items.s: BANSTEAD HOSPITAL TROPHY Report of the Banstead Hospital Trophy meeting on 29 July, won by Belgrave with 55 points from six other clubs. On July 29th, at Banstead Hospital, there were seven competing clubs with nine events to be decided. Gordon Lowers gave us a good start by winning the 100 yards, with Dicky Barlett in fifth place. Basil Walden won the 220 yards with " Ginger " Holtum in third place and then Alan Picton won the 440, beating Ede of Epsom, the international runner. Derrick Burfitt and Ches Walker were first and second in the 880 yards, and Bill Lucas won the 1 mile with Vern Blowfield in third place. Len Herbert won the 2 miles race in 9 min. 34.4 secs., but we were beaten in the team race by S.L.H. Thus from the running events we were well in front on points and although we only managed to score a fourth place in the Weight and a similar position in the Long Jump with no competitor in the High Jump, we still managed to come out on top. Final points for the Trophy were: 1, Belgrave H. 55; 2, Walton A.C. 41; 3, Kent A.C. 28; 4, South London H. 25; 5, Surrey A.C. 20; 6, Epsom & Ewell H. 19; 7, Sutton & Cheam H. 1. items.s: THE CLUB TRACK CHAMPIONSHIPS—TOOTING, AUGUST 5th Report of the Belgrave club track championships at Tooting on 5 August. A large crowd was present to witness (although we say it) a well-conducted meeting. The 100 yards senior event saw two heats with the holder, M. H. Broadbent, not competing, and the final was won by D. J. Merrett, with Lowers second and Alan Sexton third. In the 100 yards (under 19) we only had five runners and Frank Kemp was the winner in the good time of 10.4 seconds. We made up two heats in the 100 yards Boys (under 16) race and the final was won by Don Clements from Malden. Mike Stearman was present to defend his 880 yards Junior title, but he was beaten by a newcomer to our ranks in Gerry Trower, with Bob Wolton third. In the 880 yards senior race the holder, J. T. Cope, was not competing, and Ches Walker won a good race from Archie Bedford, with Len Bishop running well for third place. Frank Kemp made a double of it by winning the 220 yards Junior race, beating Dave Marshall, who is the Surrey champion at this distance. Alan Sexton was defending his 220 yards senior title, but owing to his service in the R.A.F. was not up to last year's form and was beaten into second place by D. J. Merrett, with Alan Picton a good third. The 440 yards Junior is a new club championship and we are indebted to Mr. Plummer for a very fine trophy for this event, and the first holder proved to be young Dan Godfrey who looks a most promising prospect at this distance. The holder J. T. Cope was not defending his 440 Senior title and Jim Heathfield proved the new champion with I. W. Odde second and Tom Underwood third. Ray Tooby beat the holder M. J. Stearman in the 1 mile Junior as did D. G. Maclean and Ray's time of 4 min. 28 secs. beat the old record by no less than 20 seconds. Derrick Burfitt was not defending his 1 mile Senior title and Jack Brown ran a good race to beat Len Herbert with Bob Taylor gaining his first club championship medal in third place. Dave McMullen retained his 2 miles walk title with A. Readman second and G. Oliver third. A. Bergvalds retained his Weight and Discus titles and Charlie Melchior once again won the Javelin Throw. A new member in P. Luxon won the Long Jump and young R. Cooper won both the Junior and Senior High Jump titles. The members' children's races provided some good fun for the proud parents not forgetting " Uncle Ernie " and among the prize-winners were such well-known club names as Alan Botwright, Martin Webb, Raymond Lacey, David Cook, Christopher Smart, Susan Davies, Ann Jarlett, Rita Wilson and G. items.s: MATCH AT AYLESBURY Report of the Hazell Challenge Cup meeting at Aylesbury on August Monday, where Belgrave were third and Len Herbert set a 2 miles ground record. On August Monday we were competing for the Hazell Challenge Cup with five other leading clubs. D. J. Merrett was third in the 100 yards and Ches. Walker third in the 880, while Jack Brown finished second in the 1 mile. Len Herbert won the 2 miles event beating such runners as Lillikas, Doug. Wilson and Jimmy Wood of the Poly, in the fast time of 9 min. 12.8 secs., which was a new ground record. We finished second in the team race to the Poly and final points for the trophy were:—1, Poly H., 31; 2, Walton A.C., 30; 3, Belgrave H., 20; 4, Finchley H., 16; 5, Thames Valley H., 12; 6, Highgate H., 5. There were some Junior events on the programme and in these Gerry Trower was fourth in the 880, and in the 1 mile which was run in two sections, J. E. Godfrey was third in the 1st race and Ray Tooby won the 2nd race in the good time of 4 min. 29.6 secs., with D. G. Maclean in second place. e: Junior Match v. Herne Hill Harriers
items.s: JUNIOR MATCH v. HERNE HILL HARRIERS Report of the junior triangular match at Tooting on 9 August against Herne Hill and Blackheath, lost to Herne Hill by 14 points. This match was held at Tooting on August 9th and once again, although we did well in the track events, we scored very few points in the field events and so lost the match by a margin of 14 points. Frank Kemp won the 100 yards in 10.5 and the 220 in 23.3 which is good running for a Junior and Frank seems destined for the highest honours when he competes as a Senior. Ray Tooby running his last race before being called up for National Service, was second in the 880 yards to A. E. Hine, the Herne Hill youngster. D. G. Maclean was second in the Mile to J. Heywood of Herne Hill, J. E. Godfrey was fourth. The final scores in the triangular match were:—Herne Hill H., 44; Belgrave H., 30; Blackheath H., 14. items.sum: Report of the Legion Cup match at Upminster on 19 August, where Belgrave finished third after scoring well on the track but poorly in the field events.
items.s: MATCH AT UPMINSTER Report of the Legion Cup match at Upminster on 19 August, where Belgrave finished third after scoring well on the track but poorly in the field events. On August 19th we were to have had a match at Wolverton but owing to lack of support by the members we had to withdraw from the Midland trip. On the same day our team for Upminster was quite a good one and for the eight running events we scored 23 points, with Herne Hill 21 and Sutton and Cheam 20. There were, however, three field events and from these Herne Hill scored 10, Sutton and Cheam 7, and ourselves 2, which shows where the weakness in the club lies. Gordon Lowers won the 100 in 10.3 secs. on grass, and D. J. Merrett the 220 in 23 dead; Lowers also won the 100 yards open handicap at the same meeting. Odde could only finish fourth in the 440 and seems to lack strength over the finish but no doubt this will come with more training and experience of scratch racing. Vern Blowfield won the 1 mile match and also finished third in the open mile handicap which was won by Bill Lucas with Bob Taylor second, did I hear someone say what a Handicapper? D. G. Maclean was second in the 880 Junior event and Frank Kemp unfortunately arrived just too late for the Junior 100. Alan Bishop was second in the 880 and P. Luxon was fourth in the Long Jump and we had no competitor in the High Jump. Bill Lucas won the 2 miles race in 9 min. 48.9 secs. and as this came after his win in the open mile he thus had a busy afternoon. Final points for the “ Legion Cup ” resulted as under:— 1, Herne Hill H., 31; 2, Sutton and Cheam H., 27; 3, Belgrave H., 25; 4, Ilford A.C., 18; 5, Essex Beagles, 8. items.sum: Report and results of the first London Vidarians open 25 miles walk on 26 August, Mitcham to Lower Kingswood and back, won by W. Cowley, with Belgrave winning the scratch team race.
items.s: LONDON VIDARIANS WALKING CLUB—FIRST OPEN 25 MILES Report and results of the first London Vidarians open 25 miles walk on 26 August, Mitcham to Lower Kingswood and back, won by W. Cowley, with Belgrave winning the scratch team race. The inaugural race for this event was held on Saturday, August 26th, 1950, on an out and home course from Mitcham to Lower Kingswood and back. The course, which is a fair give-and-take one, and has plenty of turns, takes a route via Carshalton, Woodmansterne, Banstead and along the old Brighton Road to Burgh Heath and Tadworth Common, gave the competitors some good preparation for the forthcoming Brighton. The club fielded two teams and some individuals, all of whom intended to compete in the “ Brighton.” The weather at the start of the race was rather unsettled and soon after the start competitors had quite a downpour of rain to contend with, but this did not deter Jack Rutland who set up quite a fast pace and led the field for the first twelve miles when he was caught and passed by Cowley (S.W.C.) who from that point was never headed. Our team in the meantime had got themselves into a scrap with Surrey Walking Club and it soon looked like developing into a battle royal. At half distance we had a four point lead, with the “ A ” team scoring: Jack Rutland 2, Jack Bidgood 4, Jack Wakeley 9, Bert Clayton was close behind but was having an off day owing to a badly bruised heel. On the return journey some tired and lost places, but in the main, most of the “ Bels ” gained ground. The team race did develop and we eventually got home by two points. In watching the race over the closing stages, it was pleasing to note that our men looked very fit and well trained, a good omen for the future event. The prize list turned out to be a Belgrave “ Benefit.” Individual Handicap: J. Rutland, third. (Allowance 4 mins.). Scratch Team: 1, Belgrave H., 17 points. items.sum: Report and results of the London to Brighton walk on 9 September, in which Belgrave beat Highgate by one point to win the Brighton Trophy for the sixth time.
items.s: BRIGHTON WALK, September 9th, 1950 Report and results of the London to Brighton walk on 9 September, in which Belgrave beat Highgate by one point to win the Brighton Trophy for the sixth time. IT WAS A FAMOUS VICTORY!!! Fifteen of our walkers lined up in a field of over 100 to await the first stroke of Big Ben, we being the only club to start two teams. Our only non-starter was Bert Clayton who has een having some foot trouble and without Bert our chances were not quite so rosy. However this did not deter the others who all got going in nice fashion. The weather was pretty bad, with a steady fall of rain, but there was very little wind and it was fairly mild. Jack Bidgood started going up towards the front quite early with Jack Wakeley and Jack Rutland not too far back. Then there followed all in quick succession the remaining five of the “ A ” Team, Don Heath, Hugh McGreechan, “Sir” Harry Shields, Joe Wilson and Dick Frazer. Quick checks on the scoring over the first 20 miles showed that Enfield, last year’s winners, were in a very strong position with Surrey W.C. also well placed. By the time Crawley had been reached, Ruffell of Enfield had retired and Jack Rutland who had been having foot trouble changed his shoes, but in the process fell back quite a good way. Jack Bidgood was still our first man in 9th position with Jack Wakeley walking very strongly in 11th. A little further back, Hugh McGreechan and Harry Shields, both doing their first Brighton, were coming through the field like steam engines. At Peas Pottage, 31 miles, the situation was much about the same and a check of placings showed that Highgate were in the lead with Met. and ourselves second and third. A further check at 40 miles showed that Jack Wakeley was still improving, Jack Bidgood, who although he had lost no positions, was a little slower, and Mac and Harry were still holding their places. The scoring here showed that Highgate were 55 points, Met. 59 and us 60 and it was here that the whips began to put the pressure on. Our 4th man was in 22nd position whilst Highgate and Met. 4th men were 34th and 35th respectively and in the intervening gap were the non-scoring half of our Team, Don Heath, Joe Wilson, Dick Frazer and Jack Rutland, not fully recovered from his earlier trouble. These last four were then given strict instructions to keep the Highgate and Met. men pegged back and right well did they do the job. At the same time Jack Wakeley was putting on the pressure and although Jack Bidgood fell back two places, the other Jack was there to take his place. Coupled with this, Mac and Harry, over the last 12 miles, made up an additional 5 points, whilst the back four maintained their positions, thus preventing Highgate and Met. from lessening their points on the 4th man. McSweeney of Highgate, however, during the last few miles, caught and passed Jack Bidgood, thus knocking four points off their score, but this was more than wiped out by the efforts of our lads. Great was the excitement at the finish of the race, Highgate with three men in were 17 points, Met. with three men in were 24 points whilst Mac and Harry having finished in 16th and 20th positions, our score for the full team was 50 points. Highgate’s 4th man must still be in 34th position for us to win and so we waited for what seemed an eternity as the finishers came in, 28th Stroud of Poly, 29th Hart of the Beagles, 30th Rutland, 31st Frazer (our 8th “ A ” Team man) 32nd Everard, Beagles, if the next man was Longshaw of Highgate it would be a draw, and then, round the corner came Shepherd in the maroon colours of Poly and we knew we had won, but only just, for Highgate filled the next position which gave them 51 points to our 50. Once again then and for the sixth time (once more than Surrey W.C.) we hold the Brighton Trophy. But great as were the performances of our scoring four, so equally great were those of the other half of the team, on them rested our success or failure and it was their effort which brought success. Having so far mentioned only the “ A ” Team, let us now take a look back at the slower men. Unfortunately Jack Baker and Gordon Doubleday were compelled to retire owing to foot trouble before the halfway stage was reached and later, at 40 miles, Bill Urry was forced to give up. This still left us a full scoring four in the “ B ” Team and even if they were some way behind, they finished and we are just as proud of them as the winners. A very good crowd of supporters accompanied the walkers and many Club members and friends were seen on the road including Stan Manning and Jim Chalk. The cyclist attendants deserve a very hearty vote of thanks for their untiring attention to the walkers despite the uncomfortable journey they had in the pouring rain. A Club handicap, for which prizes were given by Jack Wakeley, was won by H. items.h: 50 GLORIOUS YEARS ON THE BRIGHTON ROAD
items.sum: History of Belgrave walkers in the London to Brighton walk since 1897, with the list of Club Long Distance Championship (Belgrave Cup) winners.
items.s: 50 GLORIOUS YEARS ON THE BRIGHTON ROAD History of Belgrave walkers in the London to Brighton walk since 1897, with the list of Club Long Distance Championship (Belgrave Cup) winners. Our history on the Brighton Road in both walks and Relay Runs is a very worthy one and we now give some account of Belgrave’s performances (as far as they are available) in Brighton Walks over the years. The first London to Brighton Walk took place in 1886—a year before our Club was founded. The next promotion in 1897, organised by Polytechnic Harriers, had at least two Belgrave competitors, Miles, who was sixth, and Poole, 7th, and the third open race over this course was held in 1903 when the now defunct Hairdressers’ A.C. were the promoting body. In this race the then Belgrave Hon. Secretary, H. A. Smith, finished 6th in 9 hr. 33 mins. 8 secs.—a very worthy performance over the rough and dusty road of that period. Further races to Brighton were promoted by the Polytechnic Harriers in 1906, 1909, 1911 and 1913 but our scanty records do not enable any information to be given concerning Belgrave competitors, although it is quite certain the Club was represented. The writer would welcome information from anyone able to fill in these gaps in our records. In 1914 a young Belgravian named Jimmy Bellchamber determined that the Club’s colours should be prominently carried over the 52 miles of road that year, but the outbreak of war caused a postponement of plans. In 1920, however, Jimmy was down to it again and finished third. Jimmy Bellchamber’s attendant in the Brighton of 1920 had been Bob Ricketts and Jimmy persuaded him that Belgrave could compete with distinction in such events. As a result, in 1921 we had J. H. Allen finishing 3rd, Jimmy Chalk 5th, Bob Ricketts 8th, W. J. Hawker 9th, F. M. Stone 12th, and two others to finish in S. H. Miller and W. Fuller. The race had been won by Pavesi of Italy, but it was Belgrave’s team race with 12 points (3 to score) and our popular Vice-President, Mark Stone, won the open sealed handicap. So Belgrave had really made their mark in Brighton Walks. Bellchamber did not take part in this race as he had competed in the Brighton and back race earlier in the year, finishing 2nd. In 1922 Jimmy was our first man home in the now annual Brighton Walk in fourth position. The winner was Edgar Horton of Surrey W.C., followed by two Italian entrants, Guisto and Pavesi. Then came Bellchamber, followed by J. H. Allen in 5th position and Bob Ricketts 18th, our team losing on this occasion to Surrey W.C. by three points. Two Brighton Walks were promoted in 1923 and in these events Bellchamber finished 4th and 5th, so maintaining a very fine sequence of placings which was further continued in 1924 with 4th position. Our gratitude is due to Jimmy for his enthusiasm, persistence and example. He is truly the father of distance walking in our club, and he has had the pleasure of seeing his own fine walking succeeded by that of others, until a great Belgrave tradition has been built up. In 1923 our late President, Bob Ricketts—himself a more than useful performer—presented the “ Belgrave ” Cup for a Club Long Distance Walking Championship to be held each year in conjunction with the Surrey W.C. Open Race. Some excellent walking has been witnessed and some very distinguished walkers have taken the Club Championship medals, as is shown in the summary given below:— It is interesting to note that J. Miles, the first “ Belgrave ” Cup holder, was the son of the 1897 Brighton walker mentioned above. Much could be written of Tommy Green’s magnificent performances and those of Fred Rickards, Fred Bentley and others, but space does not permit. In the 1932 race Tommy Green’s time 8 hrs. 14 mins. 59 secs., Rickards did 8.23.16 and Bentley 8.33.54 and our team scoring was 1, 2, 3, some walking! Eight and a half hours has been beaten by Belgrave men on ten occasions as follows: Green (6 times), Rickards (twice), Bentley (twice). Those to have finished the distance inside 9 hours and excluding the performances just quoted are Bellchamber (twice), Miles, Rathbone, Bentley, Martin (R.) (4 times), Bidgood (3 times), Rickards (twice), Urry (twice), Sutton (twice), Baker and Stirling Wakeley. Others, not previously mentioned in the foregoing, to have completed the distance inside 9 hrs. 30 mins. on one or more occasions include: J. Allen, E. Wall, J. Chalk, S. Manning, E. Cooper, A. White, W. Hare, A. Field, P. Khlopin, H. Thaxter, A. Readman, J. Wilson, G. Oliver, D. Heath, H. Clayton, H. McGreechan, H. Shields, R. Frazer, J. Rutland. In all there have been seventy Belgrave performances inside 9 hrs. 30 mins. Our positions in the team races from 1921 to 1950 have been as follows: 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 4, 1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2; unplaced: 1, 3, 4, 4, 4, 1, truly a record of which we can be proud. In 1929 four a side team scoring was introduced and the “ E. Knott ” Memorial Shield first awarded and we have now won this trophy on more occasions than any other club. This is our record in Brighton Walks of which we may be justly proud, and with this year’s encouraging performance of eight walkers inside 9½ hours, we may well face the future with confidence and anticipate more honours in ever increasing measure on the Brighton Road. items.sum: Extracts from a letter by long-standing member Stan Manning on loyalty to the club and respect for its officers.
items.s: EXTRACTS FROM A LETTER RECEIVED Extracts from a letter by long-standing member Stan Manning on loyalty to the club and respect for its officers. The urge to write this will at least have proved the truth of my old saying which I thought I coined long ago, but as all of us old members feel that the “ Club ” gets us alike, several may challenge its originality when I repeat “ Once a ‘ Bel,’ always a ‘ Bel,’ as long as life lasts.” . . . Just as the letters “ R.N.” are as mystic and powerful a draw to many of us for life, so is to be a “ Bel,” tradition in each case being the magnet. I have no intention of mentioning any names, but I do know that to young and old members alike, those we read of as Presidents, Life Members, Officers and Committeemen, fire us with ambition, hopes and respect, and if later in life we find that our lesser abilities or greater disabilities prevented us joining those illustrious lists, we read those names with even greater respect than when we first joined the Club. . . . Good health and success to all connected with the Club. Sincerely yours, STAN MANNING (whose membership dates from 1920). Stan Manning STAN MANNING membership dates from 1920 STAN MANNING

items.s: L.C.C. TRACK CHAMPIONSHIPS Report on Belgrave performances in the finals of the L.C.C. (All-London) track championships. Our members that had qualified at the various area championships, did quite well in the finals of these All-London events. Gordon Lowers retained his 100 yards title in the good time of 10.6 secs, on a very heavy track, and then Ches Walker won the 1 mile in 4 mins. 28.8 secs. with Bob Taylor in second place. Jack Bragginton was third in the 3 miles run which was won in a new record time, while in the Junior events we had D. G. Maclean 2nd in the 1 mile with Ray Tooby, now in the Army, finishing third. Maurice Jones, perhaps better known as “ Glimpy,” finished third in the Junior 880 yards with his usual strong burst down the straight and should do well next season. items.sum: A. H. Bruce’s impressions of the European Championships at the Heysel Stadium, Brussels, and the British team’s performances.
items.s: THE EUROPEAN CHAMPIONSHIPS 1950 A. H. Bruce’s impressions of the European Championships at the Heysel Stadium, Brussels, and the British team’s performances. Having returned from an exciting week at the Heysel Stadium, Brussels, it is good to reflect upon some of the outstanding events during the Games. The organisation, overburdened with too many officials, functioned reasonably well apart from the Walk in which we were definitely robbed of a title, and of a bad slip in the lap numbering in the 10,000 metres. The track events proved most encouraging for Great Britain and our team, supported by a very noisy British contingent in the Stadium, rose to the occasion in practically every event. Highlights were Shenton’s wonderfully improved running in the 200 metres, in which he never looked like being beaten, Derek Pugh’s lion-hearted win in the 400 metres and his equally fine 46.2 flying start quarter in the relay. For the British contingent in the Stadium, however, the 800 and 1,500 metres were the biggest revelation. After the 800 metre heats the Belgian newspapers said that we only had a chance if it was a slow-run race, to which I must say “ some slow race!” In the 1,500 metres both our men ran above themselves. Bill Nankeville running especially well as he always does on the big occasion and with a little luck he might have been second. For the cross-country enthusiast perhaps Frank Aaron’s run in the 10,000 metres was the most interesting. Running in his uusual dogged style he returned a time equivalent to 29.25 for six miles, which is some running! After reading Geoff Dyson’s reply to his critics with regard to John Disley’s running in the A.A.A. Championships, it seemed strange to see Disley forcing the pace in a much higher class race—with the invitable disastrous result. The two Hurdle races gave us two very welcome third places with Angus Scott very unlucky in not reaching the final. The field events were, as expected, the weakest part of our team’s performances, although Paterson’s high-jumping was magnificent and Savidge in the shot, Geoff Elliott in the decathlon and McDonald Clark in the hammer, all performed well. Our girls showed that they can hold their own with the rest of Europe and only Blankers-Koen and the Russian “ heavy ” brigade prevented us winning more titles than we did. Probably all these successes were helped in no small measure by the great win of Jack Holden in the Marathon on the first day of the meeting, and it must have acted as a great morale-raiser to the rest of the team, so perhaps we can now look forward to Helsinki with a certain degree of confidence. As a matter of interest to any statisticians, if all the 5,000 metre finalists had run the last 5,000 metres with Zatopec in his epic 10,000 metre “ gallop,” only three would have beaten him! A. H. items.sum: Report of Belgrave’s third successive win in the Surrey County Road Relay at Old Woking on 23 September, taking the Underwood Trophy.
items.s: SURREY COUNTY ROAD RELAY Report of Belgrave’s third successive win in the Surrey County Road Relay at Old Woking on 23 September, taking the Underwood Trophy. At Old Woking on September 23rd once again our team proved too good for the opposition and thus we won the “ Underwood ” Trophy for the third year running. Ches Walker went off first for us and he beat Stone of Dorking and Martin of Walton A.C. to give Jack Bragginton a useful lead, and his time of 14 mins. 12 secs. beat the previous course record. Bragginton did 14.38 to further increase our lead and then Len Adams returned 14.48 and when he handed over to Stan Davies the next team was not in sight. Stan did 15.16 but can feel very satisfied with the thought that he is our only runner to have been in all three of our winning teams. Archie Bedford was our next runner and he returned a time of 14.26 which beat the old record of 14.30 and then Bill Lucas took over for the final “ leg ” and he did 14.11 which was only beaten by Chataway of Walton, who put up a new record time of 14 mins. 2 secs. for this course of 2.94 miles. We thus led throughout and with Len Herbert, Derrick Burfitt, Vern Blowfield and Jack Brown to call on, it is a pity that the “ National ” Brighton Relay has been put off until April, 1951. The leading teams and times in the above race were: 1, Belgrave H., 1 hr. 27 mins. 31 secs.; 2, Walton A.C., 1.28.6; 3, South London H., 1.28.38; 4, Herne Hill H., 1.29.21; 5, Surrey A.C., 1.31.28; 6, Dorking St. Paul’s A.C., 1.32.29; 7, Mitcham A.C., 1.32.31. items.sum: Report and full results of the club three miles road run handicap at Wimbledon on 14 October, won by 16-year-old G. J. Goode, with Bill Lucas fastest.
items.s: THREE MILES ROAD RUN HANDICAP Report and full results of the club three miles road run handicap at Wimbledon on 14 October, won by 16-year-old G. J. Goode, with Bill Lucas fastest. At Wimbledon, on October 14th, there was a field of 68 runners. This was not so good as last year but Bert Footer saw fit to take out a training pack over the country and we can only assume that the chaps concerned were not interested enough to support the club race. George Still, who joined the club in 1899 was the first man away, followed by Jimmy Flatt and our past-president Bill Webb, but once they were caught they soon dropped to the rear of the field. The winner was a very promising youngster, G. J. Goode, who is just turned 16 and bearing in mind that Derrick Burfitt won this race when about the same age, we hope that Goode will prove to be as good a runner as Derrick turned out to be. The second man home was another youngster in R. Linstead, who first started as a walker but has now changed over to running and promises to develop into a very useful member of our teams. Dick Tobin, now almost in the veteran stage, was third and was followed by S. G. Brooks, Arthur Bruce, who put up the 4th fastest actual time, and another veteran in Tom Morrell. Bill Lucas was “ clocked ” at the fastest actual time of 15.20, which was five seconds outside the record set up by Len Marchant. Times and placings are given hereunder and in view of the size of the field and also the manner in which they arrive at the finish, the ideal handicap is, of course, for them all to finish in a straight line, it would seem that we may have to arrange for a “ funnel ” finish as is done in the open cross-country races. items.s: FIVE MILES CLUB HANDICAP WALK—WIMBLEDON, October 14th Report and results of the club five miles handicap walk at Wimbledon on 14 October, won on scratch by Syd James and on handicap by R. Frazer. In spite of the Chippenham-Calne Open in which we entered a team and the Police v. Stock Exchange Race which took all our Police members, we had a surprisingly large field of 24 for the race. We were especially pleased to see four new members and we know they will develop into good clubmen. The scratch race was won by Syd James who promises to have a successful season. George Oliver snowed that he will be among ’em, too, in the opens and Jack Rutland, who had been thinking of having a rest, finished third in great style and now thinks resting a waste of time. We were pleased to see Dick Frazer among the prize winners after his gallant effort in the “ Brighton ” and H. Jeffery’ who also performed so well in that race. Handicap: 1. R. Frazer 2. S. James 3. items.sum: Brief report of the Chippenham to Calne six miles walk on 14 October, where G. Gregory finished second and Belgrave’s scratch team was third.
e: Chippenham to Calne Open Six Miles Walk
items.s: CHIPPENHAM TO CALNE OPEN SIX MILES WALK, October 14th Brief report of the Chippenham to Calne six miles walk on 14 October, where G. Gregory finished second and Belgrave’s scratch team was third. Despite the fact that 24 of our walkers turned out at Wimbledon for the Opening walk and a further 7 police members, were engaged at Imber Court in their annual match with the Stock Exchange, a further 7 made the journey to Chippenham. Unfortunately, G. Gregory was ruled out just after the start whilst taking a very awkward bend, but continued to walk and finished second to Harry Churcher. Gerald Warr continued to show improvement and for the first time was in our scoring scratch team which was placed third. Details of placings and times are not yet to hand. G. Gregory G. Gregory ruled out after the start but finished second Harry Churcher Harry Churcher winner Gerald Warr Gerald Warr first time in scoring scratch team Chippenham to Calne Open Six Miles Walk Police v. items.s: ONE HOUR TIME TRIALS Report of young Belgrave walkers in the new one hour time trials at Sutton, Tooting and Esher for R.W.A. badges. Sutton and Cheam Harriers at Sutton — July 27th. Surrey Walking Club at Tooting — August 9th. Walton Athletic Club at Esher — September 30th. A number of our young walkers have taken part in the newly instituted one hour time trials for which R.W.A. Badges are awarded. In the race promoted by Sutton and Cheam Harriers at Sutton on July 27th, three of our walkers, G. Beecham, E. Hall and F. Rolfe competed. Beecham walked exceedingly well to finish 2nd to an ex A.A.A. Track Champion, Vic Stone, in the time of 55 mins. 43 secs., with Eric Hall 3rd and Fred Rolfe 16th. A fortnight later Beecham and Hall were again 2nd and 3rd in the Surrey W.C. race at Tooting Bec with H. Jeffery 4th.. A few weeks later, in the Walton A.C. promotion, Wally Ives was 3rd in 55.32, R. items.s: FINAL CLUB TRACK MEETING—TOOTING, September 16th Report of the final club track meeting at Tooting on 16 September, with club handicaps, the 3 miles club championship won by Jack Brown, a novices' mile and complete results and standards. We had a varied programme of club handicaps, the 3 Miles club track championship, and an open race for Unattached Novices. In the 3 Miles championship, the holder, Vern Blowfield, was not defending and with Bill Lucas and Len Herbert also absent, the race was a very open one. Jack Brown, however, had other ideas and with a lap to go he went well ahead to win in 15 min. 19.2 secs., with Jack Bragginton just beating Archie Bedford for second place. The 1 Mile run for the novices brought out a good field and the winner, Pte. Newell, who is stationed with Doug. Briggs, is a useful performer. Both the first two men home have now joined the club and we wish them every success in our ranks. In the 100 Yards (under 19) handicap we had another poor turn-out and the winner was K. Hewitt, a new member who should prove very useful next season. The 880 Yards handicap saw M. F. Jones produce another of his whirlwind finishes to catch D. P. Elliott who unfortunately collapsed a few yards from the tape and so was not placed. In the 2 Miles walk, Gordon Waddingham, our recruit from Coventry Godiva H., proved a good winner with G. Oliver and Syd Jarlett once again gaining the minor placings The 220 Yards handicap saw the scratch man Don Merrett run through his field in easy fashion to record 22.8 and he should be up with the best next season on the track. We had a new innovation with a 120 Yards Low Hurdles handicap, and John Briggs the scratch man was just beaten by Les Christmas with Peter Hunt in third place. Alan Law won the Shot Put handicap with the scratch man, A. Bergvalds, in second place and Bert Machell who was third also won the Hop, Step and Jump handicap. items.sum: Report of the Maidenhead Road Relay on 30 September, where Belgrave's A team finished second to Reading A.C. inside the old record.
items.s: MAIDENHEAD ROAD RELAY Report of the Maidenhead Road Relay on 30 September, where Belgrave's A team finished second to Reading A.C. inside the old record. Held on September 30th in bad weather. and times were consequently on the slow side. There was a field of 16 teams and our “ A ” team did well to gain second place behind the strong Reading A.C. side. Most of our “ cracks ” were not eligible to run owing to numerous barring clauses, but even so our team's time of 2 hr. 16 min. 2 sec. was well inside the old record of 2.17.44. Archie Bedford ran well to give us the lead over the first “ leg ” but Len Adams had to relinquish this to the Reading runner although putting up third fastest time. Reg Bolam went next and he kept us in second position doing the same time as the leader. Arthur Bruce was our next runner and although he did second fastest time the Reading man increased his side's lead. Jack Bragginton then went off and ran well to gain half-a-minute on the leader but our last runner, Ches Walker, had J. C. Green of Reading, to chase and never looked like catching his man. Our “ B ” team finished eighth and our “ C ” team eventually failed to finish owing to their last man going off the course. items.label: No. 110
items.sum: Notice welcoming members to the cross-country season at Belgrave Hall and Wimbledon Common, quoting Athletic Review on the sport and appealing for officials.
items.s: OVER THE COUNTRY Notice welcoming members to the cross-country season at Belgrave Hall and Wimbledon Common, quoting Athletic Review on the sport and appealing for officials. With the cross-country season now upon us we welcome all members to Belgrave Hall and hope they will sample the enjoyment of a run over Wimbledon Common, with a hot bath to follow and a cup of tea and cake to round off the afternoon. Our Club Championships are being held on the usual dates, a new addition this season being the 3 miles Youths Championship, which is due to be held on January 13th and we hope for a good entry to this race. Many people have tried to explain the attraction of cross-country running but we think the following remarks from a recent issue of “ Athletic Review ” just about sum it up. “ Conditions for the competitor are frequently unpleasant, sometimes they are extremely severe. Yet remarkably few fail to turn out whatever the weather or the course may be like, and of those who start nearly all will go through to the bitter end with dogged perseverance or cheerful disregard as the case may be. Nor do the spectators often find conditions in their favour. But hail, rain or snow, they are there squelching through the mud, facing the rigours of a biting wind, yet withal keeping astonishingly cheerful and maintaining a lively interest in the racing from start to finish. Many of them, probably the majority in fact, are runners of other days. They have been through it all themselves and long association with the sport has provided them with a philosophy which is proof against anything. No! we do not think we are wrong in our assertion that cross-country running is a sport of true greatness. It receives scarcely any publicity in the press and still less ‘ over the air,’ yet, because of the intense enthusiasm among all concerned, its popularity is growing as a comparison of our present day championship programmes with those of past years will confirm. Sometimes we are apt to overlook the important part played by our loyal band of officials in the organising of cross-country running as a sport. Far more spare time goes into even ordinary club work than is generally realised. When the staging of big championships is undertaken it will be appreciated what a tremendous amount of work is called for, both before and on the day. Just think of what it means to stand out in the open for a couple of hours on a cold, and perhaps wet, winter's day, putting down numbers or times with benumbed fingers, or standing out on one of the bleak outposts of the course acting as a marshal. The fact that there can be found men willing to take on such work voluntarily is in itself an indication of the fundamental greatness of this most amateur of all our winter sports.” Such words as these say far more than I can find to put into words in order to induce our members to sample the “ enjoyment ” of cross-country running and even those who cannot go out for a run will find a Saturday afternoon trip to Wimbledon Common well rewarded. We are always pleased to receive assistance as regards officials for both running and walking events and can always find a job for you to do. Entry fee to all club handicaps is 1s., payable on the day of the race, and all entries and any enquiries as to fixtures, etc., should be sent to our Running Hon. Secretary, as under:— E. A. Duffett, E. A. Duffett E. A. Duffett Running Hon. Secretary Club Cross Country Championships Belgrave Hall Wimbledon Common

items.s: DID YOU KNOW THAT— Profile of J.G. (Jovial Joe) Coleman, runner turned walker, listing his club and championship record year by year from 1927. J.G. (Jovial Joe) COLEMAN first joined the Club as a runner! ! in 1927. Not content with upsetting the handicapper he has participated in club events in every section and has won pots at everything except hurdling. The reason why he has not won a prize at hurdling is perhaps synonymous with his stylish walking, it would be difficult for a man of his build to “ lift.” Apart from his pot hunting, however, he has served the club as a grand team man and has to his credit a remarkable record, as follows: 1927. Joined Belgrave Harriers as a runner. Competed in handicaps on track, road, cross-country, field events (javelin, discus, shot put, long jump), and took prizes in all events, except hurdling. 49 prizes in all. Represented Club in track and cross-country running road and track walking teams, field events teams since 1929. 1928. 3rd in 1 mile Club Open Novice Race. 1929. 3rd Surrey A.A.A. Junior 880 yards Championship. 1931. 2nd Team Surrey County Junior Cross-Country Championship. 1934. 1st Class Standard Club 2 miles Track Walk. 1936. 1st Class Standard Club 2 miles Track Walk. 1937. 3rd Surrey County 2 miles Track Walk. 3rd Belgrave Harriers 2 miles Track Walk. 2nd Horwood Cup 7 miles Road Walk. 6th Inter Counties 10 miles Road Walk. 1938. 3rd A.A.A. 7 miles Track Championship 53 mins. 23 secs. (First Englishman). Standard A.A.A. 2 miles Track Championship 14 mins. 23 secs. 2nd Surrey County 2 miles Track Championship. 1st Surrey County 10 miles Road Walk Championship. 1st (dead-heat with brother Len) R.W.A. “ Garnett ” Cup Championship. Also 1st team with record score of 16 points. 2nd Belgrave 2 miles Track Championship. 3rd Belgrave 10 miles Road Championship. 2nd Inter Counties 10 miles Road Championship. Nijmegen Shield winning team (R.W.A. 20). 1939. 3rd A.A.A. 7 miles Track Championship. Fowler Dixon Style Prize Standard A.A.A. 2 miles Track Championship. 3rd Southern A.A.A. 2 miles Track Championship. 1st Surrey County 2 miles Track Championship. 1st Belgrave 2 miles Track Championship. 2nd Surrey County 10 miles Road Championship. Also 1st team. 2nd Inter Counties 10 miles Championship. 1940. 1st Surrey County 10 miles Road Walk. 1940-45. Served in R.A.F. Won and placed in Inter Service matches. 1946. Standard A.A.A. 7 miles Track Championship. 3rd Southern A.A.A. 2 miles Track Championship. 2nd Belgrave 2 miles Track Championship. 1947. 2nd Surrey County 2 miles Track Championship. 3rd Southern A.A.A. 2 miles Track Championship. 3rd Surrey County 10 miles Road Walk and st team. 2nd Belgrave 2 miles Track Walk. 4th Belgrave 20 miles Road Walk. 2nd Belgrave 10 miles Road Walk. 6th R.W.A. Senior 10 miles Road Walk and 1st team. 1948. 2nd Surrey County 2 miles Track Championship. 3rd Belgrave 2 miles Track Championship. Nijmegen Shield Team, R.W.A. 20 miles. 1st Team R.W.A. 10 miles Senior Championship. 3rd Inter County 2 miles Track Championship. Standard Southern A.A.A. 2 miles Track Championship. 1937-38-39-47-48. Winning team Polytechnic Harriers Kinnaird 2 miles. Has been placed in individual scratch races in majority of Open 7 and 10 miles Road Walks. Has been in Bel's scratch teams in all but two races since 1937 which won all opens at 10 and 7 miles. Has won 9 open two mile handicaps. Won 1 mile race in Belgrave Inter-Club Track Walks 5 times—3 times inside 7 minutes. Second fastest recorded time in Surrey W.C. Croydon to Banstead and back, 11¼ miles, in 96 m. 27 s. Joe has served the club in many official capacities. He has been and in fact still is, an official on many associations. He is one of our Walking Coaches and is ready to instruct any new member in the sport at which he was so adept. He is insistent that a fair style is more important than a fast ragged one which often leads to disqualification and disappointment not only to the individual concerned but also to his team mates. J. items.s: Clothing Section Notice from the Hon. Asst. Treasurer on club vests, ties, badges and letters for sale, and an appeal for unwanted gear for younger members. It is with regret that I have to announce that the stock of club vests at 10s. 6d. is fast disappearing, and possibly by the time this goes to press, no more will be available. As previously stated the new stock, sizes 34, 36, 38, will be 13s. (I remember when they were 2s. 6d.). I have plenty of Club ties at 10s. 6d., coat badges 2s., vest badges 2s. 6d., sets of letters for track suits 5s. per set (sewn on 1s. extra). All these items are postage extra, 4d. on vests and 2½d. on other articles, or you can contact me at the “ Hall ” any Tuesday evening or Saturday afternoon. Older members not now active may be interested to know that I can dispose of any gear they may not be needing, amongst the younger members who are keen to have the things that go to make a runner, but find present-day costs beyond them. T. F. Morrell T. F. MORRELL Hon. Asst. Treasurer T. F. MORRELL Belgrave Hall

items.sum: House Sub-Committee notice that Belgrave Hall is now the club's property, asking members to look after it and outlining plans for work in 1951.
items.s: Belgrave Hall House Sub-Committee notice that Belgrave Hall is now the club's property, asking members to look after it and outlining plans for work in 1951. You have no doubt read that after many years of struggling and saving, “ Belgrave Hall ” has now become the property of the Club. Members visiting the hall will realise that a large sum of money has been spent on repairs and decorations for your pleasure and enjoyment, therefore I would ask all members to take care when using the property and its contents. I regret the temporary continuation of the limited bathing and lavatory arrangements, but you have my assurance that a very live “ House Sub-Committee ” will be working throughout the winter drawing up plans for work to be carried out during the summer of 1951. It is our desire and hope that the hall will eventually be rebuilt with modern and improved amenities for the members of Belgrave Harriers. The committee will be only too glad to consider any suggestions you may have to offer for your Club headquarters, so it's up to you to let us know what you want. IT IS YOUR PROPERTY, LOOK AFTER IT YOURSELF AND SEE THAT OTHER MEMBERS DO LIKEWISE. T. Morrell T. MORRELL House Sub-Committee T. MORRELL Belgrave Hall

items.s: Cycles at Belgrave Hall Notice that cycles may no longer be parked behind Belgrave Hall on Saturdays and that Arthur Whitehead has offered his garage in Lauriston Road instead. We regret that owing to lack of accommodation and serious inconvenience to members and their supporters we find it necessary to disallow cycles to be parked at the rear of Belgrave Hall on Saturdays. However, Arthur Whitehead, one of our runners, has kindly offered to all members with cycles the use of the garage at his house which is situated at the top of Lauriston Road, some 300 yards from the hall. We are really indebted to Arthur for his kind offer, this is not the first time he has come to the rescue in the matter of accommodation. Our cyclist members should show their appreciation by accepting his kind offer and thus ending this serious encumbrance to fellow members. It should be noted that the question of cycle accommodation at the hall will be taken into consideration by the Building Sub-Committee when plans for the new hall are put in hand. Arthur Whitehead Arthur Whitehead offered his garage in Lauriston Road for members' cycles Belgrave Hall Lauriston Road

items.s: “ Overseas ” Trophy Notice of the new Overseas Trophy for the Youths' Cross-Country Championship, funded partly by Percy Wright's wartime Airgraphs sales. A trophy will this year be presented for the Youths' Cross-Country Championship and will be known as the “ Overseas ” Trophy. Part of the cost of providing this trophy was the money obtained by Percy Wright during the war from the sale of Forces' “ Airgraphs,” the object being to have a trophy to commemorate our Club members serving abroad. Percy worked very hard on this scheme and we should all be happy with him now that his aim has been realised. The endeavour of our youths to win this new trophy will undoubtedly benefit the Club by encouraging and eventually producing good cross-country members. Percy Wright Percy Wright raised money for the Overseas Trophy from wartime sale of Forces' Airgraphs Club Cross Country Championships

items.sum: Notice of Athletic Review's new trophy for the best young cross-country runner of the year, judged up to the English National Championships.
items.s: “ Athletic Review ” Cross-Country Trophy Notice of Athletic Review's new trophy for the best young cross-country runner of the year, judged up to the English National Championships. This well-known sports magazine has decided to put up a Trophy for annual competition to be awarded to “The Best Young Cross-Country Runner of the Year.” This is the athlete who is adjudged the most outstanding in the Youths' and Junior ranks combined. There will also be a miniature Cup for the winner and Certificates for those gaining Honourable Mention. The competition will terminate with the English National Cross-Country Championships and all clubs will be asked to keep a record of the performances of their outstanding young cross-country runners throughout the winter so as to be in a position to submit them for consideration immediately after the National race. Here is a fine chance for the younger members of our Club and we hope that all our Youths and Juniors will make a determined effort to bring this trophy to our Club. National Cross Country Championships

items.label: No. 110
items.sum: Pen-name article urging Belgrave runners of all ages to train harder and revive the team spirit needed to regain cross-country championships.
items.s: CLUB SPIRIT Pen-name article urging Belgrave runners of all ages to train harder and revive the team spirit needed to regain cross-country championships. The cross-country season is once again upon us and some indication of our future strength has already been shown by the results of races held during the past few weeks. We have probably more runners turning out each Saturday than any other club in the country, as witnessed by the 68 starters in our road handicap on October 14th. With such numbers there is no reason why those open championships which have eluded us in the past few seasons should not be quickly regained. If clubs with fewer athletes to choose from can attain the highest team honours, it means that something is lacking in our own club that we should allow them to “ put it across us.” Your Committee are fully convinced that we have the talent and that it only requires the revival of the keenness and team spirit which won us so many championships before the war, to return us to the “ top of the tree.” Set your minds on that goal and nothing can prevent the name of Belgrave again being a power in the cross-country world. It is not enough that a small body of your members should be left to attain this object. Every runner no matter what his present standard, should strive to increase his ability and make as his greatest ambition the membership of at least one of the teams which are eventually to win back those lost honours. It may not be this year or even next, but as long as some improvement can be shown during this present season then it is a sound foundation for further achievement. Set out to train more systematically and more frequently and keep before you the object of putting those “ claret and gold ” colours in the front. Youths, Juniors and Seniors should set as their standards the winning of the respective County, District and National cross-country championships and do all in their power to attain the highest degree of physical fitness during the weeks ahead so that those standards may be achieved. The road is hard and long and may at times seem hopeless but the pleasure that can be gained by team successes such as these is immeasurable. Cross-country running calls for team spirit more than any other branch of our sport and the loss of keenness by even one of our members may deprive us of that improvement which we need so much to put us on the road back to the top. Don't let it be said that you were that one who fell by the wayside. Take every chance possible to train either with the organised packs or by yourself and do not hesitate to approach your captain or vice-captains for advice if you are not sure of your training methods. Do all the walking you can, you can even save money by walking to and from your work and this money will then assist with your expenses to away matches and you will also be attaining that fitness which is going to help both you and your club. To those that can no longer be active we say “ give us that moral and vocal support ” without which we cannot press on to victory. Come along and provide that encouragement that you yourself enjoyed in your active days and by working together and showing that “ club spirit ” without which nothing can be attained, Belgrave can succeed—make this your resolution from now onwards.

items.s: HERE AND THERE Club news column of members' performances, appointments, health and greetings, including links with Wirrall A.C. and Belgrave officials on the Southern C.C.C.A., South of Thames and R.W.A. committees. Jack Stirling Wakeley and Jack Rutland finished 4th and 5th in the Hastings—Brighton Walk on August 19th and Jack Wakeley was 3rd in the handicap. Joe Scamell won a Veterans' mile handicap at Parliament Hill Fields on August 23rd off 22 yards. Bert East won the Veterans' A.C. 2 miles Championship and was second in the Erith Open Mile on August 7th. One of our latest police recruits, J. Tebbutt, introduced by Bob Readman, won the Police 6 miles novices race at Regents Park on September 30th in the very fast time of 53 mins. 31 secs. and should prove a great asset to our “ Garnett ” Cup team this season. Welcome back to Ted Beesley who has returned to racing after a lapse of twelve months and has his eye on two or three young policemen at Ealing. Wirrall Athletic Club, Cheshire, write to say that for many years Harry Parker was a Vice-President of their Club. They do not wish to lose the link of friendship with our Club and so they have great pleasure in electing Tom Carter to be one of their Vice-Presidents. They send a hearty welcome to anyone visiting their district and Norman Graves, one of our second claim members and a member of Wirral A.C. sends personal greetings to all Belgravians. Thank you, Wirrall A.C., for your graciousness and the best of luck. Harry Churcher was 2nd in an international match London v. Gothenburg. We are happy to report that Ben Lulham, one of our A.A.A. Coaches is now out of hospital after an operation on a neck muscle and will soon be resuming his activities as Club Coach. Len Bailey won the Stock Exchange 6 miles handicap at Regents Park. Len Herbert represented London in the annual match at Gothenburg and ran well to finish 2nd in the 3,000 metres in 8 mins. 30.8 secs. Len also finished 2nd to F. Green of Birchfield in 9 mins. 17.2 secs. in the 2 miles race at the local club's floodlit evening meeting on October 4th at Perry Barr, Birmingham. Geoff Pearson gained standard award of 3 hrs. 50 mins., his actual time being 3.39.28, in the S.L.H. 30 miles road race. We congratulate Freddie Bradnum, now a B.B.C. producer in the Midlands, on finishing 12th in the recent Liverpool Marathon, and hope his duties will not prevent us seeing him at Belgrave Hall during the winter season. At the A.G.M. of the Police Walking Section Syd Roberts relinquished his office as Hon. Secretary and was elected a Vice-Chairman, joining Jack Bidgood who also holds that office. It is interesting to note that there is a strong Belgrave contingent on the Southern C.C.C.A. new committee, for not only is Les Cohen the hon. secretary with Harry Shields as his assistant, but our club vice-presidents—Joe Turner, Bert Ellsey, Charlie Munro and Ernie Duffett are all members of the general committee. This is quite a change to a few years ago when Harry Parker was our only representative and shows that we are now taking a strong part in the administrative side of the sport. Ernie Duffett is also the president-elect of the South of Thames C.C. Association while Les Cohen is on the committee, and Charlie Munro and Bert Ellsey sit as past-presidents when members of the now defunct Ashcombe A.C. We also continue to be strongly represented on the R.W.A. with Alf Harley as treasurer, and on the Southern Committee by Alf Harley, Syd Roberts, Jack Bidgood and Charlie Churcher. Brian Rice our young Junior half-miler has now been called-up and sends his best wishes to his many friends in the club. Percy Wright has now added a daughter to his family. Fred Rickards sends best wishes to all and says he hopes to be on the road again soon. In the Civil Service Championships, Jack Brown was second in the 1 mile and Charlie Smart gained a similar position in the 3 miles event. With G. Oliver being second in the 2 miles walk and Bob Jessop winning the Veterans' race our members were well to the fore. Ray Tooby won the Junior Inter-Banks 1 mile title in the record time of 4 min. 30.4 secs. and we wish him the best of luck now he has been called up for National Service. In the Triangular International at the White City on August 7th, Des Mullen was placed sixth in the 220 yards and Bill Lucas finished second in the 5,000 metres event. On August 12 also at the White City, Bill Lucas ran for Great Britain in the match against the U.S.A. and Benelux Countries and after doing most of the leading in the 3 miles race, he eventually finished third to Ashenfelter of U.S.A. with Cosgul of Turkey runner-up. It is a pity that Bill lacks a really fast finish to his races but he is certainly running better now than at any time of his career. At the same meeting Len Herbert was third to Wilson and Eyre in a special 2 miles race, and Len clocked 9 min. 12.2 secs., which is really fast running. items.sum: Editorial recalling the April 1950 call for club spirit and celebrating the season's cross-country successes, with a postscript on Steve Charlton's injury in the race that won the Ottway Cup.
items.s: Editorial Editorial recalling the April 1950 call for club spirit and celebrating the season's cross-country successes, with a postscript on Steve Charlton's injury in the race that won the Ottway Cup. Dear Fellow Belgravians, We, your Editors, are inclined to give ourselves a little praise. It would appear that our Editorials are not only read, but digested. We quote briefly from our Editorial of the April, 1950, issue—"And now for a subject that is causing some people concern—our defeats over the country . . . Let us not worry unduly . . . and now that we have been vanquished, shall we say temporarily, let us turn about and endeavour with all the enthusiasm we can muster to regain once again our former premiership . . . No, we are not dead yet, let us say a little unwell. Let us not try to find the cause, but certainly let us find the cure . . . Let us look upon our recent defeats in the nature of a tonic. The cure will be completed by 100 per cent. Club Spirit." Will you look up the April, 1950, issue and re-read our Editorial? We are sure, by recent results, that it did some good and that the re-reading will do even more good. This season we have won every club match, the Surrey County Championship and South of the Thames Championship—and—in spite of the doubts of many, our lads rose magnificently to the occasion and confounded the wiseacres by being narrowly beaten to second place in the "Southern." We, your Editors, who are, or rather were, walkers, but yet true Belgravians, will be forgiven if in our ignorance of cross-country running are still enthusiastic about our chances, but we do contend that any club who can win the Surrey County Championship, the South of the Thames and gain second place in the Southern, MUST stand a reasonable chance in the National Championship. It may be that by the time this is in print the National Championship will have been decided, but we are sure that whether or not our forecast has been proved correct, our lads will have once again shown that they are endeavouring to take us once more to the front in the field of Cross Country Running. Even so, re-read our quoted Editorial and carry on with a successful cure. YOUR EDITORS. P.S.—Had it not been for the unfortunate injury to Steve Charlton during the early part of the race, our forecast as above would have been almost realised. Nevertheless, we commend Steve for his courage and team spirit in finishing the course which enabled us to win the Ottway Cup. Steve Charlton Steve Charlton injured early in the race but finished, enabling the club to win the Ottway Cup Surrey County Championship South of the Thames Championship Southern National Championship Ottway Cup

items.s: In Memoriam Obituary of Norman Walker, a popular young Belgrave runner who died aged 24, with a note that junior member A. M. Bassett was killed in an R.A.F. flying accident. IN MEMORIAM Norman Walker It is with deepest sorrow that we have to report the death of Norman Walker, who passed away on Saturday, November 25th, at the early age of 24 years. Norman joined us in 1943 and was one of our most promising runners and certainly one of our most popular and likeable members. We found him a quiet and unassuming lad, who enjoyed his running, and he will be sadly missed by his many Belgrave friends. He represented the Club both on the track and over the country. He was a profound student of athletics and could discourse on almost any subject appertaining to our sport. A wreath was sent from the Club, and on Saturday, December 9th, on the day of our Championship, the President, Alf Harley, acquainted all present with the sad news and a reverent silence to the memory of Norman was observed. We are sorry to report that A. M. Bassett, one of our promising young junior members, has been killed in a flying accident while serving with the R.A.F. items.sum: The President's review of the club's cross-country, walking, track and road prospects for 1951, urging all-round club spirit.
items.s: Progress Report The President's review of the club's cross-country, walking, track and road prospects for 1951, urging all-round club spirit. PROGRESS REPORT—By Our President In the ast issue I referred to the past—now I would like to make comment on the present and the immediate future. It is good to see the enthusiasm and high morale which has manifested itself this season among our cross country men and has given us excellent wins in so many championships and second place in the Southern Championship, ahead of the holders, Thames Valley Harriers, and a mere six points behind the winners. This, too, without some of our better known men, who were prevented from turning out! Hard luck was ours also in the Southern Youths Championship, in which our own Club Champion, owing to influenza, was unable to reproduce his normal form, which would undoubtedly have given us a team win instead of 6th place of the 34 finishing clubs. However, the results are not all that important—the spirit is good and in the old tradition, and with that excellent spirit all things are possible. It should follow from the Southern Senior Championship result that we should be among the placings in the "National" once again, as we were for a sequence of ten races until two years ago. We sincerely hope so: and on the London-Brighton Relay, although not a championship event, we may expect to be very near the front when Brighton is reached on April 7th. Among our walkers, also, morale is high and if any club is to beat Sheffield United Harriers in the forthcoming 10 miles National Championship, we feel it is the Belgrave Harriers. We were within an ace of doing so last year, and with a stronger team this year may well bring back a title from Macclesfield on March 17th. Remembering the excellent walking of every Belgrave Walker in the R.W.A. 20 miles Championship last year, we can look forward confidently both to this event, the 50 kilometres in June and the London-Brighton in September. And whilst great deeds are being done at these distances, our track walkers will be showing us that at the shorter distances Belgrave still takes a lot of beating. Our track runners and field events men will already be at their early training and we look for their loyal support and first-rate performances throughout the season from them. Our programme of Club track championships is one of the finest in the country and will demand the support of all members on the first Saturday in August: and from April until September we shall be looking for the standards which have given us so many Summer International athletes in the past. Loyal and enthusiastic co-operation with our Secretaries, Captains, Vice-Captains and Coaches in the spirit of Belgrave endeavour, which is such a real thing, should enable us to surprise even ourselves! Throughout the summer, too, our road runners will be carrying our colours in various parts of the country, and we hope they may excel themselves in the marathon events. In general, let us remind ourselves that in the all-round-field of athletics, no club has, as yet, come anywhere near the performances that Belgrave can show. Let us be aware that in our numbers, in the quality of our membership, in our administration, our latent talent and proved abilities, our traditions, we have everything in good measure, that any club can desire. And let us resolve to apply to all these qualities with which we are so richly endowed, Enthusiasm, Determination, Perseverance and Intelligence—all in a spirit of good sportsmanship—and the name of Belgrave will stand even higher than it has done before! The youngest member has something to contribute, the oldest something of value to help us along, let everyone of us do his share. A. A. HARLEY, President. A. A. Harley A. A. items.s: From the Hon. Treasurer The Hon. Treasurer's appeal to members to pay their subscriptions and support the handicaps, Supporters' Club and social functions. FROM THE HON. TREASURER The matter of the Club's finances is, or should be, the concern of all members as well as of the Club's finance officials, and no Treasurer of any organisation would be satisfied until his subscriptions were paid up 100 per cent. I am giving away no secrets when I say that we are not yet in that happy state! Yes, if you've read this far, I'm leading up to that delicate question, "Have you paid?" A number of members have recently posted me remittances with notes of apology for their lateness in paying. I would thank them very much and assure them that the depths of their apologies are exceeded only by the depths of our thanks. So, if you are hesitant about sending anything I hope these few words will break down any shyness. If you think that you are in arrears, please drop me a line. We have had some good-sized fields for our cross country and walking handicaps. Let us keep it up for the track and field events handicaps—they are put on for your benefit. Do you belong to the Supporters' Club? Les Cohen or any of the committee will be pleased to give you any information required. Do you support the Club Social functions? Our social sub-committee work hard organising social events; these involve time and money, and here again—they are for your benefit. Finally, and this may also be for your benefit, the name and address is:— G. S. Doubleday, 219, West Barnes Lane, New Malden, Surrey. Thank You! G. S. Doubleday G. S. Doubleday Hon. Treasurer Les Cohen Les Cohen Supporters' Club New Malden

items.sum: Report on the club's social life: Dave Martin Shepherd's retirement as Social Secretary, Tom Carter's New Year's Eve function, the children's party and the Carnival Social.
items.s: Socials—Or Fun And Games Report on the club's social life: Dave Martin Shepherd's retirement as Social Secretary, Tom Carter's New Year's Eve function, the children's party and the Carnival Social. SOCIALS—Or Fun And Games Owing to occasional absences from town on business, Dave Martin Shepherd decided that it was not possible to carry on as Social Secretary at the last A.G.M. Dave carried out a very difficult job, a job which requires a cheerful spirit and smiling face to the customers, but one which has many worries, notably food and disappointments: these disappointments often occasioned by the apathy of those who the Social Secretary caters for and tries to please. Let us say most fervently, "Thank you, Dave," and we are pleased to learn that although not now Social Secretary you are still a pillar of strength to the social side of the Club. In Tom Carter—our new Secretary pro tem.—we have one of dynamic character, one who gets his own way by his forceful personality, one full of ideas, one not afraid of asking for others' help and one who cares not a fig for the niceties of red tape, but just gets on with it. It may be that his methods are not always exactly au fait, but they certainly do provide the social side of the Club with a very definite social side. As a result of the remarkable success of our last dinner, Tom arranged a little New Year's Eve function at the same venue for any Belgraves wishing to attend. It was unfortunate that only a few could take advantage of the facilities offered, but those that did certainly have reason to thank Tom for a really grand night, packed full of fun and with a real New Year spirit, and we can safely say that those who did attend impressed the rest of the company that they were members of B-E-L-G-R-A-V-E—Belgrave! Yes, it was a grand night and we hope Tom will arrange a repeat this year and for a larger number. On Sunday, January 7th, the Club held a Children's Party. I am not quite certain of the exact number, but I should say about 70 members' children had a grand tea from a table daintily arranged with the attractive little things that make children's eyes glow. Whoever were responsible for the tables and the fare thereon are to be thanked and congratulated. After tea many willing helpers cleared up and got the children sitting around for an entertainment by a really clever conjuror, who certainly had a way with the children (of all ages) and who also presented, in my opinion, the grandest Punch and Judy show I have ever witnessed. Many growp-ups were entranced by the expressions on the children's faces during this show. Of course, Smith (Champ) Junior, had to present the "pièce de résistance" by disclosing the procedure at his home when relatives visit on Sundays and caused perhaps the biggest laugh. After the Punch and Judy show every child was given a present by Father Christmas. I don't think I am at liberty to disclose the identity of the said Father Christmas, but he was a very popular one with the children, and he will undoubtedly be asked to grow his whiskers again in time for the next party. Again, whoever chose the children's presents are to be congratulated on the very sensible choice for so many of so many ages. It was also pleasing to see "little" Bertie Footer enjoying himself with his toy motor car on a string. We must, too, thank all those who contributed towards the party, they are assured that their donations were well used. Finally, on January 27th Tom Carter arranged our last social of the season. This was a Carnival Social and a real carnival it was. A goodly number sat down to tea, but great numbers turned up in the evening. There were streamers and cotton wool balls, hats and balloons and very jolly people, both young and old. In fact, so much did we enjoy ourselves that we asked Tom to extend the dancing to 11.30 p.m., and Tom, knowing so well that the assembly were enjoying themselves, decided to do this. Yes, we seem to be having some good times socially, but let us not forget to thank the many helpers, not only among the members, but also some of their womenfolk, and lastly, and certainly not least, our caretaker, Mrs. Savage, and her family. After all this, Tom Carter still insists on being known as Social Secretary—pro tem.—or should it be sine die! Dave Martin Shepherd Dave Martin Shepherd retired as Social Secretary at the last A.G.M. items.sum: F. H. Elson's report of the February 17th film show and 'Pep' talk at Belgrave Hall, where Charlie Jones criticised the Field Events Section and the coaches aired their complaints.
items.s: Cinema Show—And Straight Talking F. H. Elson's report of the February 17th film show and 'Pep' talk at Belgrave Hall, where Charlie Jones criticised the Field Events Section and the coaches aired their complaints. CINEMA SHOW—AND STRAIGHT TALKING Belgrave Hall, February 17th As a means of attracting the people for whom this "Pep" talk was intended, the film show seemed deemed to failure, but as a means of entertaining some sixty members from different sections of the Club it was definitely a success, and we do thank Charlie Jones for the arrangements. A film of the 1950 European Games and of the 1950 Poly Marathon was shown and a running commentary was given by Charlie Jones. As I have already said, the show was very entertaining to those present and after listening to the talk afterwards, it became obvious to everybody that the Field Events Section was primarily affected, but on looking round we saw very few of those members present. In presenting his list of moans, for moans they certainly were, Charlie Jones did not pull his punches. Let us be honest. It is very definite that with the exception of the very few stalwarts the Field Events Section is letting us down. We hate to admit it, but if we face up to it and manage to jar these laggards into a sense of duty to the Club of their choice we shall get better results. Those present were asked for any ideas for the improvement of the Club, but few were forthcoming. Is it because the members are so completely complacent or could it be that everything is perfect? I believe that many members have suggestions, but are a little timid in presenting them in person at a meeting. Let me say that if this is the case, as Editor, I would be very pleased to have them and either publish them or present them to the Committee. Mention was also made of non-replies to postcards sent by officials. Again I will be outright and say that this is not only unprincipled and rude, but also a waste, not only of Club officials' time, but also of Club money, which, in effect, is your property. The coaches then had a little moan about late or non-appearance of their pupils. This again is a source of annoyance to those gentlemen who are prepared to give their knowledge and time to assist the young Club members and who should show their appreciation of the coach by turning up regularly and early. I was sorely tempted to intervene here, but decided to use my words as a winding-up of this report. As Walking Coach I think I am the only coach without a grouse. At the last coaching school I had a regular and very prompt attendance of nine walkers each evening. Again our Walking Captain and Secretary always receive answers to all postcards and letters. Our lads invariably turn up for all races, whether selected or not, and we are a very happy and chummy crowd. Perhaps it is because they have a very keen sense of duty to their Club and fellow Club members, and in closing I would recommend the Field Events Section to study our methods of clubship, and we shall soon be hearing praise once again for their section. F. H. ELSON. Charlie Jones Charlie Jones arranged the film show and gave the commentary and talk F. H. Elson F. H. ELSON Editor and Walking Coach European Games Poly Marathon Belgrave Hall

items.s: Match v. Thames Valley H. Report and Belgrave placings from the October 21st five-mile cross-country match against Thames Valley Harriers at Wimbledon, won by Belgrave 1,847 points to 2,075. MATCH v. THAMES VALLEY H. This was held at Wimbledon on October 21st and as there was a field of 90 runners it was decided to score 44 a side. First man home over our usual five-mile course was Les Field, of T.V.H., and he was followed by a club-mate in K. Norris. Bill Lucas came next and he was followed by Jack Brown, Vern Blowfield and Ches Walker, who came in together, with Bob Taylor and Ted Stimpson close behind, and this laid the foundation of our win in the team race over our old and friendly rivals. P. G. Newell, who won our novices one mile back in the summer, finished well up and looks like being a decided asset to our ranks. Alec Olney, of T.V.H., took things steady and was content to finish in 14th place, as did A. Miles in 22nd position. G. J. Goode, who won our three-mile road race, also ran well, and with careful handling should be a champion of the future. Placings and times of our runners are given hereunder:— 3, W. E. Brooks, with the Royal Military Police and Veterans' A.C. also competing. CLUB 5 MILES C.C. HANDICAP In this race, at Wimbledon on October 28th, we had the Royal Military Police from Woking and the Veterans' A.C. also competing. First man home was John Bromley, of the Police, and he was closely followed by Bill Lucas, with Steve Charlton and Archie Bedford also well up. We were pleased to welcome Ray Tooby, on leave from the Army, also Denis Brickwood, the well-known Mitcham A.C. runner, who has now joined us first-claim. The handicap was literally a "walk-over" for S. G. Brooks, who ran far above any previous form, and Tom Morrell gained second place, with J. E. Godfrey and E. S. Udall, both juniors, dead-heating for third place. Scoring 12 a side in the match, the scores were:—Belgrave H. 99 pts.; Royal Military Police 270; Veterans' A.C. 297. items.s: Highgate Harriers 7 Miles Open—October 28th Report and results of the Highgate Harriers seven-mile open walk on October 28th, where Belgrave lost Harry Churcher and Bert East to disqualification and finished third in the scratch team race. HIGHGATE HARRIERS 7 MILES OPEN—OCTOBER 28th Congratulations are offered to Highgate Harriers on their successful Open Walk, successful not only from the organisation point of view, but also in competition. First man home in record time, first scratch team, first handicap team, is quite a good day's sport. A record entry for opens of 270, a record number of starters, 230, and a record number of finishers, 217, was a magnificent start to the season's Opens. Coleman got away to a very fast start, followed by our Harry Churcher, who, at about 1¼ miles, was disqualified. We feel that Harry was definitely unlucky in being so ruled and with Bert East also suffering disqualification in the last half-mile of the race our team was too depleted to be a danger, and we feel that we did very well to finish third in the scratch team race. Gerald Gregory walked splendidly throughout to finish in the fifth position and will certainly be a power to our teams when he qualifies. Syd James was well up, with McMullen, Bob Readman and Bert Clayton constituted our team. Gerald Warr had a battle with Gordon Waddingham and George Oliver. J. Norton, one of our new members, did very well to finish in the centre of the field and should feel bucked at beating such old campaigners as Joe Wilson and Jack Baker.
