items.label: No. 116
items.sum: Account of the Nijmegen Four Days' Marches of July 1952, where Jack Wakeley marched in the R.W.A. team and five Belgravians in the M.P.A.A. police team, with lessons learned.
items.s: NIJMEGEN MARCHES—1952 Account of the Nijmegen Four Days' Marches of July 1952, where Jack Wakeley marched in the R.W.A. team and five Belgravians in the M.P.A.A. police team, with lessons learned. Among the 10,000 participants in the Annual International Four Days' Marches held at Nijmegen, Holland, from July 22nd to 26th, were six Belgravians; one—Jack Wakeley—in the R.W.A. Team, which took part in the 55 Kilos event, and five in the M.P.A.A. Team marching in Police uniform with a small (1 kg.) pack in the 50 kilos section, which the writer had the pleasure of leading. Jack Wakeley, the present English 100 miles Champion, with previous experience of the Marches behind him, was naturally one of the stalwarts of the R.W.A. team, and as Billy Baker's tribute in the Race Walking Record shows, he did the job in true Belgravian fashion, helping the English team to maintain its usual 100 per cent. performance and win a team award. Hugh McGreechan, Frank Jarvis, Sid Spencer, Jock Ferguson and I, with 13 other members of the M.P.A.A. met with a few of the troubles which first timers in the Marches encounter, but came through with only one casualty and so secured the coveted Corps Medaille. Inexperience led me to put our tallest men in front on the first day, with almost disastrous results for the shorter men of whom Jock Ferguson came off worst; so severely were both his feet blistered that after the second day of what must have been crippled agony (he was never heard to complain) he had to be ordered, on the doctor's advice, not to walk on the third and fourth days. Sceptic blisters are not funny and, how he finished on the second day is a mystery and a tribute to his grit. Sid Spencer had few competitors for the title of fittest man of the whole team, whilst Hugh McGreechan, who found it all well within his capacity, was heard to complain only when the singing stopped. Frank Jarvis had one difficult patch on the first half of the fourth day, but was as usual full of chirpiness and was never in danger of failing to finish. I had one or two patches of heavy weather, but found it well within the range of anyone reasonably fit. It was certainly great fun and a truly wonderful experience. We found that the 11 hours allowed each day for the 31 miles was ample. Marching at about four miles an hour with two or three stops, totalling 1½ to 2 hours, left us with 60 to 90 minutes to spare. There is of course no question of racing and, in fact, fast marching is frowned upon. One team which got in very early on the first day were made to wait about for nearly an hour before being booked in! The Marches were as usual magnificently organised, and the Dutch clearly have immense pride in them. It is a fact that the Nijmegen Medal awarded to those who complete the marches is authorised to be worn in their own armed forces with an individual's gallantry and campaign medals. Among the lessons we learned were:— (a) First and foremost must be the care of the feet. Shoes or boots must be comfortable; big enough to allow for at least some swelling of the feet and really stout in the sole, if only for the occasional cross country stretches. All regular marches seem to make Rule 1 that of strapping the heel and the ball of the foot with narrow strips of plaster, slightly overlapping, with similar protection for the large and smaller toes. I tried this after the first day and thereafter had no trouble at all, which seemed to be the general experience. (b) The next care is to have plenty to eat. We found Dutch fare very good indeed, but of course different from English in some respects and liable to cause a few people in times of extreme tiredness to lose their appetite. Ten hours of open air exercise leave no doubt about the importance of this however, and quite obviously it is a Team Captain's No. 2 care to see that no one neglects his feeding. (c) No. 3 is the question of rest. My team gave no trouble at all and we all had an hour or two in bed as soon as we had finished, and most were down to it again by ten o'clock. Rising at 3.15 a.m. for a 4.30 start makes this a vital matter. (d) Marching in step proved best for us and to music better still; whether to a mouth organ or to our own, at first, unaccustomed and hesitant voices. Tipperary got a little too thoroughly plugged, but like “She'll be coming down the mountains” is quite international and both were sung by almost every foreign unit we came across. Also internationally popular was one beginning “Roll me over,” which I had not, I think, previously heard. Everyone in the M.P.A.A. team seems quite determined to go next year and enquiries about chartering a plane again have already been made; which one feels is recommendation enough. With care, i.e., spending little on beer or presents, the week's trip can be done for about £17 to £18, which is no more than a week at the seaside. Individuals may enter on their own, subject of course to the usual consent of the A.A.A. or join the team which the R.W.A. organises every year. Better still, if I may make a suggestion, would be a Belgrave team; we need only ten and it really is almost child's play to those who are reasonably fit—as of course most Belgravians are—people like Bert Footer for instance!!! But if he goes, I go with the M.P.A.A. again. items.sum: Frank Simmons' message to the club's juniors congratulating them on the season, urging winter training at Battersea Park and Belgrave Hall, and welcoming new members.
items.s: To All Juniors Frank Simmons' message to the club's juniors congratulating them on the season, urging winter training at Battersea Park and Belgrave Hall, and welcoming new members. First let me congratulate the Junior athletes of the Club on their performances throughout last season. It was a pleasure to me to see so many support our fixtures and indeed, I had a job to fit everyobdy in. But I like it that way, for it shows we have in the making good club members who will turn out on any and every occasion. Some of you may still be at school and if you have a school match on the same evening as the Club, then your first loyalty is to your school. Loyalty to me means, if you have a duty to perform, whether at home, at school or in the club, then do your utmost to carry it out. This brings me to a point which I wish to make clear—the making of promises. Many of you promised me that you would train during the winter, well what about it? I have not seen many who made this promise, or was it made just to stop me badgering you about training, for believe me, you will not and cannot improve on broken promises and no training. The weather may be bad, good or indifferent: wet, dry, warm or cold; but we are always at Battersea Park Track on Saturday afternoons from 1.30 p.m. to 4.30 p.m. and Sunday mornings from 10.30 a.m. to 1 p.m.—that is of course, those who are keeping the promises they made, and myself, with Franz Stampfl, who has never failed to turn out for his coaching sessions. I hope those who made this promise to me will have a great sense of guilt in not keeping it. Those who have come along so far can, I am sure, honestly say they have enjoyed themselves in the happy company of Belgravians assembled and on their behalf I extend a cordial welcome to all those who wish to come along and have a rattling good time at our coaching and training sessions. John Jones, Dave Ansell and C. R. Jones are three who have trained regularly and industriously so far and I am looking for great improvements in these and many others in field events. I cannot stress too much the importance of training and ask you to get down to it NOW. You cannot afford to waste any time. I am holding Wednesday evening indoor coaching at Belgrave Hall from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. and a programme has been worked out which will cover all angles of field events. You do not have to pay anything extra for this—it is all included in the very small annual subscription which you pay. Make it worth me giving up my time, often at cost to myself and the other coaches who are willing to assist you in your chosen events. To the Cross Country juniors and youths, on behalf of the track boys, I wish you every success this winter and hope you will exceed all your expectations. Make Mickey Pyer a happy man by winning the National Junior C.C. He is a grand fellow whose first consideration is YOU and such a great success by Belgrave Juniors will be much appreciated, especially by Mickey. To the Junior walkers—“Keep 'em down” and have a go. You have a great tradition behind you that should be enough to spur you on to great heights. To follow in the footsteps of Tommy Green, Harry Churcher and many others too numerous to mention. To those who are now entering the Senior ranks of the Club, carry on the grand work which you started as a Junior, and to those just joining the Club as Juniors, we give you a hearty welcome and want to make you happy in this happy band of Belgravians. Finally to all juniors in the Club, may your successes be great and your disappointments few. May we all go forward together along the road of high endeavour to make this our greatest year so far in the Club's history. Frank Simmons FRANK SIMMONS Franz Stampfl Franz Stampfl coach at Battersea Park Track sessions John Jones John Jones junior, training regularly Dave Ansell Dave Ansell junior, training regularly C. items.sum: Progress report on plans to rebuild Belgrave Hall, which may close for the summer of 1953 if a building licence is obtained.
items.s: Belgrave Hall Progress report on plans to rebuild Belgrave Hall, which may close for the summer of 1953 if a building licence is obtained. After many months of legal wrangling, with letters by the dozen, things have at last sorted themselves out, our dreams for rebuilding the Hall are now beginning to take shape, plans have been prepared, builders are estimating, with a general easing of the labour market, and a more plentiful supply of material, there is every possibility of our obtaining the necessary licence, if this is forthcoming, we plan to start building at once, this will mean, that the hall will be closed for the summer months, members normally using the hall, are asked to make alternative arrangements, while no definite date of completion can be given, members can rest assured that every effort will be made to have the hall ready for the beginning of the winter season 1953. T. F. Morrell T. F. MORRELL Hon. Sec. "House" Sub-Committee Belgrave Hall

items.sum: Club news column: births, Jack Chappell's elections, members' track and walking successes, National Service postings and G. Walsh's running in Singapore.
items.s: Here and There Club news column: births, Jack Chappell's elections, members' track and walking successes, National Service postings and G. Walsh's running in Singapore. Although a little belated, but none the less sincere, we send heartiest congratulations to Alf and Mrs. Harley on the birth of their twin daughters and we are glad to know they are all progressing favourably. Congratulations to Jack Chappell our Field Events Hon. Secretary on his election to the office of President of the South of the Thames Cross Country Association and Vice-President of E.C.C.U. and S.C.C.C.A. Among the successes by our members during the past track season were—Ray Tooby who won the Junior Inter-Banks 1 mile race in 4 min. 28.2 secs. Jack Brown 2nd in the Civil Service 1 mile with Bob Taylor 3rd in the 880 yards. J. D. Benstead was 3rd in the Southern Junior 220 yards, while Frank Wright was 3rd in the A.A.A. Junior 880 yards and also finished 3rd in the Junior half-mile at the British Games meeting in the fine time of 1 min. 57.4 secs. Jack Brown also ran 2nd to [illegible]oger Bannister in the A.A.A. v. Combined Services match in 4 min. 16.6 secs., and also finished 3rd in the 1 mile event at the Highland Games held in Edinburgh. Bert Jordan won the 7 miles road race handicap at the Oxted meeting on August Monday. Ian Badiali won the Shipping A.A. 440 yards championship in 52.1 seconds, and Len Rolls won the Veterans A.C. 880 yards championship. Ted Smith won the London Transport 7 miles Walk Championship at Wembley in record time. Harry Shields was third. Quite a number of our lads are now having to join up to do their National Service training and recent joinings include—Peter Casselton to the R.A., Charlie Henn to the R.E.M.E., Peter Courtney who managed to get placed in the half and mile at his Depot Sports. Brian Trower writes us from the Fighter Plotters School at Middle Wallop, while J. Hills is with the R.A.S.C. at Aldershot, and Don Maclean is now with the R.A. in North Wales and says he is hoping to get in some running while there. Vern Blowfield also writes to say that his family are now with him at Oxford, but that he hopes to come up for some training runs and says he is looking forward to having a good season and takes it as a good omen that the Southern is at Aylesford, as in 1948 at the same venue he was 3rd in the individual race, while we won the team championship. A feature of the finish of the Southern London to Brighton Road Relay was our large crowd of supporters holding a club banner, made by the President's wife for the occasion, and it is hoped to include a photo of this in the programme for next year's race. G. Walsh, a Corporal in the A.C.C. in Singapore is apparently making his presence felt out east. As there are no English Athletic Clubs, he has joined a Chinese one. Members include Indians, Tamils, Malays, Eurasians, Dutchmen, Chinese and a few Army personnel. The Club is called the “Swifts” and competing in their colours he won four cups in the Annual Singapore A.A. Championships at Jalan Besar Stadium. items.sum: Editorial acknowledging a lean season without Surrey County titles but urging Belgravians, after the example of Frank Thomson and the club's pioneers, not to be pessimistic.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial acknowledging a lean season without Surrey County titles but urging Belgravians, after the example of Frank Thomson and the club's pioneers, not to be pessimistic. Dear Fellow Belgravians, In reading this issue it may be you will notice a slight undercurrent of melancholia. We are unable to report many successes in any section ; on the contrary, among other things, for the first time for many years, we are not now the Surrey County Champions at either Cross Country or Walking. But, do these reverses give us cause for the rumblings of pessimism we hear. Your Editors do not think so ! In our Editorials we endeavour in a few sentences to review many aspects of the Club and we feel our intended words of wisdom do much to emphasise the necessity of certain things and alternately to soothe any unwarranted apprehensions. Frank Thomson (whose obituary is published in other pages) with other pioneering Belgravians, were, in their days never deterred by pessimism, although they were up against tremendous odds. With due respect to those Belgrave stalwarts of yore, there was no possible chance to achieve anything much more ambitious than a club match win. Yet cheerfully they kept at their task and the full fruits of their endeavours were eventually realised in our many championship successes. Why, then, should we be pessimistic because we are having a few reverses ? What Frank Thomson and his colleagues did in the early days with a handful of enthusiasts we can do again, particularly with the splendid team of up-and-coming youngsters which we now have. So, away with the blues. We are still at the top of the tree in all branches of sport, the only difference being that we are sharing that position with others. Let us welcome this new state of affairs, and let it give us a greater incentive to regain our lost honours in the knowledge that it will be a much more praiseworthy achievement. YOUR EDITORS. Frank Thomson Frank Thomson pioneering Belgravian; obituary in this issue Surrey County Championships

items.label: No. 117
items.h: YOUR PRESIDENT SPEAKS ON THE WINTER SEASON
items.sum: The President reflects on the club's poor winter season in open events, blaming retirements, studies and marriages, and calls for members' support to put the club back on top.
items.s: YOUR PRESIDENT SPEAKS ON THE WINTER SEASON The President reflects on the club's poor winter season in open events, blaming retirements, studies and marriages, and calls for members' support to put the club back on top. The winter season just passing has not shown the Club in a very good light as regards successes in open events. Both our runners and walkers have sadly declined in performance as reckoned on previous years, but on reading through a copy of the December, 1931, issue of the "Belgravian," I came across the following comment, which seems to me to meet the present situation :— "The true strength of any club is its numbers, enthusiasm, sportsmanship, and standard of ability, which are the true index to a club's pre-eminence, and we need have no misgivings on these points." As I stated in our last issue, we have unbounded enthusiasm as regards our Youths and Juniors, ; we also have the numbers, as witness our large fields in Club races. I do not think that anyone would question our sportsmanship, and I think our standard of ability is quite high. What, then, you may ask, is the reason for the apparent decline both in our running and walking sections ? Firstly, I think, is the inevitable retirement of some of our well-known members in both spheres, and their places are hard to fill right away, although we have the right material coming along. Then we have the numerous studies being undertaken by our members in order to help their business careers, which curtails their training time, and then we have the marriages, which are bound to come along and unless they can "school" their wives to take an interest in athletics, any time taken for training is naturally resented by their better halves ! It is rather ironic that I mentioned our cycle of successes in the last issue, but it does seem that for the moment our run of victories has been halted, although some people may think this is good for the sport as a whole. That we shall triumph again I have not the slightest doubt, but it does require the support and co-operation of all our members, which I sometimes think has been lacking in certain quarters, and let us hope that next season we shall see the "Bels" back on top once again in both the running and walking worlds. E. A. DUFFETT, President. E. A. Duffett E. A. DUFFETT President E. A. DUFFETT

items.label: No. 117
items.sum: Obituary of Frank Thomson, sprinter, long-serving club official, Belgrave President and President of the Road Walking Association, who died on February 1st in his eightieth year, with a tribute from "Timber" Woodcock.
items.s: F. G. THOMSON Obituary of Frank Thomson, sprinter, long-serving club official, Belgrave President and President of the Road Walking Association, who died on February 1st in his eightieth year, with a tribute from "Timber" Woodcock. Once again the Club has suffered a very heavy blow in the death of Frank Thomson, which occurred on February 1st, in his eightieth year. Frank was not a Founder Member of the Club, but joined Belgrave—he was a Westminster resident—in its early days. He had many successes as a sprinter and, as was the custom in those days, he entered races at all distances and "had a go" at most. He played an important part in the management of the Club and in 1893 was accorded the honour of Life Membership. In 1895 he was Assistant Hon. Secretary to F. A. Bool, happily still alive and living in Chelsea, and was also a Vice-President and Hon. Auditor. In 1903 he had an operation which cut short his active career, and business and other interests claimed his attention in the years that followed. In the early 1920's Frank returned to his first love of Amateur Athletics and it is doubtful if anyone worked harder in the cause of our sport during the next twenty years. Almost every day throughout spring and summer he was at Battersea Park Track, and during the winter season he was always to be found at our mid-week quarters on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and at our Wimbledon Headquarters on Saturdays—and always working in the Club's best interests. For a while he was our Gen. Hon. Secretary, when the Club was bounding ahead, and later became Hon. Treasurer of the Surrey County A.A.A., building up the first bank balance that Association had ever known. For several years he was (jointly with F. W. Blackmore) Hon. Handicapper for Road Walking events in the south and in permanent demand as chief scoring judge at most big walking events. He was well known as a member of the Southern Committee A.A.A., and had special interests on the handicapping Board of Control. In 1935-36 Frank became President of the Road Walking Association—the first Belgrave Harrier to hold that high office. He was a Past Chairman of the R.W.A. Southern Committee and highly honoured by being elected to Life Membership of the Road Walking Association and of Les Marcheurs Francais, in tribute to his work for walking internationally. He became President of the Belgrave Harriers as the war clouds burst upon us. A partial breakdown in health in 1941 caused his retirement from business and removal to the Slough area. But still his interest in athletics persisted and he was frequently to be seen at our events. He was at our track championships last year, at the Club Dinner in October and our Open Walk in November—still showing that keenness which had always epitomised all his activities. He derived tremendous satisfaction from the Club's successes over the years with its succession of Championship titles and prominent performances, which had sprung from the few enthusiasts of the early years of the Club. Many of us will have plentiful and rewarding recollections of our old friend. We recall Frank wielding the megaphone at our track meetings, giving helpful advice to members on training nights explaining the rudiments of the Field Events and his assiduous work at our various races and on the results sheets. He will be remembered for his self-less work at some of the early Nijmegen Marches and for his hours well spent in fostering and fathering the Southern Amateur Athletic League Field Events competitions, which may truthfully be said to have been the forerunner of the greatly improved performances we see to-day. We shall remember him with the open-top bus he hired for us on Brighton Walk and Brighton Relay days ; as Trustee of the Club, conscientious and hard-working for the Club's ideals. We shall think of him, only a few months ago, with sponge and drinks at Slough Feeding Station on the Bath to London Walk, where he spent many hours helping competitors. Above all, we shall remember Frank Thomson as a great Belgravian who attained high office in the realms of athletics, yet worked effectively and unceasingly for Belgrave in fair weather and foul. Increasing years did not dull his enthusiasm, and his example is one we can all well take to heart. Frank's daughter has kindly offered us a trophy in memory of her father, and this we shall gladly accept as a perpetual reminder of one who served the Club so well and so long. R.I.P. A. A. H. Expressions of sympathy and appreciation were received from the Amateur Athletic Association, Road Walking Association, Surrey Walking Club and many who had worked with Frank over so many years. The following is an extract from a letter received from "Timber" Woodcock, Surrey W.C., and typifies the enthusiasm for our sport which Frank always showed :— ". . . I remember when I first started walking in 1930, Frank Thomson was known to me as the Southern Handicapper. In 1931, when I was a member of the Surrey Team to go to Nijmegen, I well remember that Frank was in charge of the R.W.A. Team and, with our Capt. Wilmot, he took great care of our welfare while in Holland. I remember a nine o'clock foot inspection at the end of our beds just before lights out every night. Who was first up every morning ? Why, Frank Thomson. We usually woke to find him fully dressed and having a go at those who were inclined to stop in bed at 3 a.m. Who looked after the team when on the road at check points ? Why, Frank again. And when it was all over he was the proudest man at the final ceremony when the awards were made. . . ." F. G. Thomson F. G. items.sum: Note on the illnesses of Jack Stirling Wakeley, Dick Murphy and Len Rollins.
items.s: OUR INVALIDS Note on the illnesses of Jack Stirling Wakeley, Dick Murphy and Len Rollins. Since our last issue, Jack Stirling Wakeley was taken suddenly ill and had to be rushed to hospital for an operation. We are pleased to report that he is now fully recovered and hopes to be out training again soon. Dick Murphy has been very ill, but as far as is known, he also is on the way to recovery, but has retired from business. Len Rollins, one of our very keen members in pre-war years and one who still takes a very live interest in Club activities, has also been ill. We wish both Dick and Len an early recovery. items.sum: Report of an informal meeting of about 25 runners called by Cross-Country Captain Jack Brown to discuss the section's progress, pack running, fixtures and planning for future seasons.
items.s: CROSS-COUNTRY MEETING—FEBRUARY 14th Report of an informal meeting of about 25 runners called by Cross-Country Captain Jack Brown to discuss the section's progress, pack running, fixtures and planning for future seasons. With a certain amount of trepidation, it is ventured to state that an informal meeting to discuss cross-country racing was called for the first time for some years by the Cross-Country Captain, Jack Brown. The idea basically, was to stimulate interest in winter activities and to this end two items appeared on the agenda :— 1. The progress of the Cross-Country Section this winter. 2. To discuss plans for the future. At this juncture it would probably be as well to say that there was an attendance of about 25 runners, and conspicuous by their absence were some of the great names of the Club. The meeting was opened by Denis Brickwood outlining the somewhat docile outlook of the runners to-day which had its reflection in a degree of Club stagnation. This was not to imply that we were worse than any other club—in fact, we were still more virile than most. Progress, he pointed out, could be divided into two sections : 1, The progress in ability of the individual. 2, Progress in Club outlook and spirit. He had decided that there was progress in the ability of certain runners and this implied that the training had been good. There was nothing particularly controversial about this and most speakers agreed. This naturally led to the second type of progress and Ted Stimpson, soliloquising on the past glories of the Club, said that the spirit which led them on then, was required now. Efforts had been made to get people to run in organised packs and the outcome was poor. A view was expressed that various groups did their own training which did not differ in any way from organised training. Doug Briggs and George Stace spoke most ably in their own defence, but at the same time did not disagree with the necessity for having an organised run with the pack once a week. Jack Brown, the Captain, whilst not doubting the truth of Ted Stimpson's views, ventured to say that the nature of athletics had altered in some degree and the individual performance was now considerably more important than before the war. Perhaps this was not desirable, but you had to keep pace with the times. On pack running it was explained by Denis Brickwood that it was an opportunity for the selectors to see how men were running, and this non-attendance on Saturdays had caused mistakes in selection to be made. During the season changes had been made in the organisation of packs, such as changing pace-makers periodically, but it was surprising that some members were not aware that this was being done. It had to be explained that the pack-leader ran in the body of the pack and was able to watch individual runners. The pacemakers were varied in order to afford experience and add variety to the runs. In addition, of course, it did tend to teach judgment of pace and it certainly kept the pace at a pretty high rate. To those that had not indulged in these packs, Denis Brickwood extended a cordial invitation, and assured possible clients that they would benefit from it, and even enjoy it. Passing on to the future, there was a general feeling that more thought could be given to the season before it actually started. It was conceded that the responsibility for about everything was left to Ernie Duffett, and whilst this was appreciated it did mean that, when anything was not to members' requirements, it just had to be Ernie's responsibility as no one else was involved. This was unfair and it was up to members to come forward and give their ideas to those concerned. George Chantler said that the Captains and Vice-Captains were elected to do a job and it was up to the runners to back them up. He knew the day when, if the Captain said, "We're going to run 10 miles," everyone did it. He wanted to see that once more. On fixtures, it was reported that support had been pathetic and it was lucky that there were three Bishop brothers and Bob Taylor. The average turn-out was about seven per away fixture and this was not good enough for a Club of our size. Perhaps this type of fixture was not wanted, or was it the venue ? A suggestion from Ernie Duffett was that fixtures be confined to clubs south of the Thames, and this was, in the main, agreed on by the meeting. Another point raised was the desirability of nominating the Captains well before the Cross-Country season started, so that they could take some part in making plans for the ensuing season. It was even suggested that a small Committee should be formed to properly organise the season's activities. The suggestion almost amounted to heresy in club official circles, but it was considered that it would make members more conscious of the work that was necessary in a club of our size and which was now done by a matter of half-a-dozen officials. The meeting discussed many other matters and it would take many pages to put it into print. The meeting was undoubtedly a success, and although it lasted about 1½ hours, it could have gone on much longer. It was somewhat difficult to end the meeting, but it was obvious that those who wanted to let off steam had had their chance. And now a final word to those who were not able to be present. You must have some views on cross-country running—you must have given it a thought. So, watch the notice boards, or the press, or News Letters, or this admirable magazine, for the date of the next informal meeting. items.sum: The Field Events Secretary previews the 1953 season, praises winter coaching at Battersea Park, announces entry for the Sward Trophy and urges selected members to turn up for matches.
items.s: FIELD EVENTS The Field Events Secretary previews the 1953 season, praises winter coaching at Battersea Park, announces entry for the Sward Trophy and urges selected members to turn up for matches. We are now approaching the Field Events season and I am hoping that the members of this section will get together and support George Powell, Captain, and P. Luxon, Vice-Captain. We have a very full programme, and I trust it will prove a successful one. Plaques are to be awarded, as suggested last year, for Club records. As you must know, to win one is very hard work, but it can be done and I hope 1953 will give you the opportunity. I must say that Frank Simmons and Franz Stampfl have worked hard all the winter on Saturdays and Sundays at Battersea Park, and I am sure they will be all the more pleased if their work produces good results. We have received and accepted an invitation to compete in the Sward Trophy (all field events) next May. The Club has not yet won this trophy, but we can win it if the field events men train hard enough. The events are 120 yards hurdles, 220 yards hurdles, 440 yards hurdles, 2 miles steeplechase, long jump, high jump, hop, step and jump, pole vault, discus, javelin, and hammer and shot. Entries will be sent in by the Club in April. We should very much like to cover every event, so carry on with the training and see what you can do. Further particulars can be obtained from Frank Simmons or myself. One important thing I would ask of you, and this applies equally to every member of the Club : If you are selected to represent the Club in a match, do please turn up and give us your support, or else let your Hon. Secretary or Captain know in good time so that they can fill the vacancy. Many valuable points have been lost in the past, merely because we had no one to represent us, so, whatever you do, don't let the Club down. Here's wishing you good luck and good sport. J. CHAPPELLL, Hon. Field Events Secretary. P.S.—Will any non-active members who are willing to act as officials, please get in touch with me before the track season starts ? items.s: CLUB OPEN 7-MILE WALK, November 29th Report and placings of the Club Open 7-Mile Walk on November 29th, a record entry of 267, in which Belgrave were outside the prizes for the first time, Harry Churcher their first man in 6th, and Woodford Green A.C. won the Berman Trophy. Once again our Open Walk was promoted with outstanding success, that is, if we overlook the race results. Although this was Jack Goswell's first big job in his new office as Hon. Walking Secretary, he tackled it with great enthusiasm and brilliant organising ability. We thank him for his diligence in every detail and also add our thanks to Mrs. Goswell, who helped in so many ways. The prizes, as usual, were admitted by all to be grand value and were greatly appreciated by the successful competitors. As to the race itself, the results below will tell their own story, but mention must be made of the gallant effort of Harry Churcher, who was not fit, but finished in 6th position to be our first man home. Another fine performance was that of J. Haynes, who, we feel, will eventually prove a very fine team man. For the first time in the history of this race we were right outside the prize list, and this should give us food for thought as to the necessity of obtaining new blood. However, we should gain great satisfaction from the fine walking of our Juniors, particularly J. Haynes, E. Hall, and B. Eglington. items.s: "BLACKSTAFFE" SHIELD RACE Report and full results of the Club 7 miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield on Wimbledon Common on December 13th, won by Jack Brown, with the handicap and a six-a-side match against Cadogan A.C. The Club 7 miles c.c. championship was held on December 13th over our usual 2-lap course across Wimbledon Common, and although the field of 29 starters may be good by comparison with other clubs, it was a poor turn-out so far as the last two races for this trophy are concerned. Notable absentees included previous winners in Vern Blowfield and Len Herbert, and we had Eric Herbert running in the Civil Service race on the same day. Len Adams, who has recently married, and Archie Bedford, also P. G. Newell, who had been mentioned as a probable winner. Eddie Short was running for the R.A.F. in a match against the U.A.U. and Midland Counties, and Bob Taylor, who was indisposed. In mentioning the above names we are not attempting to detract from Jack Brown's running in winning the race, as his time was well up to standard and he finished in comfortable fashion in front of Chas. Walker and Bill Lucas. Mike Stearman ran well seeing that, under the new E.C.C.U. rules, he is still a junior and he pays tribute to the way he was helped along by Denis Brickwood, who seems to be regaining some of his old form. The handicap was won by George Stace, with "Jumbo" Masters in second place and Denis Brickwood third, and Masters ran very well seeing that this was his first appearance over the country this season. In a six-a-side match with our Middlesex friends, Cadogan A.C., we were easy winners and it seemed a pity that Ted Stimpson and Dick Tobin, both former stalwarts of this Club, preferred to go out for a training spin rather than run in the race. items.s: "HORWOOD CUP" 7-MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP (JUNIORS) Report and results of the Horwood Cup 7 miles junior walking championship on December 13th, won by Gerry Warr from Eric Hall and George Beecham. December 13th A good field of 20 Junior walkers, that is junior in performance, faced the starter and a very interesting race followed, with Gerry Warr and George Beecham battling all the way for first position. Eric Hall walked a very brainy race, being content to hang a little way back from the leaders. Towards the last mile George began to feel the effect of his recent foot injury and had to give way to his training comrade of their early days, thus enabling Eric to gain second place. Gerry Warr walked well and strongly right to the end and proved a worthy champion. Ted Smith had an off day, but Eglington and Ferguson showed improved form. Charlie Speechley, our evergreen at sixty-five years of age, again showed he can still show the youngsters how. We were glad to see W. Emery with us again and hope to see more of him, and L. Demmon, one of our latest acquisitions, will undoubtedly prove a useful walker with more training. Results as follows :— Handicap—1, E. Hall; 2, B. Eglington; 3, G. Warr. items.s: MATCH v. WANDSWORTH SCHOOL Report of the cross-country match against Wandsworth School at Wimbledon on 13th December, won individually by Frank Wright but lost by Belgrave on points. This was held on 13th December over our usual 3½-mile course at Wimbledon and, owing to the fact that the fixture had been arranged at the last minute, we had a job to muster a team. The School appeared to turn up in force and it was agreed to score 7 a side, which meant all our runners counting. Frank Wright was first home in the good time of 21 min. 27 secs., closely followed by Darchambaud, of the School, and this lad was at one time on our books, but has since joined South London H., and is running very well for them. A. C. McLean, our new member from the North Shields Poly., finished in 3rd place and he has shown a big improvement since he joined our ranks. J. Mitchell, 5th, and E. Cronk, 8th, also ran well, and if we had made it 4 to score we would have won with 17 points against the School's 19, but with 7 to score the points were: Wandsworth School, 49 ; Belgrave H., 56. items.s: MATCH AT BEXLEY Report of Belgrave's one-point defeat by Cambridge Harriers in a cross-country match at Bexley on 20th December. On 20th December, against the local club, Cambridge Harriers, it was unfortunate that our captain, Jack Brown, turned up just too late to take part in the race. Holden, of Cambridge, was first home, followed by Chas. Walker, with Cass, of Cambridge, third. Then followed Bob Taylor, Denis Brickwood and J. E. Burr, but the Cambridge lads packed in well behind these and so came out winners by the narrow margine of 1 point. The course was not too well marked, and Len Bishop went off the course and this, plus Jack Brown's absence, was really responsible for us losing the match, with Cambridge scoring 40 points and ourselves 41. items.s: BOXING DAY MEETING Report of the Club's Boxing Day handicap meeting at Battersea Park, with sprint, walk, 2 miles and weight handicap results. Although the weather was not too good, a large number of Club members turned up to compete in the various events at this meeting held at Battersea Park. It was a pity that we were rather short of officials, and we do thank the few who left the comfort of their fireside to come along and help make the meeting a success. L. R. Truelove, the A.A.A. team manager, was present as a spectator and he must have been impressed not only by Jack Brown's fine running but also by the numbers present. The 120 yards Club handicap saw three heats, and those qualifying for the final were : R. Morrell (10), J. Benstead (5), C. R. Jones (11), D. Butler (6), A. Law (5), P. Cornish (6). The final saw the six runners finish almost in a straight line and the judges' placings were : 1, C. R. Jones; 2, P. Cornish ; 3, Butler. Time, 12.5 secs. The 3 miles walk handicap was won by the limit man, our old friend, Charlie Speechley, with George Oliver second, and Percy Wilson in third place. In the 2 miles run we saw the two back-markers, M. Whenman and Jack Brown, go right through their field and at the bell Jack left his pacemaker to streak ahead and win in the fast time of 9 mins. 21 secs. Eddie Paterson, off 290 yds., was second, with Whenman in third place. The Weight handicap saw a good muster of field event men, and the winner was D. Maddicks, our young javelin thrower, who, with 14ft. 6in., did 43ft. 3¾in. Frank Kemp (11ft.) was second, with Ian Forrester (16ft. 6in.) third, and the scratch man, Gaworski, did 41ft. 3¼in. L. R. items.s: COUNTY SENIOR C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS Report of the county senior cross-country championships on 3rd January: Belgrave third in the Surrey race in Richmond Park, and Cadogan A.C. sixth in the Middlesex race at Trent Park. These were held on the 3rd January, and the Surrey event was in Richmond Park, which was more or less familiar ground to our team. We were not at full strength owing to the absence of Jack Braughton, Len Herbert, Archie Bedford and Len Adams, and did not expect to retain our team title, which we had held for the past two seasons. Our team, however, all ran extremely well and we only lost first place by 5 points and second place by 1 point. Chas. Walker was our first man home in 5th position, then came Bill Lucas, 12th, and Bill only came into the team in order to make up the number, as he says he has retired from serious competition and declined an invitation to run in the Inter-Counties race. We then had three men, one behind the other, in Eddie Short 14th. Eric Herbert 15th, and Denis Brickwood 16th, and our sixth man was J. Masters 21st, and as this was the latter's first County race, he did very well and should improve with further experience. Placings and times were—5, C. W. Walker, 42.56; 12, W. E. items.s: MATCH v. FINCHLEY HARRIERS Report of a cross-country match at Ruislip against Finchley Harriers and Shaftesbury Harriers, in which Belgrave were second to Shaftesbury. We were pleased to renew fixtures with this old established club, one-time National c.c. champions, but only ten of our senior members made the journey to Ruislip. items.s: SURREY COUNTY YOUTHS C.C. RACE Report of the Surrey County Youths cross-country race staged from Belgrave Hall on 10th January, won by Frank Wright, with Belgrave taking the team title for the third year running. This was originally fixed for 6th December, but was postponed owing to fog, and we agreed to stage it in conjunction with the Junior event on 10th January from Belgrave Hall. There was a very good entry, with a field of about 100 lads, and first man home was Frank Wright in the good time of 20 mins. 57 secs. Gerry Lines gave him good support by finishing 4th, and then came J. B. Edgar, 6th, and Ron Linstead, 8th, and so we had scored our third consecutive win in this event. D. G. Hooper and J. F. Mitchell also both ran very well and we should have still won the team race with either of these counting in our scoring four. Placings and times of our lads were—1, F. J. Wright, 20.57; 4, G. items.s: SURREY JUNIOR C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP Report of the Surrey Junior cross-country championship at Wimbledon on 10th January, where Belgrave were fourth behind S.L.H. At Wimbledon on 10th January there was a field of about 50 runners and, seeing that the age is 18 to 21, most of those who are eligible to run are in the Forces. S.L.H. had a strong team, led by Firth and Driver, who both ran well in the County senior race a week earlier, but they only came out winners by 2 points and were only 6 points in front of us. Mike Stearman was our first man home in 6th place, then came Brian Trower 12th, Don McLean 14th, and Brian Rice 21st. items.s: "OVERSEAS CUP" RACE Report and results of the Club Youths cross-country championship for the Overseas Cup, won by Frank Wright, with the handicap won by R. J. Braine. This was the third Club Youths c.c. championship to be held for this trophy, and this year's field of 21 runners was by far the largest of the trio. Also the first three home all beat the time of 21.29 recorded by last year's winner, Geoff Goode, who is now in the Forces. In fact, all those who ran previously bettered their time this time out and this is a good sign for the future, and Mick Pyer can be well pleased with his section. Frank Wright maintained his unbeaten record over our home course, but J. B. Edgar caused a surprise by beating Gerry Lines for second place. Ron Linstead was 4th in both the scratch race also the handicap held in conjunction, but as he will still be eligible for next year's race, he should improve upon this. The handicap was won by R. J. Braine, one of our numerous members from Raynes Park County School, with M. Cunningham second, and he was making his first appearance over the country this season, and then J. F. items.s: "MACHER" SHIELD RACE Report and full results of the Macher Shield race at Wimbledon on 24th January, won by Jack Brown in 57.45, with the handicap won by Frank Mitchell. At Wimbledon, on 24th January, a field of 33 runners faced the starter, Albert Macher, and we were also pleased to see his brother, J. W. Macher, present once more. The race was two laps of our usual 5 miles course, and at the half-distance Jack Brown and Mart Whenman were running together well away from the rest of the field. We were glad to see John Bromley getting back to his old form in third place and as Whenman is only a second-claim member, and so, not eligible for a championship medal, Eddie Short took the third place award. Eric Herbert and J. E. Burr both ran well, and for the first six to finish inside 61 mins. is quite good going and compares well with previous results. The winning time of 57.45 is one of the fastest ever accomplished over this course, and both Brown and Whenman should be well up in the "National" event in March on this form. We were pleased to see Frank Mitchell win the handicap held in conjunction, a reward for perseverance, and Whenman took second prize, with J. E. Burr third. Warr. For holding this event the Club had decided on a new course this year, and it overcame the troubles of the past and we completed the race successfully. Syd James, who has been walking well this season, carried on the good work and gained his first Club trophy. George Oliver, who had been with Syd up till the last two miles, finished second, with Gerry Warr third. We were pleased to have with us P. Wright and Bobby Burns and N. Guilmant from Southampton, and sorry that Percy should be out after only 1½ miles. Bad luck, Percy. The handicap was won by G. Warr, with S. James second, and N. Guilmant third. Twenty-three started. items.s: YOUTHS' ROAD TRIAL Report of the youths' road trial on 24th January to pick teams for the Aylesbury Youths Road Relay, won by Ron Linstead. This was held on 24th January with a view to selection of our teams for the Aylesbury Youths Road Relay, and a good field turned out. McLean second, and Frank Wright third, and don't think Frank was trying too hard, as this was his third race in successive weeks. A new member in R. Brewer ran well, and it looks as if we have some good lads coming along to take their places in our teams for future road relays. Placings and times were—1, R. Linstead, 15.40; 2, A. C. items.label: No. 117
items.sum: Note that the junior cross-country match against Cambridge Harriers at Wimbledon on 31st December could not be held, and that only three members turned up for a senior match at Totteridge.
items.s: JUNIOR C.C. v. CAMBRIDGE H. Note that the junior cross-country match against Cambridge Harriers at Wimbledon on 31st December could not be held, and that only three members turned up for a senior match at Totteridge. This was due to be held at Wimbledon on 31st December and although about half-a-dozen of our visitors came along, including R. A. Butt, a past member of our Club, we only had one junior present, and so a race could not be held. To be fair to our lads, we must say that most of our 18 to 21 age group are doing their National Service training, and week-end leaves seem few and far between and one doubts whether it is worth while arranging such matches in future. A week later we had a senior match at Totteridge with Shaftesbury H. and T.V.H., but only three of our members turned up, and so could not count in the match, although they had a run. It does seem as if away fixtures are not welcomed by our runners and that our fixtures for next season will have to undergo a drastic alteration in make-up. R. A. Butt R. A. Butt past member of the Club; among the visitors Wimbledon Totteridge Cambridge H. Shaftesbury H. T.V.H.

items.label: No. 117
items.sum: Report of the South of Thames cross-country championship at Milford, near Godalming, on 7th February, where a depleted Belgrave team was third behind Bristol A.C. and Herne Hill H.
items.s: SOUTH OF THAMES CHAMPIONSHIP Report of the South of Thames cross-country championship at Milford, near Godalming, on 7th February, where a depleted Belgrave team was third behind Bristol A.C. and Herne Hill H. Held at Milford, near Godalming, on 7th February. There was a record entry of 26 teams. Clubs are only allowed to enter one team of 12 to run with 6 to score, and in the eight races since the war we have only been unplaced on two occasions and have won the team race four times. As the winning team is barred from competing again, it will be seen that fresh men have constantly to be found and we think our post-war record speaks for itself. We thought we should improve on last year's 7th position, but as we were without P. G. Newell, A. H. Bruce, B. L. Hudson, A. J. Snoad, and Mike Stearman, down with 'flu, we did not fancy our chances of getting a place. The winners of the team race were Bristol A.C., which was a just reward for their long journey, and who should be with them but our old past President, Teddy Gordon, and you can imagine his pleasure at their success and in our getting third. The individual race was won easily by "Lofty" Holden, of Cambridge H., and our first man home was Bob Taylor, 17th, our other scorers being Mick Porter, 27; John Burr, 32; Ray Tooby, 38; Len Bishop, 57, and George Stace, 61. Ray Tooby was suffering from split heels and found he could not wear his spikes and ran in rubber shoes, which no doubt was partly to blame for his backward position Our other placings were : D. Briggs, 73; J. Masters, 76 ; A. H. Bishop, 109 ; K. G. Stimpson, 111 ; E. M. Bishop, 208 ; and Eric had a pulled tendon and did well to complete the course. We were expecting Mike Stearman to arrive on the Brighton A.C. coach, but, instead, got a letter from him saying that he was down with 'flu, and this meant that we could not field a full team of 12 runners and so qualify for the "Colman" Cup, which was won by Herne Hill H. This brings up the point about all those entered who can turn out should come along with their togs in case they are required, and in any event, they can do a good job of work round the course in their track suits, as did Denis Brickwood at this race. items.s: AYLESBURY YOUTHS RELAY Report of the Aylesbury Youths Relay on 7th February, where Belgrave's A team was second to Southgate Harriers by 16 seconds. This Relay was held on 7th February, and we entered four teams for this event and actually fielded three full teams. Our "A" side ran well to beat their winning time of last year, and yet were beaten by 16 seconds for first place. A. C. McLean ran the first leg and handed over in 4th place, then Gerry Lines took us up into second position. Ron Linstead did the third fastest time of the afternoon to take us into the lead, but J. B. Edgar, running in place of Frank Wright, who was down with 'flu, could not hold his opponent over the final stage. Our "B" team ran well to finish 8th, while our "C" side were placed 13th out of an entry of 28 teams, which proves how popular this form of racing is with the clubs. The winners were Southgate Harriers, who are very strong in both Youths and Juniors, and in third place were the R.A.F., Halton, boys, and their Sports Officer is none other than our own member, Eddie Short. Times of our lads were as under :— "A"—McLean, 18.33; Lines, 18.37; Linstead, 18.09; Edgar, 18.40. "B"—Hooper, 19.13; Mitchell, 18.53; Boreham, 19.06; W. Bird, 18.59. items.s: SOUTHERN R.W.A. GARNET CHAMPIONSHIP, 7th February, 1953, at Woodford Report and results of the Southern R.W.A. Garnet Championship walk at Woodford, where Belgrave's A team finished second to Essex Beagles; the text gives Burns 15th and Kemp 17th while the table gives 16th and 18th. This was held on a very cold day and on a rather hard three-lap course, with plenty of hills, but the teams really exceeded expectations. As a well-known walker reported : “We were unfancied for a scoring place,” but whatever the day or course, the lads walked extremely well. From roughly fifth place at half-way, they fought through to finish a comfortable second, the scoring lads being G. Warr 11th, B. Burns 15th, R. Kemp 17th, and G. Beecham 21st. The other lads of the two teams were always backing up, and it was a real credit to the Club to see such a fine effort from them all. Congratulations to every one of them, especially to Bobby Burns and Ron Kemp, who had travelled up from Eastleigh for this event. Percy Wright, who keeps a benevolent eye on these lads down there for the Club, must have been very pleased himself with the result. One hundred and seventeen finished. Position Name Time 1 R. H. items.s: ANNUAL BANSTEAD MATCH WITH S.W.C., 14th February, 1953, at South Croydon Report and handicap results of the annual Banstead walking match against Surrey Walking Club in snow at South Croydon, lost 148 points to 152. What a day ! Thick snow about and temperature near freezing, but 17 lads arrived at Croydon for this event. We were pleased to welcome our old friend, Jack Rutland, out again. Hope this will lead to many more. All the lads were content to take things easy to the turn, and coming home positions changed a little, but Syd James was first man home for us, followed closely by Hugh McGreechan and G. Checkley. Alan Robins, who is beginning to find his old form, won the handicap for our members ; he walked strongly the whole way and thoroughly deserved his win. We lost a very enjoyable match by a small margin of four points, scoring 12 aside, and congratulate Surrey W. Club on their win ; also they won their match with the M.P.A.A. The walk was followed by an enjoyable Social Evening at the Blue Anchor, Croydon. Many thanks, Surrey Walking Club. Match result, 12 a side—S.W.C., 148 pts.; Belgrave, 152 pts. Pos. items.s: SOUTHERN C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS Report and Belgrave placings from the Southern Cross-Country Championships at Aylesford Paper Mills, with the seniors third, juniors fifth and youths sixth as teams. These were held at the Aylesford Paper Mills on 21st February and the venue left nothing to be desired both from the competitors' and the spectators' point of view. The Youths race was first on the programme and round the lap of the starting field Frank Wright was in the lead, but once they had gone out into the country, his lack of training, due to a bout of the 'flu, revealed itself, and Frank dropped back fast on the homeward run. Even so, his position of 17th, was quite good, as also was Gerry Lines' placing of 19th, but we then dropped a bit due to the absence of Ron Linstead, who was out with leg trouble. J. B. Edgar also lost both his shoes and thus found his running impeded, but on the whole our 6th placing in the team race out of an entry of 39 teams, was quite good. In the Senior race over 10 miles there was a field of 371 starters and after the usual fast start, Gordon Pirie and Frank Sando were out on their own, with Dennis Holden also in complete isolation in third place. Jack Brown was running quite well and was only beaten by the three above mentioned, plus Jim Peters and R. P. Ll. Morgan, the S.L.H. and Oxford University runner, and Jack's time was 55.41. Then came Denis Brickwood 30th, and as Denis was placed 22nd in the 1939 race, we think it a remarkable achievement for him to drop only eight places after a lapse of 14 years, and just shows what can be done with properly applied training methods. Eddie Short and John Burr also ran quite well, and our scoring team was completed by Chas. Walker and Mick Porter. To be placed third after our team had suffered so many setbacks was indeed a good performance and we doubt that even at full strength whether we should have beaten Thames Valley H., the winners of the team title, who gave a great display of sound team running. For the first time for a very long while we were unable to field a full team of 12 men, and so lost our hold on the “ Oddling-Smee ” Cup, which was won by Herne Hill. H. In the Junior race, Ray Tooby ran well to get 5th, as owing to foot trouble, he has not been able to train as hard as Bert Shaw would have liked him to. Brian Trower was 37th, with Mike Stearman 40th, and Mike was another just getting over the 'flu, and then came Don McLean, 65. We were pleased to see Geoff Goode out once again, and he looked short of training and has also put on quite a bit of weight in the Army. Here again we managed to be placed 5th out of an entry of 37 Clubs, and to get all our teams in the first six of each race can be looked upon as a good sign of our all-round strength, but we do need a few more chaps who are willing to “ slog ” it out, as did the Footer-Penny schools in the old days. items.sum: Report and Belgrave placings from the English Cross-Country Championships at Caversham Park, Reading, where the seniors were sixth team and Jack Brown won the Harry Parker Trophy.
items.s: ENGLISH C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS Report and Belgrave placings from the English Cross-Country Championships at Caversham Park, Reading, where the seniors were sixth team and Jack Brown won the Harry Parker Trophy. These were held at Caversham Park, Reading, on 7th March, and a large crowd saw some good and exciting racing in fine weather . In the Youths' race there was an entry of 71 teams, but owing to the 2 p.m. start, which was strictly adhered to, many of the lads missed the race owing to their late arrival. Our team were all present and Frank Wright ran well to finish 8th and he beat B. G. Stone of Blackheath, who had won the Southern Youths race. We were placed 10th in the team placings, but were the 4th Southern team to finish and were only just behind Ilford A.C., the Southern champions. In the Junior race there were 68 teams entered, and our first man home was Mike Stearman, 26th, with Ray Tooby, 30th, and the latter had a bad time owing to an attack of stitch. With better support we may have been placed in the team race, but had to be content with 10th place, which, however, was an improvement on our last year's placing. The Senior race was the big event of the day and here there was an entry of 66 teams, plus 57 individual entries and a huge field faced the starter. Jack Brown was our first man home, 34th, and so won the Harry Parker Trophy, and he was closely followed by John Bromley, 39th, and John showed a welcome return to his old form once again. Denis Brickwood ran well to finish 55th, with Eddie Short 75th, and Eddie only ran in order that we should field a full team of nine men, as he has been troubled with an ankle injury. Chas. Walker was 85th and, seeing that he was running in borrowed “togs,” owing to leaving his running kit on a bus on his way to catch the Club coach at Tooting, he can be said to have run reasonably well. Eric Herbert, 87th, was our sixth scoring man, and Eric has also been troubled by injuries and has not been able to train as often as he would have wished for a race of this description. John Burr, 99th, Alan Bishop, 219th, and Len Bishop 247th, completed our team, and but for the backward position of the latter two, we should have stood a good chance of once again winning the “ Charles Otway ” Cup, which is awarded to the first club finishing its complete team, outside the three placed clubs. In fairness to the Bishop brothers we must point out that Alan only came into our team at the last moment owing to the non-arrival of Mick Porter, while Len was spiked early in the race, and this must have affected his running. We were placed 6th in the team championship and were the second Southern club to finish, and we turned the tables on Aylesford Paper Mills, who beat us in the Southern race. items.s: R.W.A. NATIONAL 10 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP, 14th March Report and Belgrave placings from the R.W.A. National 10 Miles walking championship at Cheltenham, won by R. Hardy of Sheffield, with Belgrave "A" seventh team. A coach party of 25 walkers and supporters travelled to Cheltenham for the Senior 10 miles Championship, and although both teams were unplaced, they very much appreciated the backing of those who made the journey to give them support and encouragement. Unfortunately, we were minus one or two of our top scorers owing to various reasons, which gives all the more credit to those who upheld the “ Claret and gold.” A one-lap course of 10 miles favoured the very fast men, and after getting away to a good start, Hardy, of Sheffield, stayed in the lead the whole journey, followed by his clubmate, R. Holland, with Brian Hawkins and George Coleman in close attendance. At 6½ miles, the two Georges, Oliver and Beecham, after their excellent County performances, were in 29th and 31st positions, with Hugh McGreechan 33rd, Garry Warr 38th, George Checkley 43rd, Percy Wright 44th, Harry Kemp 58th, Bob Readman 72nd, and Bernard Eglington 77th. Sheffield made no doubt about the result of the team race, but there was a keen struggle for the second and third positions between Highgate, Woodford, Cambridge Harriers and Met. W.C. At about 8 miles George Beecham had an attack of cramp and fell back considerably. He recovered again at about 9 miles and finished strongly, bettering his county time by 20 seconds. Bad luck came when Hugh McGreechan was “ pulled ” about 200 yards from the finish. The remainder of our walkers all made valiant efforts to put the team amongst the places and improved their individual positions considerably, but not quite enough. There was no lack of “ Belgrave spirit,” and to all we say, “ Well walked.” Owing to a delayed result, the party was split up on the return journey, but some of us met at the “ local ” in Stokenchurch and a merry time was had by all, to the scent of pickled onions, and the debate between “ The baron ” and “ Sir Harry ” on his next dramatic performance. items.s: ANNUAL DINNER AND DANCE Notice of the Club Annual Dinner and Dance at Strand Corner House on 21st November, with tickets at 17s. 6d. payable by instalments. The Club Annual Dinner and Dance, the great social event of the year, is to be held at STRAND CORNER HOUSE (not Coventry Street, as last year) on Saturday, November 21st. It is regretted that owing to the continual rise in catering costs, it is necessary to charge 17s. 6d. for tickets, but to encourage as many members as possible to be present, the Social Hon. Secretary, Dave Martin-Shepherd, is arranging for tickets to be paid for by instalments, with the aid of payment cards, and he hopes that you will start paying NOW. If for any reason you are unable to attend, any money you have paid will, of course, be refunded. The date of the dinner this year has been specially arranged so as not to clash too much with the London-Brighton Relay, and the payment system can also be used by those who are hoping to join the coach party for this race. The months will soon fly by, so don't waste any time. Get your payment cards and start saving NOW for these two important functions. Dave Martin-Shepherd Dave Martin-Shepherd Social Hon. In our last issue I made a special appeal for the early payment of subscriptions, and I should like to thank all those who responded so promptly. items.s: NEW CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP Announcement of a new Junior 5 miles walking championship for Tommy Green's trophy, first held on 18th April, with a prize from Syd. Roberts for a first-time walker. A few years ago Tommy Green presented to the Club a very fine trophy, which was allocated to a Junior 5 miles Walking Championship. Unfortunately, owing to the shortage of Junior walkers, it has not been possible to hold a championship race until this year. It has now been decided to hold the first race for this trophy on Saturday, 18th April, the same day as the Club 20 miles Championship. So far there are about six Club walkers eligible, i.e., under 21 years of age on 1st October, 1952. Some of our foremost walkers in the past have started as runners and we now invite any member of the Club who is eligible by age and feels he would like to swell the entry, to take part in the race. This may attract some of our young members who are not quite making the grade at cross country, and who may be potential walking champions. As an added incentive, our Hon. Treasurer, Syd. Roberts, has offered to present a prize for the first competitor to finish who has not previously competed in a walking race. Why not have a go and see what you can do ? Make a note of the date NOW : Saturday, 18th April. Tommy Green Tommy Green presented trophy for Junior 5 miles Walking Championship Syd. Roberts Syd. Roberts Hon. items.sum: Preview of Belgrave's summer 1953 track and walking fixtures in Coronation Year, naming Len Marchant as new track captain and E. A. Duffett as the contact for entries.
items.s: THE SUMMER SEASON Preview of Belgrave's summer 1953 track and walking fixtures in Coronation Year, naming Len Marchant as new track captain and E. A. Duffett as the contact for entries. This is Coronation Year, and we can expect the usual crop of additional meetings due to this fact. We have already been invited to take part in meetings on Coronation Day itself, but do not think our members would appreciate having to turn out on such a day. Our first Club meeting will be at Battersea Park, on Saturday, 2nd May, and the Surrey County 7-mile track walk will be included in the programme. On Wednesday, 6th May, we visit Paddington Track for a match with Queens Park Harriers ; start at 6.30 p.m. Then on 9th May, at Battersea Park, will be held the Surrey County Youths Track Championships, with the 6 miles run and Pentathlon also at this meeting. 16th May, at the new Wimbledon Park Track, is the date fixed for the Brockman Trophy meeting, and on the same day we are holding our open 20-mile road run from Belgrave Hall, start at 3 p.m., and we are hoping for a good entry. On Monday, 18th May, we have a Club meeting at Tooting Bec, and have a Senior and Junior match against the Polytechnic H. and South London H. ; start at 7 p.m. Whitsun Saturday and Monday we see the C.A.U. and British Games meeting at the White City, and there are also the usual number of “ open ” meetings on this day. 30th May is the day fixed for the Surrey County Senior Track Championships at Motspur Park, with the Junior and Youth Relays, also the Junior Hammer Throw. On the same day we have accepted an invitation to compete in a Coronation Sports meeting at Aylesbury, with the usual generous six prizes in each event given by the Hazells Club. 6th June sees more County Championships, also a glut of Coronation meetings, and we have promised to support a meeting at the newly-opened track at Carshalton, and also to visit Walton A.C., at the Stompond Lane ground for an inter-club match. On Wednesday, 10th June we have a Club meeting at Battersea Park, start at 7 p.m., and hope to put on our annual Schools Relay at this meeting. Saturday, 13th June, is “ Kinnaird ” Trophy day, with our Club marathon championship being decided in conjunction with the Poly. race from Windsor to Chiswick. Tuesday, 16th June, we have a match with Sutton and Cheam H., at the Sutton Stadium, and this is in the nature of a “ B ” team fixture. 17th June is the date of the L.A.C. Inter-Club Relay meeting at the White City, and it is to be hoped that our members will give full support to the various events. Saturday, 20th June, is the day of the Southern Senior Track Championships, due to be held at the White City, and owing to the past large entries it may be necessary to introduce some qualifying conditions for this year's meeting. Wednesday, 24th June, we have another Club meeting at Tooting Bec Track, start at 7 p.m., and if it is decided to include any handicap events we trust they will be better supported than in the past by our members. 27th June is the day of the Surrey County Junior Track Championships at Wimbledon Park, and the Senior relays will also be held at this meeting. Also on this day there are “ open ” meetings at Weybridge and Broomfield Park, Southgate, which should attract good support. Wednesday, 1st July, we have a match at Victoria Park against the local club and the United Hospitals A.C. On Saturday, 4th July, we have the “ Heathfield ” Trophy meeting at Stompond Lane, Walton-on-Thames, and we are the joint holders of this trophy. Also on this day will be held the Southern Area Junior Championships, the venue for which has not yet been decided upon. Wednesday, 8th July, is the date fixed for our open Inter-Club Walking Competition at Battersea Park Track, where the accent is on competing for one's club, with no awards given. 10th-11th July we have the A.A.A. General Championships at the White City and tickets for the Club stands will be available from Frank Webb, as in past years. On 18th July there is the “ Waddilove ” Trophy meeting at Birmingham and we have also promised to send a team to Guildford on the same day, which should give a chance to all our members. Wednesday, 22nd July, we have a Club meeting at Tooting Bec Track, and hope to include some members' handicap events on the programme. The A.A.A. Junior Championships, also the Marathon and Relay Championships are due to be held on 25th July at Maindy Park, Cardiff, and the question of fares will come into what support our members can give this meeting. Saturday, 1st August, is Club Championship day at Battersea Park. See summer fixture card for list of events, and we hope our members will support the various events, for which standard medals are awarded. August Monday we have the “ Hazell ” Trophy meeting at Aylesbury and, seeing that our members did so well last year, I am sure that we shall not lack support for this fixture. Wednesday, 5th August, we have a Senior and Junior match at Charlton Park Track against Cambridge Harriers, and although this is the holiday season, we hope our members will endeavour to turn up for these matches. Monday, 10th August, we have a Club meeting at Tooting Bec Track, and as the evenings are drawing in at this time of the year, we shall only have a small number of events at this meeting. Saturday, 15th August, we visit Alperton for a match against Thames Valley H. and Mitcham A.C., and our Committee have agreed to the “ Doris ” Shield being put up for competition once again. There will also be a Junior match at the same meeting and as we have several members in this area this should give them a chance to represent the Club. 22nd August is the date of our final Club meeting, due to take place at Battersea Park Track, and we have arranged a Senior and Junior match with Cambridge Harriers, and it is likely that the Club 3 miles track championship will be decided at this meeting. On Saturday, 5th September, we visit Imber Court for a match against the Metropolitan Police A.C., and this will more or less wind up the track season, except for the evening floodlit meetings at the White City and the L.C.C. Championship finals, which are due to be held at Battersea Park on 12th September. We have a new track captain in Len Marchant, who most of our members will remember as a half-miler of near international class and, together with vice-captain, Dicky Bartlett, they will do their best to make sure that every member is given a chance to show what he can do. It is to be hoped that members will avail themselves of the opportunities offered them by the Club, and if any new member is in any doubt as to the method of approach, I shall be only too pleased to advise him in this direction. All entries for Club events should be sent to me at least ten days in advance of the meeting date. A card will do, and any handicap fees can be paid on the day of the meeting. Any enquiries can be sent to : E. A. Duffett, 57, Harcourt Road, Thornton Heath. Frank Webb Frank Webb Club stand tickets for A.A.A. e: Portsmouth A.C. open 5 miles road handicap
items.s: HERE AND THERE Club news notes on members' successes in other races, National Service postings, rugby, committee elections and club comings and goings. Archie Bedford was first home in the British Workers' 5 miles c.c. championship, with Ron Mitchell in second place. John Burr won the L.B.H. Novices c.c. race, and Eric Bishop was second in the Inter-Banks Junior event. Brian Trower finished third in the Portsmouth A.C. open 5 miles road handicap race, with a start of 3 min. 10 secs., and has also been running with the R.A.F., Sopley. E. T. Paterson is another doing his National Service training and has been running for the R.A.F., Yatesbury, team. Another member to do well in R.A.F. events is P. N. G. Gilbert, and he captured the course record at Hednesford and also broke the R.A.F., Padgate, record. He has also twice run second to Sgt. McMinnis, the R.A.F. champion, and as he is still a junior, he should do well in future events. P. J. Rossiter is now in the R.A.F J. Hills finished second in the R.A.S.C. c.c. championship, but has now been posted to the Middle East. R. D. Knights also writes to say that he has been posted overseas with the R.E.M.E., and sends best wishes to Alf Taylor and S. Jefferson. Geoff Goode is now with the Royal Signals at Catterick, and ran in the Northern Command championships and finished 8th, and as K. L. Norris, of T.V.H., was 4th, it was evidently quite a hot field. Brian Rice, who is at Cambridge University, was reserve in the 4 x 880 for the Inter-Varsity Relays in December last, and Alan Sexton ran for Cambridge in the 4 x 110 yds., 4 x 220 yds., and the 4 x 440 yds., and led his team to victory in the latter event. A. J. Snoad was sixth in the London University c.c. race, and it is a pity that studies have prevented him from turning out for the Club, but he hopes to remedy this for next season. P. R. Bagnall was first home in an Inter-College race when running for S. Mark & S. John, and he beat several well-known runners, and should be an asset to our teams on the road and over the country. Congratulations to George Oliver on winning the Civil Service Road Walking championship, and he beat R. Carpenter, the holder, with A. H. Cotton, the Olympic walker, in third place. Syd James was second in the L.B.H. 7 miles road walk at Wembley Park, with Harry Churcher, the holder, a non-starter. We were pleased to see that B. C. Michez and M. A. Phillips, two of our youngsters from the Raynes Park County School, were selected to represent Surrey Schools XV. While on the subject of Rugby, we see that Basil Walden and D. R. Childs are playing for the very successful Streatham R.F.C., and J. Powell-Jones has now joined this club, while Alan Sexton recently turned out for his Old Boys' side There is a rumour that L. N. Bailey, the Streatham club's full-back and Surrey County player, is going to join the Club, as he wishes to go in for half-miling on the track. We send our best wishes to Vernon Blowfield, who, now that he has permanently moved down to Oxford, has resigned from the Club, and has joined the local Oxford City A.C., of which club Derrick Burfitt is also a member. items.sum: Editorial announcing the Jimmy Belchamber Memorial Trophy and the Frank Thomson Cup, bringing the club's trophies to about 35.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial announcing the Jimmy Belchamber Memorial Trophy and the Frank Thomson Cup, bringing the club's trophies to about 35. Dear Fellow Belgravians, The " Jimmy Belchamber Memorial Trophy " Fund has now been closed, and a fitting trophy to perpetuate the memory of Jimmy will shortly be purchased and awarded for an event to be decided by the Committee. At the same time we place on record our gratefulness to Mrs. Smith, daughter of the late Frank Thomson for the presentation of a very beautiful cup, which will keep Frank's name for ever connected with the Club he so ably and unselfishly served, and which will also be awarded for an event to be decided by the Committee. With the addition of these two trophies our total of Club Cups and Shields will be brought up to the splendid total of some 35, and now cover every event in our curriculum of Athletics. It should be noted by all members, especially the newer members, that these trophies bear the names of illustrious Belgravians, some of them happily still with us and, we hope, for many years to come. We ask you, when admiring your trophies, to give a moment of thought to the donors who are still with us, and a reverent thought for those who have passed from us. These gentlemen and their colleagues of yore are those who pioneered so steadfastly to give you the Belgrave Club, to which you must surely be proud to be a member. The inscription on The Frank Thomson Cup reads : " Life Member for 60 years.—President, 1940-1942.—Presented as a token of life-long service to Athletics." It is truly so, and let it be an incentive to you—you for whom he did so much, many of whom he never knew. Let it never be said you knew not of him or his contemporaries or of what they did. YOUR EDITORS.
