items.s: CLUB 10 MILES C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP (MACHER SHIELD) JAN.25TH Report and result of the club 10 miles cross country championship for the Macher Shield, won by Charlie Walker, with Bob Plummer taking the handicap. This year's race,held on a cold damp day, ran true to form with Charlie Walker, who always performs so well over our own courses, the winner by the comfortable margin of 47 seconds. Dave Baulch took second place, 53 seconds ahead of Eric Gebbett who had earlier in the season won the seven miles championship. This was the order which had been maintained almost throughout the race and the fact that, for the second year, the course was inadvertently shortened by missing out the lap of the starting field in the middle of the race, obviously made no difference to the result. The back markers in the handicap could well complain, for if the full distance had been covered there is little doubt that Walker and Moore would have been among the prizes. John Moore (the second), in his first season with us, has made his mark upon us and will soon be taking a leading place in our races and should bolster up our teams both on track and country. His fourth place in this event was well earned, for he has been a keen performer since he joined us. Archie Bedford returned for one of his rare visits and, by finishing fifth, proved he still has the capacity to gain a place in our first teams. Eddie Short ran well to take sixth place and that "little potterer" Joe Dooley followed close on his heels with Jim Heathfield, only a few yards behind. Bob Plummer, better known for his exploits over the marathon distance, took advantage of the handicapper's generosity to win the handicap by a good margin. Another long marker, Reg Bolem, took second place and John Hilton, a newcomer, made good use of his 9½ mins. start to secure third place. 1 C.W. Walker 52.57 2 D. Baulch 53.44 3 E. Gebbett 54.37 4 J. items.sum: Report and result of the South of the Thames senior cross country championship held from Belgrave Hall, won by Blackheath Harriers, with Belgrave 9th and George Flanagan 13th.
e: South of the Thames Senior Cross Country Championship
items.s: SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP FEB.1ST Report and result of the South of the Thames senior cross country championship held from Belgrave Hall, won by Blackheath Harriers, with Belgrave 9th and George Flanagan 13th. This race was held from Belgrave Hall in honour of Les Cohen who this year is President of the South of the Thames Cross Country Association. He must have been proud of the efficient manner in which this event was organised and our thanks go out to Arthur Whitehead who took all the responsibility for course marking and the provision of starting and finishing pens upon his experienced shoulders. The number of barring clauses in this event precluded the fielding of our strongest team, but on paper our lads, with a mixture of experience and youthful exuberance, appeared to have a chance of a place. Unfortunately we were again to be disappointed as we could finish no better than 9th in the team race with the mammoth score of 461 pts. George Flanagan was the only one of our runners who excelled himself and he should be pleased with thirteenth position. John Moore, by finishing 52nd, gained good experience in a large field and Robin Weate, in his first year with us, showed that he is possessed of more than his fair share of pluck to finish 88th. Robin, still a junior, always gives of his best and is a great asset to us - with regular and correct training he should follow in the footsteps of that courageous little man, Bert Footer, who did so much for Belgrave in the years preceding the last war. Bob Glover, also in his first season, improves with every outing and in finishing 111th can be said to have performed well and should benefit from this experience. Ken Jones, running in the colours of the Metropolitan Police A.C. ran very well to take 33rd place and will be a tower of strength in these races when we have his services. items.h: SOUTHERN COUNTIES SENIOR C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP at Parliament Hill Feb.15th
items.sum: Report and result of the Southern Counties senior cross country championship at Parliament Hill, won by South London Harriers, with Belgrave a disappointing 9th, plus notes on the Southern youths and junior races where George Flanagan was 5th.
e: Southern Counties Senior Cross Country Championship
items.s: SOUTHERN COUNTIES SENIOR C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP at Parliament Hill Feb.15th Report and result of the Southern Counties senior cross country championship at Parliament Hill, won by South London Harriers, with Belgrave a disappointing 9th, plus notes on the Southern youths and junior races where George Flanagan was 5th. A return to the course over which the National was held last year saw one of the biggest fields ever set off on the long trek of nine miles over hilly grassland with a fair proportion of mud and slush. Toward the end of the first of the three laps Eric Gebbett was our first scorer way back in 49th place followed closely by Charlie Walker 55th. Then followed a string of runners before we again saw a Belgrave vest filled by Eddie Short who had John Moore and Jumbo Masters close on his heels, all of them in the 130's. Pete Hitchcock, Clive Shippen and Len Bishop were next, in the 170's while the rest of our men were back in the 200's. The next view of the field was soon after the first lap had ended, and Walker had moved up to Gebbett and Short and Moore had also progressed about fifteen places and were running well. Masters was making very heavy weather of it and was slipping back steadily, Hitchcock and Shippen were 152nd and 167th respectively with Len Bishop and D.Baulch in close attendance. At the conclusion of the second lap Walker had left Gebbett and was now 44th but was having great difficulty in making any further progress. Although Gebbett was slipping back gradually, Short and Moore were still making up ground and were now 103rd and 104th. Our other men however, were making little or no improvement with the exception of J.Dooley who had started very slowly and was now beginning his late excursion through the field. On the last lap Moore made up another ten places and Hitchcock put in a good run to move up nearly thirty places. Dooley seemed to enjoy himself at this stage and must have passed about fifty runners in the last three miles. The others seemed to have got themselves well bogged down. The final count gave us ninth place with the astronomical score of 591 points, which must have been our lowest place and highest score for a good many years. The impression one gets from this fiasco is that most if not all of our runners are short of the type of training needed to keep pace with the leading performers. On examining the final positions one cannot fail to notice how many athletes, possessed of far less ability than our lads, finished well up the field and assisted their clubs to secure good places - the moral is obvious. Result :- Individuals :- Also held at Parliament Hill on the same day were the Southern Youths and Junior championships. Our juniors ran very well to finish fourth in the team race. An outstanding performance was that of George Flanagan in being placed fifth, a performance which qualifies him for a Junior Honours Badge. Another good run was that of Robin Weate who was 21st. In the youths race Belgrave were 10th.The only other news we have is that C.Thompson was 26th and J.Thresher 48th. 1st South London Harriers 136 pts. 2nd Thames Valley Harriers 142 " 3rd Woodford Green A.C. 206 " 9th Belgrave Harriers 591 " 47 C.W. items.s: COUNTY 10 MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIPS - FEB.22ND. Report on the county 10 miles walking championships: Eric Hall won Surrey with Belgrave taking the team race, the Club (as Cadogan A.C.) was second team in Middlesex, and Stan Vickers won Kent for the third year running. The splendid performances of our walkers in county championships gives every promise of Belgrave repeating last year's record of winning all three major R.W.A. titles. Again those two great ambassadors of the sport, Eric Hall and Stan Vickers, retained their titles in a convincing manner. A feat probably never equalled by any other club was that of ten Belgrave walkers gaining their county colours. Surrey at Walton-on-Thames. A splendid race was won in immaculate style by Eric Hall who was just over one minute ahead of Dave McMullen.Then followed three other Belgravians which meant that the team race was won with the minimum score of ten points. It is interesting to note that our"B" team finished in third position which gives a startling indication of Club strength. 1st Belgrave "A" 10 pts. 2nd Surrey W.C."A" 39 pts. 3rd Belgrave"B" Middlesex at Enfield A full team plus two individuals, as Cadogan A.C., represented the Club, and right well the performed to finish second team to Metropolitan Walking Club, beating Highgate, Polytechnic and many other fancied clubs in the process. A particularly fine effort was that of Ted Smith in finishing fourth and George Checkley sixth. Kent at Hayes This might be described as Stan Vickers benefit, which he won for the third year in succession (not running!), walking completely on his own, with the ease and style which have become the standards whereby all others are judged. items.s: MATCH v. FINCHLEY H. & ORPINGTON A.C. FEB.22ND at Wimbledon Report of a 7½ mile cross-country match at Wimbledon which Belgrave won with 46 points despite moved marking flags sending Clive Shippen off course. About forty runners faced the starter for a race of 7½ miles in which there was a great preponderance of Belgrave Harriers including a number of old stalwarts. At the end of the first lap Clive Shippen was leading with Moore and Short well in attendance. A quick check showed that we were well in the lead and should have no difficulty in holding our position. Unfortunately a number of small boys on the Common thought otherwise and on the second lap the marking flags were found to have been moved with the result that Clive Shippen went well off course and was left with too much ground to make up to regain his early lead. John Moore and Eddie Short soon discovered their mistake and all was well once more but the whole character of the race had been changed. Nevertheless we gained a comfortable win, scoring seven a side, with 46 points against 82 by Finchley and 103 by Orpington. items.sum: Report of the Gosport Open Seven Miles Walk, won by Eric Hall by 14 seconds with Belgrave taking the team award, followed by an account of a Sunday stroll from Croydon the next morning.
items.s: GOSPORT OPEN SEVEN MILES WALK.MARCH 1ST Report of the Gosport Open Seven Miles Walk, won by Eric Hall by 14 seconds with Belgrave taking the team award, followed by an account of a Sunday stroll from Croydon the next morning. We sent a small team down for this new venture, and after a rough sea crossing we were not quite so sure we should have bothered. After being "Security Cleared" we changed in a barracks, no autograph hunters were allowed just in case we looked like volunteers. The course itself was flat and Stan Vickers soon showed the way, followed by a large of local lads. Soon the pace began to tell and at two miles Eric Hall had moved through and was breathing very heavily down Stan's neck with Norman Read just behind. Nick Milsum had a bad time, but fought back well to regain lost ground near the finish. At four miles Eric moved away and Stan fell back to third, but not for long however, as over the last mile he closed right up again and Eric just got home by 14 seconds. Ray Hall had a great fight all the way and used bluff to finish 8th. Terry Clark was always handy and he was followed by Joe Coleman who took first veteran's prize. Nick Milsum was third in the handicap and of course we won the team award - a very successful pot hunt. Harry Shields made his mark by leading others astray on the pretext of having tea - result - we had four minutes to swim 200 yards, sprint half a mile and jump six feet. It was a good job we were fit or we'd have missed that train. 1st Belgrave H. 16 pts. 2nd Trowbridge 55 " 3rd Gosport 69 " The following morning six of the above considered themselves fit enough to go strolling. At precisely 0936 we left Croydon led by Harry Shields (shortly to explore Birkenhead) and a steady pace was maintained for six or seven miles by which time we were above the snow line. The leading bunch must have had skis, as they moved away very fast, led by "Sherpa" Clark, followed by Stan and Nick Milsum. The inevitable happened, and when Harry took a sun shot we found that the intrepid trio were hell bent for somewhere about a mile off course. Much signalling resulted and they eventually rejoined the main group in time to buy refreshments. Stan was by now sporting Club colours - he was looking alternately purple and yellow! We ascended the south Col of the downs shortly after this and made good progress to our next camp, where we waited for one straggler, who must remain nameless, then after dropping Terry Clark and Stan, the survivors pushed on over Hayes Common where Harry deviated too much to the right and was lost without trace. The two Halls were left to complete this epic, incident packed march on their own No matter what you have done on the previous day, a Sunday stroll with the Boys is the best tonic you can have. A. items.s: BELGRAVE OPEN FIELD EVENTS MEETING. MARCH 1ST Report of the club's second winter open field events meeting, with 82 individual entrants, noting the discus second place of D[illegible]szo Audorka and thanking the officials. Our second Winter Meeting was better supported than last year and even more successful. There was an entry of 82 individuals and an event entry of 128. This included some of the best performers in the country and a contingent from Cambridge University. The day was not an ideal one perhaps, but after the snowy weather in the early part of the week we were lucky indeed to be able to carry the meeting through. The javelin, perhaps, suffered most from the conditions and we really must try and persuade the L.C.C. to put down a cinder approach. Better support could have come from our own members, although we were represented in all the events except the Shot. It was pleasing to see two of our javelin throwers getting in the first six despite this being our weakest event. Bill Couzens was disappointing, especially after his good performance in the T.V.H. meeting.He is really still a novice as far as the javelin is concerned but is showing promise and must improve during the summer. Our best performer was undoubtedly D[illegible]szo Audorka with a fine throw in the discus for second place after a neck and neck battle with the winner who only widened the margin between them to four feet with his last throw. We hope to see him doing some 160's or more in the summer. Our thanks are due to the Surrey County Judges, Messrs. Reed, Fairfoul and Reeve and to Mr.E.F.Housden, the old pole vault Champion, for their assistance, together with the Club members who came along and particularly to Dick Savage who acted as Referee. items.s: NATIONAL C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS. BIRKENHEAD MARCH 8TH Report of the National cross-country championships at Birkenhead covering Belgrave's youths (12th team), seniors (15th team, Pat Newell 39th) and juniors (16th team). An unusually small band of runners and officials availed themselves of the special transport put on by British Railways for this the premier cross country event of the year. Event one, the youths race over 3 miles started in bright sunshine, most unexpected after the violent snow showers which greeted our arrival.In a large field, Arthur Penny's youngsters performed quite creditably, our first man home being Thresher in 77th place.Having partaken in a schools race the day before, Eric Penny can be said to have run well to finish 127th. Other positions:- C. Thompson 105 T. Hart 108 D. Crooks 124 Team result :- Belgrave H. 12th,414 pts. 53 teams closed in. The senior event, always a race to stir a feeling of awe in the spectator, was soon seen to be an S.L.H. "benefit", for they had three men in six at one stage. What is it about men like Firth, Driver, Pirie and company which enables them always to strike the front within half a mile or so? Pat Newell, running in his first cross country race this season, clung tenaciously to a good start and was always placed around the forty mark. He eventually finished 39th, ahead of international Harry Hicks and many other performers of high rank. Next man was Charlie Walker, 77th, an improvement on recent form, with ever consistant Eric Gebbett 134th. A special mention must be made of Clive Shippen who has been short of training. He put in as much work as possible between the Southern and this race and reaped the benefits. To finish 175th in this field was no mean performance. The rest of our men finished outside the two-hundreds. In the team race we were 15th and the only consolation that can be got from this is that Birchfield were 16th - how are the mighty fallen! Positions :- 39, P.Newell 77, C.W.Walker 134, E.Gebbett 175, C.Shippen 200, P.Hitchcock 264, D.Baulch 288, J.Dooley 307, E.Short 319, L.C.Bishop The junior race saw a new Frank Aaron in the northern youngster Alan Cocking. To establish a lead of almost 200 yds by two miles and then coast home from a good class field was a meritorious performance. George Flanagan seemed unable to get going. One had the impression that his long-striding action was out of place on this type of going; he faded to 52nd. Whilst Geoff Stevens 118th, and K.Miller 1[illegible]6th improved on their Southern running our other lads found the pace too hot. No one was disgraced, however, and in them we have some good material for the future. Other positions :- C.Dabbs 115 R.Weate 142 R.Braine 208 Team position :- 16th The return journey was a little boisterous, but lets remember that we were all young once. items.sum: The cross country secretary laments the club's worst cross-country season since the war, urging harder concerted training, support for club matches and replies to his communications.
items.s: CROSS COUNTRY SECRETARY'S NOTES The cross country secretary laments the club's worst cross-country season since the war, urging harder concerted training, support for club matches and replies to his communications. We have reached the end of another cross country season and I regret that I can raise little or no enthusiasm for our performances. When the results of the major championships are considered it has been our worst year since the war and probably our worst since the early 1930's. Take a look at the following. South of Thames Junior 7th Surrey County 4th South of Thames Senior 9th Southern Counties 9th National 15th I realise that many clubs would be only too pleased to have such a record but it should be remembered that we have one of the largest memberships in the country and should therefore produce a higher standard in our teams. I am convinced that the talent is with us but the spirit to succeed is missing so far as cross country races are concerned. The whole atmosphere changes, however, when the road relay races start. Why can't we carry the enthusiasm shown on the Brighton road into the harder grind of the mud baths. It was a great joy to see us go from 18th to 2nd in the Southern Brighton relay last October; this proves that we have first class performers. This type of performance, however, is not repeated in the large fields of the major cross country races against the very same opposition. Why is this??? I feel that we are neglecting the well balanced training that is necessary to attain the fitness required for good cross country running. Two or three outings each week is not enough - daily training is essential, with a basic amount of really hard work combined with as much speed work as possible. We have all seen the Piries and Drivers at work at Tooting and know that such methods succeed; their followers too, benefiting similarly, even though missing the same limelight, but nevertheless becoming fit enough to bring their clubs into good positions in open races. These lads are no different to any of our members; they are all flesh and blood with the thrill of athletics in their bodies.Perhaps we fail because the concerted training runs in large packs at least three times a week no longer take place. Individual training on Saturday mornings is not necessary - we must all get together and use our efforts for the benefit of our fellow members and the Club as a whole. I am firmly of the opinion that it is quite wrong for an athlete to train continuously for months on end without an occasional race to test his ability. Our Club matches, for the past few years, have been very poorly supported, especially those away from Wimbledon. In our heyday everyone turned out, and it was not necessary for the Secretary to have to remind members to turn up, the fixture card alone was sufficient to guarantee at least thirty runners at every match. These races are planned to fit in with the advance of fitness throughout the winter season and from my own experience they can be very helpful in assessing ones progress. So many of our members fight shy of races on the score that their performances in the championships will suffer but just look at these performances and you can see that this contention is far from justified.I hope we shall all give our training considerable thought in the Summer months with a view to a considerable improvement next Winter. Now I feel that I must attack those members who habitually ignore all the communications I send out. Do they realise the hours spent in writing cards and letters for their benefit and also the cost to the Club for stationery and postage? I have been disgusted with the ignorance shown by many members in taking no notice whatsoever of my cards, especially those regarding the Ilford and Bexley road relays. In the former event we failed to finish a "B" team through the absence of a number of members who failed to give me sufficient notification of their inability to attend. At Bexley we finished only one complete team out of three just because the following failed to write or phone me despite sufficient warning :- R.Linstead, S.Charlton, S.Boreham, G.Lines, D.Manning and R.Braine. In consequence those members who ran in incomplete teams turned out with no object but to finish the course, and spent money on fares unnecessarily. In addition the Club spent 10/- per team on entrance fees. I can only hope that the people concerned have sufficient conscience to avoid a recurrence. Out of this season come a few bright prospects. In John Moore, Ken Jones and Robin Weate we have a acquired runners of high quality and Club Spirit and the improvement of George Flanagan, Peter Hitchcock, Clive Shippen and Bob Glover promises well for the future. It is around these boys that our future teams will be built, plus the experience of those diehards who go on for ever. The foregoing remarks may seem rather direct and caustic but they are intended for the good of the Club and I hope you will all take them in the right spirit. It is my ambition that Belgrave should again rise to the top of the cross country world and I want everyone to analyse their approach to Club matters and resolve to do everything in their power to bring the "Claret and Gold" to the fore for many years to come. items.sum: Report of the R.W.A. 10 miles championship at Victoria Park, Hackney, where Belgrave's Stan Vickers and Eric Hall were the first two home.
items.s: R.W.A. 10 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP MARCH 15TH Report of the R.W.A. 10 miles championship at Victoria Park, Hackney, where Belgrave's Stan Vickers and Eric Hall were the first two home. We were strongly represented in this race, held at Victoria Park, Hackney on March 15th, fielding three teams - a goodly proportion of the 227 starters. Moreover most of our men reported fit and well, although we should have liked to have seen Bob Newson, Syd James and Roy Switzer in the field. The course consisted of five laps of approximately two miles each on level roads within the park and as expected the pace was fast and furious, and many had cause to regret their earlier speed work as they neared the end of the race. Our Stan Vickers, the Championship holder, started at a tremendous pace and at one mile had a lead of about thirty yards over a small group consisting of Eric Hall, Matthews (Sutton Coldfield) and Norman Read(Steyning), the Olympic 50 kms. Champion. At three miles Stan's lead had been reduced by Eric and Matthews, whilst Read had fallen back slightly and already there were some huge intervals between walkers. Gradually Hall and Matthews overhauled Vickers and this trio were together for quite a while, each having his nose in front momentarily. As the last lap was approached Matthews showed signs of his earlier efforts and faded out somewhat, eventually to finish sixth. Our Stan and Eric continued together, lapping numerous competitors in their progress. This passing of other walkers who had been lapped nearly proved Eric's undoing for as our two passed a group of three walkers, one on each side, one of these walkers stepped to one side (presumably to allow the faster men through) but only succeeded in knocking Eric off balance and out of rhythm - and this with less than half a mile to go. But for this the race would have been even closer for the individual title. However, we were delighted to have the first two home, repeating last year's effort. Well done, Stan and Eric! Meanwhile, what of our other team men? Dave McMullen walked a very even race indeed and was always in the first twenty. His 17th position at the finish was one of the soundest pieces of team work he has given us, and they have been many. He was in our winning team in 1947 and it says much for his efforts that he can again score all these years later. We hope to see him emulate some of his Father's performances over 20 miles in the near future. Ted Smith and George Checkley found the start a very fast one indeed and early on they seemed well back, but towards the finish they were gaining many places and claiming their rightful positions. Ray Hall did well on a course that was never to his liking and we look forward to a first class "20" from him soon. The nature of the course and the speed at which the race was walked, combined with very cold conditions towards the end, gave rise to many disqualifications. We lost Nick Milsum and Terry Clark of our first team men, but their turn will come. Nick was particularly unfortunate for he was our fourth man, on the last lap and, in the view of many, walking splendidly as he came through the field. Of our others Ray Middleton, D.J.Stevens and J.Keown show promise for the future and allin all we were well satisfied that all our walkers of A, B and C teams carried the Club colours with great credit on this difficult day. Naturally we were proud indeed to retain our hold on the London Shield and to have the first two men home. They were also first and second in the Inter Counties Race, and Eric Hall, Dave McMullen and Ray Hall were in the Surrey team which was placed third. items.sum: Vice-President Frederick Mark Stone ("Rodney"), decorated Metropolitan Police officer and 1920s club walker, was the subject of the B.B.C. television programme This Is Your Life on March 3rd.
items.s: "THIS IS YOUR LIFE" Vice-President Frederick Mark Stone ("Rodney"), decorated Metropolitan Police officer and 1920s club walker, was the subject of the B.B.C. television programme This Is Your Life on March 3rd. On March 3rd, a popular Belgravian Vice-President, Frederick Mark Stone ("Rodney"), found himself the centre figure of the well established B.B.C. television programme. Rather unwillingly he was persuaded to leave the audience for the platform by Eamonn Andrews, when Paul Bennett V.C., Mrs. Stone, Fred's two sons and many former colleagues and friends from all stations of life (including our own Past President, Harry Evans) outlined those assets of character, courage and sportsmanship which have endeared him to such a wide circle. The programme culminated in the presentation of a testimonial cheque by the Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, Sir John Nott-Bower on behalf of the members of that great body to "our Rodney", who has been well described as the "bravest Metropolitan Policeman ever". Mention was made during the programme of his winning of the Kings' Police Medal for Bravery in jumping from Westminster Bridge to save life, of the award of the Royal Humane Society Medal for life saving, of supreme courage during an air raid which brought the award of the British Empire Medal, and of his success in preventing a smash and grab raid (when on sick leave and in plain clothes) which resulted in Fred being beaten over the head with an iron bar - but his man did not get away! His courage and devotion to duty gained recognition when he received the George Medal from the hands of Her Majesty the Queen - but his severe injuries unfortunately resulted in his discharge from the Police. Fred was in many of our long distance walking teams in the early 1920's and was a great worker for the Club always, and it was pleasing to see such a combination of many virtues (and many could only be lightly touched upon) on television, exemplifying a life - with many more years yet to run, we trust - which could well serve as a model for the younger man of service, courage and personality. items.s: PORTRAIT GALLERY Profile of Bill Lucas, the club's cross country secretary, a 1948 Olympic 5000 metres runner and Tommy Green Trophy winner who never won a club championship. What stranger than to have represented Great Britain in the Olympic Games, gained international vests for track running and yet be denied a single Club Championship during a distinguished career lasting almost twenty years? Such is the case of Bill Lucas our present cross country secretary. Unlike some stars, who shot into their orbit from the blue, but who faded into obscurity with equal rapidity, Bill progressed steadily in the post war years, representing the Club on every possible occasion and proved that good track running is not adversely affected by cross country racing. 1946 saw Bill win the South of the Thames Junior C.C. race at Cheam and the following January he gained his County vest by finishing fourth in the Surrey C.C. Championship. He also finished well up in the South of the Thames Senior race and in the same year finished second in the Surrey 3 miles track race. Although not listed amongst the probables for the 1948 Olympic Games, Bill sprang a surprise by gaining third place in the A.A.A. 3 miles and earned selection for the 5000 metres in the Games, where he ran well, probably the best of our representatives. Two international races were to come for Bill, when in 1950 he finished second in the 5000 metres in a triangular match at the White City, and at the same venue, versus U.S.A. and Benelux Countries, was third in an event of the same distance won by Ashenfelter of U.S.A. For his great three mile time of 14m.11.6s. in the A.A.A. Championships of the same year Bill received the coveted Tommy Green Trophy for the best performance of the year by a Belgravian. Bill's record in the London to Brighton relay is second to none; he was consistently in the team from 1947 to 1954. Possibly his best performance was in giving Max Jones of Birchfield 31 secs. start on the last stage in 1948 and finishing twenty yards in front of him to give us a great win. On four occasions Bill had the honour of handing the baton to the Mayor of Brighton after finishing first on the last stage of this classic relay race. Although he took a long time to prove he meant it, Bill retired in 1955, only to increase his Club activities even moreso in official capacities. Rather outspoken, but that is what is needed in our Club, Bill has earned the respect of all Belgravians for good work. Perhaps the greatest tribute one can pay him is that he moves with the times and recognises today's runners for what they are worth, one never hears him make unfavourable comparisons between present and past and few know of his distinguished war career when he was decorated for service with the R.A.F. items.sum: Report and full result of the club 5½ miles road race, the last trial for the London to Brighton relay team, won by Dave Baulch from Eric Gebbett.
items.s: CLUB 5½ MILES ROAD RACE. MARCH 29TH Report and full result of the club 5½ miles road race, the last trial for the London to Brighton relay team, won by Dave Baulch from Eric Gebbett. In perfect conditions a field of thirty-four was started on its way by Past President Tom Morrell. This race is the last chance for London to Brighton relay aspirants to prove their worthiness of being included in the team for this classic race. As a consequence the selectors are given more than a few headaches - this year being no exception. Eric Gebbett was, as usual, quickly in the lead and he, together with Charlie Walker and Dave Baulch, took the field along at a very brisk pace. After about two miles these three became detached from the rest of the struggling mass and it was soon obvious that the winner could only be one of this trio. With about a mile and a half to go, Charlie had a lead of fifty yards and it seemed all over bar the shouting. However, the stiff climb up Pepys Road slowed him down to such an extent that he was quickly passed by his two opponents, Baulch and Gebbett, who went on to finish first and second respectively. The winning time was the third fastest ever accomplished and Dave must be congratulated on a very fine performance. Eric, in beating 29 minutes, can also be said to have run exceptionally well. Another to show much improved form was Clive Shippen. Perhaps the most meritorious performance was that of Charlie Smart, now forty eight years of age, in returning the splendid time of 30.26. But for a mishap with his glasses, which he dropped while cleaning them, his time would have been considerably faster. Congratulations Charlie and may you continue for many more years! items.h: CARSHALTON CORONATION TROPHY MEETING. EASTER MONDAY
items.sum: Report of the Carshalton Coronation Trophy Meeting where Belgrave finished third behind T.V.H. and Mitcham and were presented with a plaque for three successive wins.
items.s: CARSHALTON CORONATION TROPHY MEETING. EASTER MONDAY Report of the Carshalton Coronation Trophy Meeting where Belgrave finished third behind T.V.H. and Mitcham and were presented with a plaque for three successive wins. Held on a cold, blustery afternoon, this event which we have won on three previous occasions, saw us finish third to T.V.H., who fielded almost an international team. We were beaten by Mitcham for second place by one point, a creditable performance considering our sadly depleted field events representation. Charlie Jones was our highest points scorer, finishing 2nd in the 220 yds. to Segal, who won in the fast time of 22.1 s. He also provided our only win of the day by cleverly taking the 440 yds. in 53.2s. Clive Shippen clocked 9m.47.2s., his fastest, in the two miles to enable us to secure third team place. D.Ansell showed good early season form in the long jump, with four jumps over 20 ft; his best, 20'6½" gained him second place. Special mention must be made of S.Boreham, who, recovering from a bad cold reluctantly competed in the mile, finishing 3rd in 4m47s. and having been persuaded to start in the two miles to complete our team, hung on to the end, finishing in a state of collapse. Our other competitors were Holtum, 3rd in the 100yds, and Pepe and Edwards 4th in the 880 yds. and javelin respectively. In recognition of our winning the trophy for three successive years, Carshalton Council made a nice gesture by presenting us with a special plaque. items.label: No. 135
items.sum: Editorial praising the quality of track performances, including Brian Morris and John Davies, but lamenting thin club representation and asking for timely reports.
items.s: Editorial Editorial praising the quality of track performances, including Brian Morris and John Davies, but lamenting thin club representation and asking for timely reports. Dear Fellow Members, From reports so far received, our track performances have been notable for their quality, if Club representation has been lacking in quantity. In the wide sphere in which we compete, we provided champions in six counties; a pretty remarkable achievement. Some great running has come from Brian Morris, with a 48·9s. quarter to his credit when representing the South against the North and Midlands and from John Davies (4m.10·6s.) for Middlesex versus Cambridge. But it is sad to note that in the majority of cases the same old faces turn up, whilst new talent seems to be lacking ( our youth and junior county results bear this out). On paper we have a powerful team at all events, but our inability to muster this strength in matches is poor advertisment and does not show respect for our opponents, let alone for the patient officials. A well meaning anonymous member sends us reports for youths and junior cross country events for which, he states, no reports appeared in the Belgravian. Whilst we appreciate the effort, such items are of doubtful interest after such a lapse of time. This must not be taken to mean that we do not require news, we do! It must be stressed, however, that it should reach us not later than a fortnight after the event occured. items.s: Cambridge Harriers Road Relay March 22nd. Report of a poor twelfth place in the Cambridge Harriers Road Relay, and a win for the Belgrave veterans' team. The less said about this event the better,for Bill Lucas looked an extremely harassed man as he juggled with the very inadequate forces at his disposal. The inevitable happened, in that our "B" team was incomplete and that the "A" team contained men, including the writer, of obvious "B" team capacity. Clive Shippen and Len Adams ran quite well on the first leg for the "A" and "B" teams respectively, but apart from a good run by Ken Jones on the third stage there were no outstanding efforts. Twelfth position in this event was not mediocre but downright shameful. In the veterans relay over four stages our team of E. Stimpson, L. Rolls, D. Brickwood and Charlie Smart had a very easy win, with the last named showing great form in returning a lap time of 19.46. items.h: Stock Exchange 25 Miles Walk at Hayes, Kent. March 29th.
items.sum: Appreciation of Ray Hall's record-breaking win in the Stock Exchange 25 miles walk, with Dave Stevens fourth.
items.s: Stock Exchange 25 Miles Walk at Hayes, Kent. March 29th. Appreciation of Ray Hall's record-breaking win in the Stock Exchange 25 miles walk, with Dave Stevens fourth. Reminiscences hardly have a part in club life, yet who can say what part "Footerisms", "Harleyisms" and all the other "isms" have in creating the spirit of comradeship, sportsmanship and will to achieve that which is such a part of a true Belgravian. What luck I had in attending to Ray Hall on what I am sure is only the first of his many victories in "Claret and Gold". With pride I watched him breast the tedious climb out of Westerham and shatter the opposition,and saw the tenacity with which he stuck to his task when in the doldrums and the whole world looked black and unsmiling. With pride I witnessed the comeback of a true champion as his strength returned and he started that fight against the watch, as not only victory but one of the most difficult records of the walking calender came within grasp. Such was my fortune and pleasure in witnessing one of our younger school display such fine characteristics and have his name added to the long list of champions this Club has produced. Congratulations also to Dave Stevens for his performance in finishing fourth. Result:- 1st R.C. Hall 3hr.39m.08s. 4th D.J. Stevens 4 " 02" 28" Previous record 3hr.41m.51s. H.W.S. items.h: Match v. Hercules A.C. & S.L.H. at Tooting. April 23rd.
items.sum: Report of the mid-week track match against Hercules A.C. and S.L.H. at Tooting, with Belgrave second in the senior match and third in the junior match.
items.s: Match v. Hercules A.C. & S.L.H. at Tooting. April 23rd. Report of the mid-week track match against Hercules A.C. and S.L.H. at Tooting, with Belgrave second in the senior match and third in the junior match. Our first mid-week fixture of the season, although blessed with fine weather and excellent conditions, did not produce results quite in the same category. However, our performances were not entirely displeasing. Brian Morris, in serious preparation for a coveted place at Cardiff and Stockholm, sharpened his speed by running in both the 100 and 220 yds. events; comfortably winning the latter by a yard from Gerry Leroy in 23.2s. This event produced our only points maximum of the evening. Henry Martin produced a promising early season effort in the quarter when running a close second to Woodland of Hercules(52.0) and, although only placed fifth, it was good to see Jim Heathfield running quarters once more after his third retirement from the event! Apparently he hasn't yet decided between the 440 yds. and the Mitcham '15' !! Although we had four representatives in the mile they had to fill the last four places behind P.Driver(4m.19.8s.), E.Earl (4.23.1), J.Edgar and C.Wilson. Our first(?) man home was Len Orton, our second claim member from Birchfield, who recorded 4m.30.2s. Mal Ash collected his usual quota of points with a win in the High Jump (5'7") and a second in the pole vault(11'6"). Three Bels supported Mal in the high jump with 5'6", 5'4" and 5'0"; the latter performance by Roach, still only a boy. Dave Ansell(19'8") was beaten on the last jump by one inch for second place, and finished third, four inches behind the winner. Coleman collected a point here for his fourth place and a further two in the shot, which was won by Rasey, our 3rd(!) claim member from Southgate and Barnet. In the junior match our best performance was by Stan Black who ran third in the half mile to Jones of S.L.H.(2m.1.2s.) and Hamilton of Hercules(2m.3.2s.); the latter just pipping Stan on the line. This was a fine run only two weeks after the London to Brighton relay and a busy winter season. Dave Taylor earned a point for his fourth place as did D. Crookes in the mile, but with no entry in either of the sprints our points total reached a mere six. Surely we have some junior sprinters somewhere! items.s: Finchley '20'. April 26th — Great run by Eric Gebbett Report of the Finchley 20 miles road race, where Eric Gebbett was 8th and Belgrave placed 4th team in both the open and Southern Counties races. This event was favoured by its usual warm weather, but a strong wind prevailed throughout and made hard going of the first two miles of each five mile lap. A good class field emphasised the fact that this is now the top 20 of the year. At five miles, Eric Gebbett was placed 6th with Len and Eric Bishop 28th and 43 rd respectively. Our fourth man at this stage was Alan Bishop in 55th place but he didn't stay there for long, and at nine miles was overtaken by Geoff Pearson. The impetuous were soon feeling the effects of the fast first ten miles and our scoring men were steadily moving through. Eric Gebbett, although slowing somewhat on his last lap, ended up in 8th place, returning the very fast time of 1hr.50m.29s.The Bishop brothers, less Alan, who was having a rough time due to the after effects of a heavy cold, had moved up to 22nd and 25th positions. With Geoff Pearson, now a veteran, gaining 49th place, we were placed 4th team in both the open and Southern Counties race held in conjunction. Also started:- R. Bolem, A. Penstone, R.Conway, L. items.label: No. 135
items.h: International 25 Kilometres Road Walk East Berlin Sunday May 4th
items.sum: Stan Vickers' first-person account of the trip to East Berlin for the international 25 km road walk, where he led early before fading to 12th; the walk was won by Max Weber of East Germany and the run by Kantorek, with Jack Haslam third in the run.
items.s: International 25 Kilometres Road Walk East Berlin Sunday May 4th Stan Vickers' first-person account of the trip to East Berlin for the international 25 km road walk, where he led early before fading to 12th; the walk was won by Max Weber of East Germany and the run by Kantorek, with Jack Haslam third in the run. Complete with Ted Smith's speed oil, Eric Hall's soap and Jack Goswell's map of Kent, Yours Truly, OTTO VON VICKERS set out on May 3rd for East Berlin, with long-distance runner Jack Haslam and team manager Les Truelove, for the international 25 km. run and walk. After leaving London Airport at 11 a.m. and having completed some three-quarters of our journey, Jack decided to test out the little brown bag that is so conveniently placed in front of one's seat in the aircraft.However, soon after landing a good cup of tea quickly put him on his feet again. On arriving at our hotel we had tea with our hosts, and later went out to have a look at the course, which proved to consist of a mixture of good asphalt and bad cobbles. At about 8.30 p.m. we sat down to dinner, which consisted of German sausage meat plus a famous German vegetable dish known as Sauerkraut. Haslam and Vickers, however, were not going in for this special diet so we both finished up eating Eric Hall's patent wonder food (bread and jam). We then bedded down for the night, only to discover, to our amazement, that we were without pillows. So the three happy wanderers had to be content with a tracksuit for a headrest, though this is inclined to give one a sore head on awakening. At 5 a.m. a ghastly thing called an alarm went off and Vickers got up. Now this is where I made my big mistake - if only I'd kept in bed between the sheets with my head on the hard tracksuit and my rather large feet dangling over the end of the 5 ft. long bed, I would never have taken the hiding that was forthcoming later that morning. The walk commenced at 9.30 a.m. and the field consisted of many cracks from Italy, Sweden, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Finland and West Germany. The run, which was over the same course, also attracted internationals from Poland, Czechoslovakia, Holland, Finland, West Germany and Yugoslavia and commenced at 10 a.m. It was rather a cold, windy morning when the walk started and I went off very fast, taking the lead out of the stadium after doing three and a half laps of the track. I was still in the lead at 10 km., with the two East Germans not far behind. Coming up to 12 km. we turned into a vile wind which almost picked me up and blew me off to Russia and at 14½ km. Lindner of East Germany ( a very bouncy performer indeed - he was disqualified at Melbourne for "lifting") and Max Weber also of the home country came up to my shoulder and a battle of tactics as to who should lead into the wind developed. However, the Germans soon pulled away and things remained much the same until the 20 km. check point. It was here that I received a severe shock (not an electric one) as my time was given as 89m.31s. This was incredibly fast and I found out after the race that the other competitors also felt that the sighting of this point was wrong, as indeed it must have been. From the 21 km. mark we went on to the exceedingly bad cobbles and what with these, the strong wind and my over fast start I began to feel very tired and at 22km. I was absolutely whacked. After going sprawling on the cobbles, Britain's last hope was folding up badly as one by one the opposition came past me. First there was Pamich of Italy (what a wonderful stylist he is) then Dordini (again a brilliant walker) and Soderlund of Sweden - they all went by and I couldn't do a thing about it, in fact I'd have given anything to lay down in the gutter for an hour or so. Just at that moment Dr. Pavel Kantorek, the Czechoslovakian runner,came past, followed by Paavo Kotila of Finland and our own Jackie, running brilliantly in his first international. I used my last ounce of energy to shout Jack on and then somehow managed to stagger on for a while round the lap of the stadium to finish in 12th position, a very tired young man indeed. The race was won by Max Weber of East Germany in 1hr.59m., second was Lindner of East Germany in 1hr.59m.13s. and third, A.Soderlund of Sweden in 1hr.59m.26s. After a drink of my patent pick me up (warm water), I found out that Kantorek had won the run in 1hr.20m.30s. Second was Kotila in 1hr.21m.5s., beating our Jack on the run in, his time, 1hr.21m.13s. Following a good rest in the afternoon we all went to the banquet in the evening and had a very pleasant time. After the eats and speeches, not to mention drinks, Vickers wandered off with the Dutch marathon runner Jack Smits to the hotel's "open" dance, where we had a very enjoyable time with the frauleins. All was going well until Mr Smits and myself left the hotel to walk back to our lodge when somehow or other we went off course, with the result that a fifteen minute walk took one and a half hours. We managed to find the place in the end with the help of a young German couple and such was our pleasure upon finding our home of rest that we gave them all the East German cash we had (we were leaving the following day and you cannot exchange East German marks into sterling, hence our generosity). When I entered our bedroom, Les and Jack, eyeing me with an air of suspicion, enquired where I had been. After giving my story in the utmost detail, they both told me to stop shooting a line, as they had been around etc.......etc.... If you have ever tried explaining to a team manager why you have arrived home late at night with all your money gone, you'll know what I mean! However, after promising to buy them both a drink on the following morning, the past was forgotten. A rather pleasant stay with our hosts was marred when they arrived late to take us back to the airport. After going round and round in the car for an hour ( we were trying to find the German team manager who had our visas) we eventually arrived at Temlhof Airport in Western Germany, only to find that our aircraft had left some forty-five minutes beforehand. Much good work by Les finally had us flying back via Dusseldorf and Amsterdam, to arrive at London Airport at midnight. Then came a frantic dash in Les Truelove's car. First of all he dropped Jack on his doorstep, then Stirling Fangio Truelove somehow got me to Charing Cross in time to catch the last milk train home. As you can imagine, Jack and myself were very grateful indeed, especially as Les had quite a journey to his home after dropping us. Well, the trip was over, but I think it is true to say that Jack and I had the last laugh. You see, during the outward trip we were discussing air travel, and Les told us that he could openly boast that after flying thousands of miles all over the world he had never missed an aircraft by arriving late at the airport..... ...ah well, you were saying, Mr. Truelove......? I feel sure Jack Haslam will join me in saying thank you B.A.A.B. and our German hosts for a very enjoyable trip and for the experience gained. And thankyou Les Truelove for being such a jovial and amiable team manager. Stan Vickers. items.label: No. 135
items.sum: Profile of Colin Collis, tracing his club career from joining in 1943 to his Club marathon titles, his English native record in a 3 hours track race at Walton and his retirement in 1957.
items.s: Portrait Gallery Profile of Colin Collis, tracing his club career from joining in 1943 to his Club marathon titles, his English native record in a 3 hours track race at Walton and his retirement in 1957. If perseverance, courage and fortitude can produce a self-made athlete of top class, then Colin Collis, the subject of this article, is an admirable example. He became a 'Bel' in 1943 and was a contempory of the Brown, Burfitt, Short, Adams and Bishop brothers junior group, under the eagle eyes of Bert Footer and Alf Taylor. Here he learned the true meaning of club spirit, and although he was not to come to the fore until many years later, Colin competed at all distances on the track and country. In 1951 he went to London University and there beat his head against the wall endeavouring, on the mistaken advice of a "specialist", to become a half miler, with little success. Studies kept him out of the picture for some time, but by the start of 1955 it was obvious that he had been applying himself with some diligence, to distance running, for he surprised everyone by finishing 13th in the Mitcham '15' with a time of 1hr.24m.53s. But for the fact that he had been entered in the B team and walloped several A team men, Belgrave would have been placed first. Having tasted success, Colin went on to gain fourth place in the Wigmore '15' in a very fast time, and with a second in the Surrey '20' in 1hr.47m.44s.( although, let's face it, some fantastic times are returned in this Surrey race) was a strong favourite to become Club marathon champion. This he did, in record time, when returning 2hr.37m.4s. in the Polytechnic marathon that year, at the same time winning the Lalande trophy for the first man to finish who has not competed over the distance before. Following this up with a third place in the Belgrave '20' and taking the Club title in conjunction, Colin can be said to have made a very successful entry into distance running in 1955. His meticulous attention to training and his refusal to be sidetracked from what his experience had proved to him was the best method, were to pay even greater dividends in 1956. His times were steadily improving (the greatest form of satisfaction to a road runner) and he again won the Club marathon title in record time (2hr.31m.26s.). In the Autumn of the same year Colin proved that he was really better suited to even longer distances, for he returned 3hr.2m.33s. when finishing third in the S.L.H. '30' and then received an invitation to compete in a 3 hours track race at Walton. Although suffering from a cold all the previous week, he honoured his engagement and confounded everyone by breaking the existing English native record and finishing second to the renowned Arthur Keilly of Derby. Colin covered 30 miles 952 yards 2 feet; a meritorious performance. Dogged by injury however, Colin decided to retire in 1957, temporarily we hope! He has performed official Club duties for many years and has a wise head. His compilation of Club record lists has been an interesting feature of the Belgravian since 1952. Married, with a daughter of nearly two, Colin is modesty personified, but quiet confidence always lay beneath the surface; a more purposeful athlete would be difficult to recall. items.h: Senior Match v. St. Mary's College & College of St. Mar[illegible]s and St. Johns Battersea Park 14th May.
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's senior match at Battersea Park against St. Mary's College and the College of St. Marks and St. Johns, which Belgrave won with 83 points.
items.s: Senior Match v. St. Mary's College & College of St. Mar[illegible]s and St. Johns Battersea Park 14th May. Report of Belgrave's senior match at Battersea Park against St. Mary's College and the College of St. Marks and St. Johns, which Belgrave won with 83 points. The programme for this match was restricted to five track events and three field events as the Club 7 mile walking championship, a report of which will be found elsewhere, was being held the same evening. Unfortunately, however, the start of the walk was delayed and the first track event did not take place until almost half an hour after its scheduled time. This disasterous start was somewhat remedied, so far as our guests were concerned, by the speed with which the events were carried out, and the whole evening ended on quite an amicable note. As was to be expected, with a number of first team members, we proved to be much too strong for our opponents and we provided six first and five second places. In the shorter distances our members won their respective events; Ron Holtum taking the 100 yds in 10.6s. and Brian Morris the 220 yds in 23.2s. Gerry Leroy and Henry Martin finished first and second in the 440 yds with 51.7 and 52.0s. respectively, although Gerry was rather disappointed with his performance, being hampered in training by a recurrent leg injury. Our visitors provided the winner of the 880 yds, Steve Boreham being a good second in 2m.3.2s.; he was just unable to get on terms with the winner despite his characteristic final burst. The mile proved to be an interesting race between Shipley and Len Orton, both second claim members, who finished first and second respectively in 4m.29s. and 4m.33s. Len Orton took the lead from the start, going through the three quarters quite easily,only to tire rapidly on the last lap, and he was unable to hold off Shipley's challenge about a furlong from the finish. The field events saw a welcome return to competition of Mal Ash who won the long jump with 20'6" and finished third in the javelin,with 135'5" behind Bill Couzens who threw 142'5". We also provided first place in the shot with Racey whose winning putt was 35'4". items.sum: Report of Belgrave performances in Surrey senior, junior and youths championships at Croydon Arena, led by a 4x440 yds relay win over Epsom and Ewell Harriers.
items.s: Croydon Arena May 17th Report of Belgrave performances in Surrey senior, junior and youths championships at Croydon Arena, led by a 4x440 yds relay win over Epsom and Ewell Harriers. A number of Senior and Junior championships were held in conjunction with the Surrey Youths championships and, generally speaking, those members who competed did so with distinction. Pride of place must go to our 4x440 yds Senior relay team of P.Pepe, C.Coxall, C.Jones and G.Leroy who, running in that order, defeated the holders, Epsom and Ewell Harriers, in 3m.28.3s. Pepe, running with great judgement in the outside lane, handed over with a two yard lead, after which our team were never headed and no doubt they would have beaten the existing best performance of 3m.28s. had Gerry Leroy not "coasted" during the middle part of the last lap. The same team with D.Gordon running in place of Pepe were placed third in the 4 x 110 yds relay in 45.5, despite a great effort by Charlie Jones over the last stage. Mitcham A.C. won the event in 44.2s. and Epsom and Ewell were second with 45.4s. Unfortunately our team were not awarded a set of medals as there were only five teams competing. Our two entries in the 3000 metres steeplechase, although not placed, performed most creditably, both beating time standard of 10m.15s; Clive Shippen finishing in 10m.3.6s. and Eddie Short in 10m.12s. Eddie was most disappointed with his performance, but when one considers his only training is done on the road he ran remarkably well In the junior events J.Knifton retained his title in the one mile walk in 7m.17.4s. and Alan Black, running for his school, was second to R.J.Harvey of Croydon Harriers in the one mile steeplechase. Alan's time of 5m.5.4s. bettered the existing best performance by one second. items.label: No. 135
items.sum: Unsigned training advice piece urging moderate, regular and steadily increased training rather than copying the mileage of star athletes.
items.s: Easy does it! Unsigned training advice piece urging moderate, regular and steadily increased training rather than copying the mileage of star athletes. We all know that Rome wasn't built in a day, although when the 1960 invaders have finished with it, the locals will probably wish it could be rebuilt in that time. Likewise no champion developed overnight; Sunday newspaper journalists would have us believe otherwise, but invariably omit to record the inevitable decline of these nine day wonders. The road to the top rung in athletics, let alone to the half-way rung, is a hard one, and a sensible, moderate approach to training and racing is essential if one is to avoid the disappointment of finding oneself unable to do better times in racing than in training. Of great interest to statisticians, the published questionaires answered by the stars in their various branches of athletics may well be misleading to the uninitiated, to those aspiring to fame, or to those training to a schedule which perhaps has not yet been given sufficient time to produce the required results. The mere fact that A.S.Similate thrives on 100 miles a week plus, and as a result is a likely selection for the what-have-you games, is not the slightest justification for anyone to copy him with any certain hope of success. What the questionaire probably does not state is that the subject has only arrived at his present state after years of steadily increasing the quantity and severity of his training. One man's meat being another man's poison, moderation must be practised until some indication can be obtained as to the amount of work one's body can absorb. Whatever one's event, the importance of regular training cannot be over-emphasized. Far better do little and often than two or three mammoth sessions a week. The ideal is to become as accustomed to training as one is to daily work. Look ahead, in fact look well ahead and set your sights accordingly. Make sure that you start your races with boilers at full steam, not half pressure due to injudicious training. Training will build you up - straining will break you down. Rome

items.sum: Editorial celebrating Stan Vickers' European 20 km walk gold in Stockholm and Dave Mitchell's L.C.C. Junior 880 yards win, and thanking Alf Harley for contributing much of the issue.
items.s: Editorial Editorial celebrating Stan Vickers' European 20 km walk gold in Stockholm and Dave Mitchell's L.C.C. Junior 880 yards win, and thanking Alf Harley for contributing much of the issue. Dear Fellow Members, We are indeed proud to record the outstanding achievement of Stan Vickers in outclassing the best walkers in Europe to win the gold medal at Stockholm in the European 20 kilos. Championship. For this superb performance Stan has been awarded the "Tommy Green" trophy; it was never more gallantly earned. Since our last edition great improvements have been shewn in our track performances, the most notable being that of Dave Mitchell when winning the L.C.C. Junior 880 yards Championship in 1m.57.8s; a remarkable time for a junior. We hope Dave turns out to be a future middle distance star. We are indebted to Alf Harley for much of the material contained in this issue, but it is regrettable that one on whose shoulders rests so much responsibility on behalf of the Club, should have need to add to his duties by writing articles for this magazine. If one who is so fully occupied already can find time to do this, then we hope others will feel how small is their own contribution to the running of a Club as large as ours. Stan Vickers Stan Vickers won gold, European 20 km walk, Stockholm; awarded the "Tommy Green" trophy Stan Stan Dave Mitchell Dave Mitchell won L.C.C. Junior 880 yards Championship in 1m.57.8s Alf Harley Alf Harley contributed much of the material in this issue European Championships L.C.C. Championships Stockholm

items.label: No. 136
items.sum: New club president F.R. Webb thanks members for electing him, asks for regular training to put the club back on top, and congratulates European champion Stan Vickers.
items.s: From your President New club president F.R. Webb thanks members for electing him, asks for regular training to put the club back on top, and congratulates European champion Stan Vickers. Fellow Members, I should like to take this opportunity, through the medium of the Belgravian, to express my sincere thanks for the great honour you have paid me by electing me as your President, and I shall do all in my power to carry out the duties involved to the best of my ability. It is my hope that during the next twelve months I shall have the help of all members in putting the Club back on top, where it belongs, and this can only be done by regular training with the various packs which will be arranged by your Cross-Country Captain. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate our European Champion, Stan Vickers, on his great walking performances during the past season. Once again thanking you all very much for this honour. F.R. Webb F.R. Webb F.R. Webb President Stan Vickers Stan Vickers European Champion (walking) European Championships

Socially Speaking..... On taking over the Office of Social Secretary I would like to say a few words and to ask you for your support at all social functions during the coming year. No matter how much time and hard work is put into the arrangement of a social function such as a Dance, Dinner or Coaches for the Brighton Relay etc., it cannot be a success without your full support and encouragement. So come along and enjoy the companionship of fellow Belgravians. Social Dances Social Dances at Belgrave Hall have been arranged to take place approximately once a month, the first being on October 25th and the last in March. A licensed bar will be available on each occasion and a first class band will be engaged. Refreshments at moderate prices will also be obtainable. Games will be organised and there will be spot prizes to be won. Sausage and Mash Supper It is hoped to have a sausage and mash supper available to members and their friends after the afternoon's activities on the days of socials and dances. A list will be posted on the notice board at the hall two or three weeks before each dance and you can assist us a great deal by placing your name thereon and indicating how many persons will be making up your party. This will greatly assist us in knowing how many to cater for. Annual Dinner and Dance Tickets are still obtainable for this very important function which is to be held at Barrington House, Gresham St. E.C.2. on Saturday, November 15th. and the price - 21/- each. Report and results of the club track championships at Tooting Bec, with doubles for Clive Ryan and John Davies, a championship best for Stan Vickers in the 2 miles walk and three junior wins for Dave Mitchell. CLUB TRACK CHAMPIONSHIPS. 14TH JUNE AT TOOTING BEC. Tooting Bec gave us every encouragement on our return to its track by welcoming us with a lovely day and beautiful sunshine, bringing out our feminine admirers in all their bright best and enabling our noble band of officials to display themselves without jackets in impeccable whiteness in accordance with the well known advertisements. Although entries were only average in number a very fine Championship meeting was held and some really excellent performances were witnessed. Outstanding amongst these were the doubles of Clive Ryan in the 100 and 220 yds. and John Davies in the 880yds and 1 mile. The forward running of R. Bhatia in the latter event was particularly pleasing. Stan Vickers was again at his scintillating best in the 2 miles walk in which he accomplished a new Club Championship best performance and, of course, won the style award. In the junior events Dave Mitchell ( of whom we shall be hearing a great deal) won the 220, 440 and 880 yds. all in good times. items.sum: Obituary of race walker Bert Clayton, who died aged 39, recalling his Horwood Cup win, R.W.A. team placings, 50 km championship medals and Nijmegen Shield wins.
items.s: H.G. Clayton Obituary of race walker Bert Clayton, who died aged 39, recalling his Horwood Cup win, R.W.A. team placings, 50 km championship medals and Nijmegen Shield wins. It is with sincere regret that we record the passing of Bert Clayton at the early age of 39 years; and our heartfelt sympathy is extended to his Wife and three children. Bert joined us in 1938 and in that year won the Horwood Cup Championship. In the early part of 1939 he was a member of our winning R.W.A. Junior Championship team at Manchester; and a few weeks later figured prominently in the R.W.A. 20 miles Championship at Mill Hill. In this he was nominated as a "B" team man but was able to assist our fourth "A" team man, Harry Thaxter, to complete a Belgrave team win; and was content to finish in 17th position himself, following Thaxter in. During the war Bert served in the R.A.F. but in 1947 was again assisting our teams. He was in our 'placed' R.W.A. 20 miles teams in 1947-48-49-50 and in our winning team at Enfield in 1952. He was placed third in the R.W.A. 50 kilometres Championship at Sheffield in 1950 ( when our team was second) and second the following year at Brighton when we were the Championship winners. Bert won our Club 20 miles Championship in 1950 and 1951; and scored in our winning Nijmegen Shield teams in 1948, 1950 and 1952. It will be seen from the foregoing that Bert was a great team walker; and in addition to the strength he brought to our Championship teams he was a valuable team man in other events also. Living at Eastleigh, he travelled considerable distances for his racing, but always did so cheerfully and enthusiastically and endeared himself to a very wide circle of friends. We have lost a great sportsman and a great Belgravian - we are the richer for having known him so well, the poorer for his passing from our midst. A.A.H. H.G. Clayton H.G. items.sum: Report and results of the R.W.A. 50 km walk championship held from Belgrave's headquarters, won in a British fastest time by Metropolitan's D.J. Thompson, with Eric Hall third and Belgrave winning the team title for the third successive time.
items.s: The R.W.A. 50 kilometres Championship Report and results of the R.W.A. 50 km walk championship held from Belgrave's headquarters, won in a British fastest time by Metropolitan's D.J. Thompson, with Eric Hall third and Belgrave winning the team title for the third successive time. For the first time ever this Championship was held from our Headquarters and our thanks from the Club are due to all those who helped with the organisation of the race, which reflected great credit on Belgrave. Jack Goswell and Arthur Whitehead were, as usual, in the forefront of the arrangements but there were many others who gave assistance and made this a memorable Championship from the organisation point of view. The course consisted of five laps of the approximately one mile lap of the Common at the head of Lauriston Road, followed by four laps of our normal course ( of 6 miles 1114 yards each) taking in Park Side, Tibbetts Corner, Robin Hood Way, Coombe Lane, Copse Hill and finishing at Lauriston House There were 96 starters and [illegible]ric Hall was soon prominent among the leaders and, in fact, held the lead for a while soon after the 20 kilometres mark. At half-distance Misson(Met.W.C.) had taken the lead with Johnson(Sheffield) near at hand followed by Don Thompson(Met) and Eric, taking things reasonably easy, fourth. A few kilometres later Thompson went into the lead and rapidly went away from the field to record the fastest time yet over the 50 kilometres distance in this country. Misson whilst not quite so fast as his club mate also forged away from the field, and Eric Hall took over third position from a tiring Johnson, who was also experiencing foot trouble. Eric, realising the impossibility of cutting into the lead of the two Metropolitan walkers ahead of him, was well content with his position and the excellent start it gave to our team in their efforts to retain the Championship title. Metropolitan succeeded in taking fourth individual place with Nigel Thompson, thus having three men in the first four, but adequate backing for them was missing. Eventually their fourth man finished in 41st scoring position. Our strength is, of course, in numbers and solid team work and this was well exemplified by our supporting walkers. George Checkley did not have one of his happiest races, yet stuck to his task and, walking a tremendously fast last lap, finished in eighth position. Ray Hall started well and finished well, but there were times in between when he was very far from happy. His ninth position was of the greatest value to the team; and we are all confident that he will be a "placed" man at this distance one day. Our team was completed by Hugh McGreechan, in twelfth position, who walked a typically sound race. Four men in twelve is normally good enough to win a Championship and so it was, and our third successive win was accomplished. Near at hand was George Beecham (17th) to take over, should it become necessary. To conclude, we may derive great pleasure from this further Championship win, from the success which attended our organisation of the Championship entrusted to us and in Eric Hall's third placing which confirmed the extreme versatility and excellence of his walking at varying distances. items.sum: Report on Belgrave performances at Herne Hill Harriers' Brockman Trophy meeting, with wins for Percy Porter (hammer) and Norman Caves (hop, step and jump), seconds for John Davies and Pat Newell, and sixth place overall for the club.
items.s: Brockman Trophy Meeting 7th June Report on Belgrave performances at Herne Hill Harriers' Brockman Trophy meeting, with wins for Percy Porter (hammer) and Norman Caves (hop, step and jump), seconds for John Davies and Pat Newell, and sixth place overall for the club. Organised by Herne Hill Harriers, this meeting is always very hotly contested, and in consequence the standard of performance is particularly high. Although our field events representatives were few in number they certainly made their presence felt and in the very first event, the hammer throw, Percy Porter won with a throw of 157'5". Norman Caves won the hop, step and jump with 43'3" while in the pole vault Mal Ash did well to secure fourth place. Our track runners were more numerous, although in some of the events they were completely outclassed, notably the 880 yds, in which P. Pepe was unable to qualify for the final, and the 6 miles in which Eric Gebbett finished sixth. However, John Davies and Pat Newell came to the rescue with two very fine efforts, John finishing second to Gordon Pirie in the 1500 metres with a time of 3m.59 1s. and Pat chased John Disley home in the 3 miles to finish less than two seconds behind in 14m.39 6s. and incidently beat Langridge of S.L.H. who is no mean performer. Clive Shippen, our budding steeplechase star, was third in the 3000 metres event with a time of 10m.12s. Mal Ash was unluckly not to qualify in his heat of the 120 yds hurdles which was won in a very fast time while C.R. Jones ran into fourth place in the 220 yds final. In the 4 x 440 yds relay our quartet were fourth, behind Blackheath, London A.C. and T.V.H. Our final place in the contest was sixth. items.sum: Report and results of the Polytechnic Marathon from Windsor to Chiswick, incorporating the A.A.A. and Southern marathon championships, where Len Bishop retained the club title in a club record and Belgrave won the Southern team title.
items.s: Polytechnic Marathon and Club Championship Report and results of the Polytechnic Marathon from Windsor to Chiswick, incorporating the A.A.A. and Southern marathon championships, where Len Bishop retained the club title in a club record and Belgrave won the Southern team title. One hundred and ninety-four runners set out from Windsor Castle on the afternoon of June 28th for the annual dash to Chiswick via the country lanes of Berkshire and Buckingham. Incorporated in the event this year were the A.A.A. and Southern Counties Marathon Championships and an additional attraction was the possibility of a trip to either Cardiff or Stockholm. With the Club Championship his target, Eric Gebbett led the Belgrave contingent of nine runners for the first sixteen miles, which he covered in the rather fast time of 89m.25s. Shortly after this point he was overtaken by Len Bishop, the Club title holder, who was determined that his title would not be relinquished at any price. Eric hung on desperately for the next three miles, but Len's fighting qualities were never more in evidence than now, as he began to draw steadily away. Len eventually finished 13th in the new Club record time of 2h.30m.39s. and in fact was actually on the track at the same time as such distinguished marathon runners as E.L. Smith of Leeds and F. Norris of Bolton. Eric, in finishing 17th performed extremely well, and was comfortably inside the A.A.A. standard of 2h.35m. The third Club runner to finish was Bob Plummer, who recorded his best ever time of 2h.36m.46s. to occupy 25th position. Bob has now regained the excellent form he was showing two years ago when he was laid low by a very troublesome knee injury. The efforts of these three stalwarts won us the Southern A.A.A. Marathon team Championship which we last held in 1955. Nearly ten minutes were to elapse before our next man, Geoff Pearson, put in an appearance, and his running enabled us to secure third place in the Open Team Race. Geoff doesn't turn out for the Club very often now but when he does he can always be relied upon to put up a stirling performance. Our four remaining runners all completed the course, and special mention must be made of the running of J. MacDonald who was expected by many to be well outside three hours but in actual fact beat the new Club Standard of 2h.55m. VICTORIA PARK JULY 21ST Report of a four-sided inter-club match against Victoria Park, Deptford Park and Ilford A.C., which Belgrave lost on combined senior and junior points despite seven senior wins. We had a fairly good turn out of Seniors for this match which was a four sided affair against Victoria Park, Deptford Park and Ilford A.C. but our Junior representation consisted of only one person. As the match was to be decided on the total number of points, both Senior and Junior, this placed us at a very great disadvantage. So much so, that in spite of winning seven Senior events we lost the match. John Davies won both the half and one mile in 1m.57 6s. and 4m.23s. respectively, while Brian Morris had a narrow win in the 220 with a time of 22 7s. There were two races over 440 yds, Charlie Jones being second (52 4) in the first one and Alan Jackson winning the second in 52 6 Dave Ansell won the 100 yds in 10 8s. and the long jump with 20'7". The match resulted in a win for Victoria Park with 104 pts. Ilford A.C. were second with 96, ourselves third with 80 and Deptford Park fourth with 71. Support for this race has, in the past, been very poor, but this year saw a vast improvement with an entry of over eighty of whom sixty-four actually started. Despite this large entry the promoters only saw fit to give one set of team prizes although in fairness to them this fact was advertised freely before the race. However, one would have thought that this unexpectedly heavy support would have made them change their minds.
