items.sum: Report and results of the Belgrave Open 20 miles, where Len Bishop finished third and won the club championship in a club best championship time, and Belgrave A were second team to Thames Valley Harriers.
items.s: BELGRAVE OPEN 20 MILES RUN AND CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP AUG.16TH Report and results of the Belgrave Open 20 miles, where Len Bishop finished third and won the club championship in a club best championship time, and Belgrave A were second team to Thames Valley Harriers. A smaller than usual field of 83 was sent on its way by the Deputy Mayor of Wimbledon in weather which, for a change, was not of the heat wave variety. In fact, conditions could be described as near perfect. Belgrave's contribution to this field consisted of two teams of six runners each. Eric Gebbett was the early pacemaker from Beale of Shaftsbury and at twelve miles he was passed by Haslam(T.V.H.) and Salvat(Finchley). Len Bishop, who had been content to hang back in the early stages, now began to move up and at sixteen miles passed Eric at great speed. Maintaining his speed to the end of the race he finished a very good third in the Open Race and was a comfortable winner of the Club Championship. Eric, although taken aback by this burst of speed was still an easy fourth, exactly two minutes ahead of the next man, Harry Dennis of T.V.H. With Bob Plummer running well for twelfth place our team was narrowly beaten by T.V.H. Mention must be made of Ron Linstead and Joe Dooley, who were running in their first 20 mile race. To beat 2h.5m. on this course was a particularly good effort. Once again Bill Bird and Arthur Whitehead plus their numerous assistants must be congratulated for the way the race was organised. items.sum: Report of a small Belgrave team's successful visit to a minor meeting on a muddy grass track at Bishop's Stortford, winning the 440 yds, 220 yds and 4 x 440 relay.
items.s: Report of a small Belgrave team's successful visit to a minor meeting on a muddy grass track at Bishop's Stortford, winning the 440 yds, 220 yds and 4 x 440 relay. On Saturday Sept.20th a small team visited Bishop's Stortford on a minor "pot hunt" with considerable success. The grass track was very soggy and in some parts was just plain muddy. Hence the rather slow times. In the 100 yds. heats our only competitor, C.R. Jones, came through at about 75 yds. and won easily in 10.5s. Starting much faster in the final (from borrowed blocks) he was only inches down on the leader at 50 yds. Everyone, including the official winner, thought he had won with his dip finish, but the judges deemed otherwise and he was given second place. Times (non electrical) 10.7 & 10.8. The 220 yds heats went off uneventfully with Brian Morris and Charlie Jones qualifying easily for the final. The next event concerning the Bels was the 440 yds which was run as a straight final, and taking part was our 4 x 440 relay team. Alan Jackson and P. Pepe started rather fast into the mud while Brian Morris and Frank Wright went off steadily. At the half-way mark Brian was leading slightly from Frank, but Pepe and "Jacko" found the heavy grass track not to their liking and decided to save their energies for the relay. Brian and Frank continued running very strongly and drew away from the field to finish first and second in 51.4 and 51.6 respectively. Twenty-five minutes later came the 220 final. Charlie,in the fourth lane, started well, catching Brian coming off the bend and holding his lead to the finish. Brian, although feeling tired after his "quarter", finished close up in second place, giving the Bels another maximum. Time 23s.? The "quarter" men next performed as a team in the 4 x 440 relay and showed their superiority by finishing more strongly than their opponents who, however, put up quite a fight. Belgrave first again, time 3m32s. The team then headed back to civilization in cars, motor-bikes and scooters. C.R. Jones C.R. Jones won 100 yds heat 10.5s.; 2nd in final Brian Morris Brian Morris won 440 yds 51.4; 2nd 220 yds; 4 x 440 relay Charlie Jones Charlie Jones won 220 yds final Alan Jackson Alan Jackson 4 x 440 relay team P. items.label: No. 136
items.h: Some notes on the A.G.M. Sept.25th.
items.sum: Wry account of the club's Annual General Meeting, covering the Hon. Secretary's report, interruptions from members, elections and Charlie Munro's election to Life Membership.
items.s: Some notes on the A.G.M. Sept.25th. Wry account of the club's Annual General Meeting, covering the Hon. Secretary's report, interruptions from members, elections and Charlie Munro's election to Life Membership. The A.G.M. opened (apart from the reading of previous minutes and noting apologies from absentees) with the Hon. Secretary's Report from which we were encouraged to learn that apart from a temporary setback in cross country and middle distance running (formerly our main strength) we nevertheless had reason to be proud of the Club's overall contribution to the sport. Thanks to our walkers and late season form of our track relay men, our record last year was quite a good one. The adoption of this report was temporarily delayed by the snarling interruption of a rather incoherent member who seemed rather concerned that a first claim Belgravian had competed for another club. He quickly subsided - still muttering - on learning that his outburst was out of order at that stage. We were then taken through the accounts and there followed the usual rather dry proceedings until we came to the election of officers, and this was marked by the efforts of current holders of office to transfer their mantels to other shoulders. We learned, among other things, that while the job of auditing the Club books was small, the journey from Chislehurst to Edmonton was long. This piece of information prompted a former Hon. Treasurer to jump to his feet and to question whether the audit had been properly carried out. His feigned criticism was an attempt to inject a note of humour into the otherwise rather dull proceedings, but he was perhaps rather unwise in attempting to draw a comparison between the somewhat more arduous and complicated accounting of his day with that at present obtaining. This brought quite a storm about his head from the platform, and whilst this forced him to hastily resume his seat with apology, he was re-assured by the accompanying applause that not all members were devoid of a sense of humour. The election of a new committee followed uneventfully and it was not until "any other business" that the meeting once more briefly came to life. Again it was the incoherent member who seemed anxious to repeat his previous uninformed comments regarding the first claim Belgravian, and went on to discuss the merits of our distance runners generally and our 3 and 6 milers in particular. Whilst most of this was rather incomprehensible, one could not escape the impression that the speaker was not altogether satisfied with their performances, but before he got very far, another member interrupted - rather violently it was thought - to discuss, not athletics, but some sort of ball game. It was all very bewildering. The meeting ended having elected, among others, a new President, a new cross country caption, a new social secretary, a new committee, but not a new junior section secretary, probably the most important job of them all. Charlie Munro was elected to Life Membership. One came away from the meeting with the feeling that without the presence of the General Hon. Sec. the A.G.M. could well have got out of hand. He has held this post for a long time and while he repeatedly expresses the view that a younger member should be considered to take over this important job, it is evident, that for the present at least, there is no one of sufficient stature to replace him. Charlie Munro Charlie Munro elected to Life Membership A.G.M. Chislehurst Edmonton

items.s: A few words from your Track Hon. Secretary The Track Hon. Secretary looks ahead to the 1959 season, asks for more support from distance runners and thanks second-claim member Len Orton, who is returning to Birchfield. I look forward to the 1959 season with confidence and the expectation that our teams will be much stronger in all departments. Particularly would I like to see more support from our two and three milers. This year we have missed the assistance of Chas. Walker, Dave Baulch, Brian Hallowell and others. We must thank our second claim member, Len Orton, for his support at our fixtures. I understand that he will be returning to his first claim club Birchfield very soon and I feel sure that he carries our best wishes for his future, both in his athletics and his career. D.M.S. D.M.S. items.label: No. 136
items.sum: Report and results of the club road race over the Common, won comfortably by Pat Newell, with Clive Shippen second, Ken Stimpson winning the handicap, and a plea for winter cross-country training.
items.s: CLUB 5[illegible] MILES ROAD RACE SEPT 27TH Report and results of the club road race over the Common, won comfortably by Pat Newell, with Clive Shippen second, Ken Stimpson winning the handicap, and a plea for winter cross-country training. A spectacular return to form by Charlie Dabbs, a defiant battle against "father time" and injuries successfully overcome by Archie Bedford, and an extraordinary run by Clive Shippen were just a few of the highlights to emerge from this event, considered by some to be an unofficial "Brighton" trial. With so little having been seen of our key road-relay men this summer there was considerable speculation as to how they would fare against the fitness of the long distance men and the speed of the middle distance track runners on this both tough and fast course. To add to the uncertainty Archie Bedford and Len Adams were reputed to be making a determined effort to regain their long lost places in the London-Brighton relay team. So, on a fine day and in ideal conditions, our new President, Frank Webb, sent the 40 odd runners on their way. After one lap of the Common very little had been decided despite the faster than usual start; Pat Newell slightly led a pack of about eight runners, with a few more in close attendance. No sooner had the second lap commenced than Pat decided to increase the tempo, only Dave Baulch attempting to go with him. However,on leaving the Common for Copse Hill Pat was way ahead and increasing his lead with every stride; the role of pack leader being taken over by Eric Gebbett. On entering Cambridge Road with the hills still to come this group had been reduced to Gebbett, Walker, Baulch, Robinson and Shippen. Dave dropped back at the approach to the first hill and Malcolm likewise at the turn into the second; the remaining three staying together until approximately 400 yds. to go when Clive Shippen sprinted ahead to gain second place, 25 yds. ahead of Charlie Walker, with Eric a further 35 yds. down. Charlie Dabbs proved his unexpected fitness by finishing strongly, only 10 sec. behind Gebbett. Pat Newell must be congratulated on his fine solo effort; he ran comfortably throughout and was at no time fully extended. Bob Glover ran in this event for the first time last March when he returned a time of 30.35. His time today? 29.38! Establishing himself as a runner of note in such a short time makes one wonder how much potential he has yet to realise. Special mention should also be made of Archie Bedford on his most welcome return to form, and of a fine performance by young Radford. The handicap was won by Ken Stimpson who produced a time considerably faster than his usual. Second place went to Glover and a deserved third to Dennis Jones who is running better than ever before. Once more we are on the brink of another winter season and if all of today's competitors take an active part in the programme, it should be a successful one; and 1959 could take us out of the "fifties" on the same triumphant note with which we entered them nearly ten seasons ago. Belgrave possesses almost unlimited depth but, as yet, no stars. An enthusiastic winter season could well remedy this weakness. To those who are dubious of working hard over the country it might well be worth mentioning names like Herb Elliott, Derek Ibbottson and John Merriman. Ibbottson's "failure" this season followed a winter of negligible cross-country work, whereas his triumphant summer of 1957 was produced by a winter in which he won major international cross-country races during an extremely active season. items.sum: Report of the Road Runners Club London to Brighton run, where Bob Plummer was tenth with a first class standard and Belgrave's four runners took third team prizes behind T.V.H. and Derby and County.
items.s: LONDON TO BRIGHTON RUN, SEPT. 27TH. Report of the Road Runners Club London to Brighton run, where Bob Plummer was tenth with a first class standard and Belgrave's four runners took third team prizes behind T.V.H. and Derby and County. (Promoted by the Road Runners Club) On the first stroke of seven, some forty-eight runners, including four Belgravians, started from Westminster. The weather, a little cold and damp at the start, developed into a good day for this type of race. At five miles our four, Alan Bishop, Joe MacDonald, Bob Plummer and Wally Wortley were running together at just inside seven minutes a mile. At ten miles Bob was nearly a minute ahead of our other three who came through steadily. The next ten miles on towards Redhill saw Bob still running strongly whilst our others had spread themselves out a little, the order being Wally, Alan and Mac.Times of our runners at 20 miles:- Bob(2h.15m.27s.),Wally (2.22.28.), Alan(2.22.38.) and Mac(2.22.53.). At thirty miles Wally had some trouble with his back and stopped for a while and was passed by Alan and Mac, Alan having a lead of over four minutes on Mac. On to Handcross, with eighteen miles still to go, Bob was still going well and Wally was losing ground to Mac. The road after Handcross, in spite of its downward trend,has often troubled the best and Bob and Alan both had bad patches along this stretch. Alan told me afterwards that he was short of training and in consequence he had several miles of slow running. So to the finish, Bob Plummer, full of running again, was tenth in 6h.22m.2s., his best ever with a First Class Standard. The team race (3 to score) was already won by T.V.H. with fourteen points, but we had hopes of a place. Wally Wortley, who was still three minutes behind Mac. at Pyecombe and had passed Alan two or three miles back, had made a grand recovery and finished strongly in fifteenth position with a time of 7h.00m.33s. Joe MacDonald was next man in in 7h.02m.53s, he had had a hard run over the last few miles and seemed very glad to finish. Our team was in with 31 points, but Derby & County and Orion had two men well placed and could still beat us. Derby's third man made their score 22 points, so it was Belgrave or Orion for third place. Meanwhile Alan Bishop had finished nineteenth in 7h.15m.39s. and although not scoring added a point to the Orion score which, when their third man did arrive, equalled our own. With our third man in front of Orion's third man we were awarded the third team prizes. Alan was not unrewarded, as he gained a Second Class Standard as did Wally and Mac. The day was rounded off by having tea with the Mayor of Brighton (who has threatened to run in next years' race) and the presentation of well earned awards. G.D. Crawley 30.6m. Handcross 35.1m. items.label: No. 136
items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's notes: Ted Good's recovery and club history since 1897, Eric Hall's walking record in 1958, John Sams's hurdles titles, Dave Mitchell, the W.J. Pepper Memorial Cup, relay finals, John Palmer's illness, and Stan Vickers's Tommy Green Cup with Harold Whitlock's praise of his European Games walk win.
items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S CORNER The Hon. Secretary's notes: Ted Good's recovery and club history since 1897, Eric Hall's walking record in 1958, John Sams's hurdles titles, Dave Mitchell, the W.J. Pepper Memorial Cup, relay finals, John Palmer's illness, and Stan Vickers's Tommy Green Cup with Harold Whitlock's praise of his European Games walk win. We congratulate Ted Good on recovering from a very serious illness and wish him well for many years yet. Ted was sustained in his battle for life by the fighting spirit he acquired fifty years earlier in the Club teams and, he writes, in his delirious condition he re-fought his team battles over and over again and they gave him the desire and strength to win through, and satisfy his doctors. Ted joined the Club in 1897. He was then a young man who listened to his foreman (a Belgrave Hon. Secretary) talking of sporting walkers at lunch time, and enquired how he could join Belgrave. He was told that the first step was to sign a nomination form and submit it with a shilling entry fee. To do this, Ted who lived at Chelsea and worked at Baker Street, got up earlier each morning and walked to work, thus saving the two-pence a day allowed him by his mother for workman's fare. Thus in a week he saved his nomination fee and became a member in 1897 ( when his wages were 10/- weekly for a sixty-hour week! ), and was elected to Life Membership 54 years ago. Ted Good, who was an Hon. Editor in 1908, now lives at Brighton; and weather permitting, tries to get to the finish of all the big athletic events in the hopes of seeing a Belgrave win. Eric Hall's versatility as a walker can never have been surpassed in the history of the sport; and his record in 1958 of not having been further back than fifth in any of the five major championships ( three on the road and two on the track) must be unique. The performances are :- What a magnificent record! Our heartiest congratulations go to John Sams on winning the A.A.A. and Southern 200 yards Hurdles Championships, and the L.C.C. junior 100 yards Championship. John may be booked for the Army soon but we look forward to seeing him in our senior teams in the years ahead, and have every confidence that his ambition to win an A.A.A. 440 yards Hurdles Championship will be realised one day. Another junior whose future looks bright is Dave Mitchell who put up a personal best time in winning the L.C.C. Junior Half Mile Championship very cleverly from a good class field. We derived a great deal of pleasure in winning the "W.J.Pepper Memorial Cup" for the Club gaining the greatest aggregate of points in the L.C.C. Championships; for Bill Pepper had very close associations with our Club going back many years. Our former President, Bob Ricketts and Bill were great friends, and Bill always had a very warm spot in his very warm heart for Belgrave. We were also pleased in the manner of winning, for our Runners, Field Events men, Walkers and Juniors all shared in the effort - which is Club spirit at its best. There was also pleasure in seeing our teams finish second and fourth respectively in the 4 x 110 yards and 4 x 440 yards A.A.A. Relay Championships. Only two clubs could qualify for both finals, and we were one of them! John Palmer has resumed light training and we would hope that perhaps in twelve months time he will be claiming a place in our teams. After showing great promise as a Junior, John did his National Service with the Army in Germany, where he had many close races with J. Merriman who has subsequently distinguished himself both on track and cross-country in the highest company. Most unfortunately, John Palmer was found to have a kidney complaint on his return to civil life, and this has necessitated long treatment which appears to have been successful, as was forecast. Meanwhile every time Merriman runs it serves to underline the potentialities of our John Palmer; and we hope his cure will be complete and permanent. The "Tommy Green" Cup for the best athletic performance of the year by a Club member has been awarded to Stan Vickers for his magnificent win in the 20,000 metres European Games Walk. Could there be any argument? The following comments from Harold Whitlock, a former Olympic and European Games Champion himself, who acted as Chief Walking Judge at Stockholm will be read with pride by all Belgravians. "I arrived back with the British Team last evening after a good week in Stockholm. The team was one of the happiest that have taken part in any of these events. That was the opinion of the athletes themselves, and much of the credit must go to the officials with the team for their handling of the group. Without doubt the Team's success sprung from the inspiration given them by Stan Vickers, whose performance was the best piece of race-walking I have ever seen. He was always the master, even when behind the leaders in the initial stages, and when he decided to go they just could not match him, and in trying to do so two of them suffered disqualification. Belgrave have good reason to be very proud of Stan and I can tell you that I, too, felt very proud when the judges congratulated me on his success and said that he was without doubt the best walker in every respect. As an Ambassador of British walking he is likely to open up avenues that have eluded us in the past, such is his prestige among the walking nations". items.sum: New-year editorial urging members to support the club and train harder, singling out junior C. Thompson as a promising athlete.
items.s: EDITORIAL New-year editorial urging members to support the club and train harder, singling out junior C. Thompson as a promising athlete. Dear Fellow Members, Although a little late, we take this opportunity of wishing all members a happy and successful new year. Doubtless many resolutions have already suffered their inevitable fate, but at least two should still be foremost in our minds. Firstly let us resolve to support our Club in as many events as possible, whether as competitors or officials and secondly,we must resolve to train harder, this applies especially to our youths and juniors. The amount of punishment a properly trained athlete can absorb is fantastic. If we remember that most fatigue is purely psychological, then perhaps we can drag ourselves out for that training session which, although dreaded, invariably becomes most enjoyable. Certain members stand out as likely to perform exceptionally well in Belgrave colours this year, and among them is C. Thompson, a junior, whose improvement during the last year has been great to see. He has a fine future ahead of him provided he is able to distinguish between good and bad advice as regards his training and choice of events. It is a pity that so much harmful advice is often given to young athletes when their careers are in the infancy stage. C. Thompson C. Thompson junior, praised for improvement

items.s: TED GOOD Obituary of Ted Good, a member for over half a century, who died after a serious illness. In our last issue we gave news of Ted Good, whose years with the Club extended over half a century. We now learn with sincere regret of his death; it is evident that he never fully recovered from his most serious illness of a few months ago. Ted's passing means the severing of yet another link with our early history and it is pleasing to note that he was so recently able to put into proper perspective, for many of us, the early days of the Belgrave Harriers and those who made up the Club in those days. Our sincere sympathy goes to Ted's widow. A.A.H. Ted Good Ted Good death; member for over half a century A.A.H. A.A.H.

items.sum: Obituary of George Still, a familiar club figure for sixty years and former Highgate Harriers runner, who died aged 82 after swimming.
items.s: George Still Obituary of George Still, a familiar club figure for sixty years and former Highgate Harriers runner, who died aged 82 after swimming. We mourn the passing of one who had been a familure figure in the Club dressing rooms and over our courses for sixty years and more. Many of us had our first run over Wimbledon Common with George, and listened to his reminiscences of races and athletics of years gone by with glowing interest. George had his first race at the age of eighteen at the Putney Velodrome in the 1890's and he continued to run for the next sixty years. Latterly he had contented himself with his second love - swimming and diving; and death came to him on the 4th of October when, after swimming three lengths at the Baths, he collapsed and died at the age of 82 years. In his heyday George was a member of the Highgate Harriers teams which dominated the Southern Cross Country Championships for a decade, and he was a member of their winning "National" teams in 1904 and 1905. He was a more than useful performer at any distance from 880 yards up to the Marathon, and was honoured by an invitation to compete at the Olympic Games, but this he had to decline for domestic reasons. We shall remember George Still with affection as a great character and sportsman and as a link with our early days when there were cross country courses to be found in the Battersea neighbourhood. items.s: To George Still of the Belgrave Harriers Farewell poem to George Still by L. Fabre, a 70-year-old Belgrave runner. I taught you how to swim, you taught me how to run, What a clean life it was, for it was full of fun, You started before me George and you never did pause, But watch for me Georgie for I am very close, And again full of fun, We may meet for that final great run, Farewell George, you were a great sport and I respected you. items.s: POLY. HARRIERS ROAD RELAY (8 x 3 miles) SEPT. 20TH. Report of the Poly. Harriers road relay, where Dave Baulch set a club best and the Belgrave A team was 5th. Conditions were perfect and personal bests cut by 30 sec. were the order of the day. On the first leg Dave Baulch ran 13.42 to set up a new Club best, only to be 250 yds. behind the leader, Roath(Walton), who sliced 16s. off the course record with a magnificent 13.01. A notable feature of the 'A' team was the fine running of R. Bhatia, who should be a great asset on the Brighton road. The 'A' team finished 5th. The 'B' team were 9th (second 'B'team), and at half-way they were still ahead of the strong Herne Hill 'A' team. Ken Miller, despite little training, looked very fit showing 14.08 - fastest of the 'B' team. The 'C' team finished 25th of the 31 starting teams. items.label: No. 137
items.h: LONDON TO BRIGHTON RELAY (SOUTHERN CLUBS) OCT.11TH
items.sum: Stage-by-stage account by Eric Hall of Belgrave's sixth place in the London to Brighton road relay for southern clubs, with a call to rebuild the club's running and the stage times.
items.s: LONDON TO BRIGHTON RELAY (SOUTHERN CLUBS) OCT.11TH Stage-by-stage account by Eric Hall of Belgrave's sixth place in the London to Brighton road relay for southern clubs, with a call to rebuild the club's running and the stage times. The Brighton, I am informed, is almost always held in fine weather, and this year was no exception. October 11th. was the sort of day when a trip to the sea is just what Doctor Brighton would order. As I am a newcomer to this business of road-relays, I needed quite a lot of persuading to enter into the spirit of things. After much coaxing I was waiting at Big Ben for the first stroke of ten to set 20 lightly clad figures on their way. At last Big Ben warmed up and the chime rang out clearly and they were off. (Thought - what happens if there is a false start? Perhaps they go home and wait till next year). That was that, I thought, as they disappeared out of sight but my chauffeur was already revving his car after a Le Mans type start, so I joined in the chase. Down Millbank and across Battersea Bridge where Brian Hallowell was nicely placed in ninth place after a leisurely start. Then satisfied that Brian knew what he was doing, we sped on to Clapham Common for the first change-over. Brian had moved up to seventh and away went Charlie Walker. Portsmouth had a slight lead from Brighton and T.V.H. Charlie did well in the early part, but was being closely followed. However, on arrival at Mitcham he had moved up to sixth. We had dropped further behind the leaders and the gaps had begun to appear. Lewis(Woodford) and Pape (Portsmouth) were in contrast here and it was surprising to see Pape go away quite easily. Dave Baulch, usually on a later stage, was having a change of scenery this year but as he was surrounded by Internationals he not surprisingly had to relinquish two vital places. At Purley it was Clive Shippen's turn to take his medicine and at nineteen miles we took a rough time check; Portsmouth led Woodford by thirty seconds with Herne Hill moving up well seventeen seconds behind. Then came a long gap until T.V.H. and Walton followed by Aylesford and Essex Beagles with Clive chasing hard. We were now four minutes behind Portsmouth - not a very bright outlook. When we eventually caught up with the runners again, (those motor driven coaches are a greater nuisance than the athletic type) we found Jim Masters in command. The manner in which he tackled the long climb through Redhill was ajoy to watch, he made short work of two of the intruders and we were back to sixth again. John Davies had the shortest trip of the day (hardly worth the bother of changing John!) and at Salfords Woodford had taken over from Pompey, we had improved slightly and were now three minutes and twenty seconds in arrears; it was felt that this was still too large a gap. The next man to show his paces was newcomer to the Brighton road, Mal Robinson. He had what I consider to be a very unpleasant stretch past Gatwick Airport; he held on to our position but unfortunately the gaps grew wider. Our next glimpse of the race was after Crawley, and Portsmouth were back in the lead. Pat Newell was doing the first of the two long legs for us and he was being closely followed by Ilford, Polytechnic and Hampstead in a bunch which looked rather ominous. However, Pat didn't let us down and we held our position. Just outside Bolney we had a grand view of the race and Pompey led by over a minute from Woodford. Eric Gebbett was doing his utmost to hold on to our place but the fifth team, T.V.H., were over three minutes in front. Harry Hicks was on this leg for Hampstead and looked very dangerous but Eric refused to be panicked and towards the end was moving away slightly. For us the race was now over, as the gaps were such that we required at least three top class three-milers; we could only hope that our remaining runners would hold our position. Charlie Dabbs had other ideas and put up the third fastest time for the tenth stage. He was relieved on the tricky Dale Hill stage by "veteran" Archie Bedford who put us well clear of the rest of the field. The last man, but by no means the least, was John Moore. Not for him a dramatic finish as for some previous Belgravians, nor the feeling of truimph, just the steady plod home unheralded save by the faithful supporters who had cheered their club-mates all the way from Mitcham. Our sixth position entitles us to compete in the National next April, but as we finished six minutes and forty-two seconds in arrears I do not hold out much hope for a Belgrave victory. This year's race was not particularly fast and we lost an average of eight seconds every mile. The supporters as always did a magnificent job of work, but only those with long years of service can remember a Belgrave win. Surely its about time they had another? I am not a very senior member, but when I became a Belgravian in 1948 we were National Cross Country Champions. We had many fine runners and as now a great tradition. Of recent years we have slipped rapidly down hill, but every club has its ups and downs, so what about an all-round effort; some serious training, then and only then will the results follow. Our walkers have proved that it can be done. Only a few years ago we weren't figuring in the results, so Jack Goswell thought it was about time we got back to our rightful position. Someone could do the same for the runners. All it requires is a large back and the ability not to take no for an answer. We have enough men capable of handling this job of welding the lads into a TEAM and thereby getting the results that the "old timers" achieved. This is not a new recipe, it is one which brought Belgrave fame in the past and will do the same again we hope in the near future. Eric Hall. Stage times with stage rankings in brackets:- 1 B. items.sum: Report of the five-club cross-country match at Dartford, where Belgrave won both the five-a-side and eight-a-side matches.
items.s: MATCH AT DARTFORD - 18TH OCT. Report of the five-club cross-country match at Dartford, where Belgrave won both the five-a-side and eight-a-side matches. This five-sided fixture involving Dartford H., City of Rochester A.C., Maidstone A.C., Kent A.C. and, of course, ourselves was the first event of the cross-country season, and following so closely on the London to Brighton relay was expected to be something of an anti-climax. Also, with our forces split between the Walton "10" and the organisation of our own open Youths road relay, a strong turn-out was not envisaged for such a distant fixture. However, all predictions were proved wrong with a splendid turn-out of seventeen, but which included only three of the previous week's twelve Brighton men. Once again we illustrated our great depth by winning both the five-a-side and eight-a-side matches. Owing to the uneven apportionment of Juniors in the five clubs it was decided to run both grades in one senior scoring race over 5½ miles. Despite the brisk start up a half-mile incline, John Moore wasn't satisfied with the pace and, accompanied by Bob Glover and J. Lyne of S.L.H.(2nd claim Kent A.C.), forged ahead to establish a clear lead of thirty yards after 1¼ miles. Shortly afterwards he had the misfortune to go off course at a point which should clearly have had a marksman rather than a flag. By the time he had been called back and rejoined the race he had dropped to 25th place. It says much for his determination and ever improving form that he was able to fight his way back to fourth place at the finish. Approaching the end of the first lap Miller, Thompson, Glover, Bedford and Shippen were in close attendance around tenth position with John Moore moving through fast after his mishap. Morrison of Dartford and Ellam of Rochester were sharing a lead of 75 yds. Ellam eventually pulled away to win by eighteen seconds in a new course record time of 26.12. Shippen moved through well over the last mile and he was closely followed by Archie Bedford who had run steadily throughout. Bob Glover found out too late that one mustn't underestimate the finishing speed of those behind, especially when they include an accomplished half miler like Gerald Batty of Rochester! With Miller, Thompson and Bob Taylor backing up very closely Belgrave were assured of the team race. One of our recent recruits, John Collier, ran well in his first race for the Club and should soon become a more than useful runner. If the remainder of the winter fixtures are supported as well as this one, then Belgrave is indeed on the road back to their all-conquering past in cross-country running. Result:- 4,J. items.s: HIGHGATE OPEN 7 MILES WALK 25TH OCT. Report and result of the Highgate open 7 miles walk, where Stan Vickers was second to record-breaker Ken Matthews and Belgrave won the scratch and handicap team races. The first open race of the season must inevitably cause some anxiety as to how our teams have weathered and how they are likely to fare in subsequent championships. This worry was soon dispelled however, as our team, led by Stan Vickers, quickly established themselves amongst the leaders. A great race for individual honours took place between Ken Matthews of Royal Sutton Coldfield and Stan, with the former just getting the verdict in a time which shattered the previous course record by more than two minutes. The remainder of our team walked extremely well and with Ray Hall, Ray Middleton, George Checkley and John Knifton we easily won the scratch team race. We also won the team handicap, which is an important feature of these open walks, with Stan, R. Hall, R. Middleton and J. Knifton. It was an added pleasure to note the good walking of our younger men, particularly that of Brian Cornick and Robert Barns. 1st Belgrave H. 45 pts. 2nd Highgate H. 57 pts. 3rd Woodford 62 pts. 2 S.F. items.sum: Report of Belgrave's eighth place in the Chelmsford road relay, their first visit since winning the trophy in 1952, with stage-by-stage account and times.
items.s: CHELMSFORD ROAD RELAY 25TH OCT. Report of Belgrave's eighth place in the Chelmsford road relay, their first visit since winning the trophy in 1952, with stage-by-stage account and times. This was our first visit to Chelmsford since 1952 when we won the magnificent trophy for the second successive year. Unfortunately, the date now clashes with our five-mile cross-country handicap, but surely six of our best men can be spared each year to at least "show face" at such an important event; and so it was. Our six were Bob Glover, Malcolm Robinson, Alan Black, Eric Gebbett, Charlie Walker and Dave Baulch; three relative newcomers to road relay racing and three "veterans". Fifty-six teams started and it was soon apparent that many clubs treat this race as their event of the year. It was good to see Bob Glover turning out for us in this type of event, and his running justified the confidence many have in him. After a mile he was still amongst the leaders and a little later began to force the pace on Lewis(Woodford), Stacey(T.V.H.) and Cornell(Chelmsford). However, he was unable to maintain this speed and finished in 12th position. Malcolm Robinson set off in great style for lap 2 and after about two miles had passed no less than seven men, being only ten seconds behind fourth place. He continued to narrow the gap before he in turn was caught and passed, after quite a battle, by Haith of T.V.H. Malcolm returned our fastest time of the day - 15.24. Young Alan Black, undeterred by the star names around him, ran a very sensible 3rd stage, dropping places only to Sando and O'Gorman, each of whom broke the course record. White took Woodford into a lead here which they kept to the end, while Bert Ingles drew away from Alan to increase the Valley's lead over us to 29s. Eric Gebbett took over in eighth position with three men in close attendance and promptly showed how well he runs in company by shaking off all three and gaining two further places into the bargain. All this over a distance which is little more than a sprint to Eric. J. Haslam, with a time only seven seconds faster than Eric's took T.V.H. into third place, five places ahead of the Bels who conceded a further place to Chelmsford. Charlie Walker set off on leg 5 and soon passed Chelmsford to regain sixth place but was eventually overtaken by Mayatt of Aylesford and Irons of Victoria Park. This was not the Charlie of old, although his time was faster than many recorded in 1952 when 15 minutes had yet to be beaten. However, when he handed over to Dave Baulch for the final leg we were still within 14 sec. of sixth place. Unfortunately Dave was nowhere near his inspired best and we had to be content with our eighth position. As a point of interest, our three experienced runners recorded an aggregate time of 46.45 while the inexperienced trio totalled 46.34! - the shape of things to come? items.s: SMITHS OF ENGLAND 12½ MILES ROAD RACE AT WITNEY. NOV.1ST. Report of the Smiths of England 12½ miles road race at Witney, where Belgrave retained the team title, with Belgrave placings. Once again our journey to the "Burfitt" domain was well rewarded as we retained our hold on the team title, winning by the fairly comfortable margin of eight points. items.s: CLUB 7 MILES C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP DEC.6TH Report and result of the club 7 miles cross-country championship, won by Charlie (Chas.) Walker from Pat Newell and John Moore. A bright but cold day brought forth a rather small field for a club of our size, but perhaps quality of individuals takes precedence over quantity of team runners these days. A notable non-starter was Dave Baulch, suffering from a heavy cold, who, despite the assertions of the old-timers that a race would do him good, wisely refrained from competing. A steady start meant a large bunch of runners in the lead for the first two miles, but as the weaker flesh fell away it was left to Chas. Walker, John Moore and Pat Newell to decide the issue, with Eric Gebbett, Malcolm Robinson and Alan Black forming the spearhead of the second bunch. At the top of the hockey field on the second lap Chas. sprinted ahead of Newell and opening up a gap ran home a fairly comfortable winner, with John Moore finishing a close third after a well judged race. items.s: CAMBRIDGE H. 7 MILES OPEN WALK. DEC.6TH Light-hearted spectator's notes ('Random notes of an Idle Fellow') on the Cambridge H. 7 miles open walk at Eltham, won by Stan Vickers with Belgrave taking the team race, with results. Random notes of an Idle Fellow The cold and cheerless afternoon afforded an excellent excuse for turning up at Eltham and exclaiming "I am resting", as a reason for standing on the side-line and offering to all and sundry, "free of charge", words of encouragement, advice or derision, according to my fancy. It was a wonderful change from ploughing my usual weary way, to achieve, after much sweat, effort and banter, some unmentionable time. The only reward being the tussle with "so and so" and the grand comradeship of those who "walk the roads". What were my impressions of this band of brothers who wear the Claret and Gold with such distinction? If pride be the prerogative of bantam cocks, then I was a very proud bantam cock when battle was joined and our contingent, led by that superlative walker Stan Vickers, flay the enemy at every level Space is too limited to more than just refer to the tenacity and pugnaciousness of Eric Hall, the daintiness of George Williams which camoufleges no ordinary resoluteness, the strength of Ray Middleton who must be a future champion, the potential powers of Terry Clark and Brian Cornick, and so through the team to our last man, Percy Wilson, who so typifies the fun and enjoyment obtained from the sport. The ten prizes awarded to our men is a measure of their success and a study of the following results will clearly show how they dominated the proceedings. In conclusion, I would emphasize the amount of fun and enjoyment that can be obtained from watching these athletic competitions and ask you, when free, to support the current fixture, be it running or walking. It will be a great encouragement to the competitors concerned and the effort will be well repaid by the comradeship obtained from a greater knowledge of your fellow members. 1 S.F. items.sum: Club news column: Ken England is very ill with disseminated sclerosis, the Coleman brothers' late-night walking training is recalled, Len Herbert has lost the urge to race, and Jack Brown writes from troubled Cyprus.
items.s: Here and There Club news column: Ken England is very ill with disseminated sclerosis, the Coleman brothers' late-night walking training is recalled, Len Herbert has lost the urge to race, and Jack Brown writes from troubled Cyprus. Many members will remember Ken England, a rather tough determined cross-country runner of a few years back. Ginger Kennedy writes to tell us that Ken is a very ill man, now hardly able to walk due to disseminated schlerosis. We feel sure that all readers will join us in wishing him a speedy recovery. They used to breed 'em tough in the old days, and the brothers Joe and Len Coleman were no exception. None of your fancy 9 to 5 hours for them; in fact at well past midnight both could have been found still hard at work in their respective trades, printing and catering. But training had to be fitted in and as both were walkers this was carried out by a brisk walk home from work at about 2 a.m. Needless to say they would both walk back to work the next morning. Can anyone beat this? Len Herbert is apparently still running several times a week but says he has lost the urge to race. His brother Eric is now married to a Dutch girl and he has now fully recovered from his serious climbing accident. Jack Brown writes to say how really difficult life has become in Cyprus; the strain on everyone is intense and being practically confined to their house Jack and his wife Betty and son Malcolm find their greatest enjoyment is derived from their record player. We hope it won't be long before commonsense prevails, bringing a return to normal conditions in Cyprus and that before long Jack will be back to don his Claret and Gold vest again to good account. items.label: No. 137
items.sum: Letter from Harry Shields, prompted by a 1934 training schedule for the Southern Counties and English cross-country championships, regretting that no member was selected for the Inter-Counties and urging members to focus training on the main championships.
items.s: SINGLENESS OF PURPOSE Letter from Harry Shields, prompted by a 1934 training schedule for the Southern Counties and English cross-country championships, regretting that no member was selected for the Inter-Counties and urging members to focus training on the main championships. Dear Fellow Members, I wonder how many of us, with the approach of "Spring Cleaning Season", suddenly become filled with a desire to have a clear out of our accumulated momentoes aquired over the ages? How many of us start, only to get bogged down in browsing over those relics of the past? Such was my fate when, a little prematurely perhaps, it was forced on me that, if domestic peace was to be maintained, then a major surgical operation was required on my heaped up store of minute books, nomination forms, programmes and all the other impedimenta gathered in club and association activities. Many papers recalling "life and death" contentions of previous years were ruthlessly destroyed, but I could not help dwelling on the three page "Schedule of training for Southern Counties and English Cross-Country Championships 1934" It commences," In the past the cross-country members of our Club have entered the New Year without any definite idea as regards training for any particular race other than running twice or three times a week as members of a pack or otherwise" Then follows a summary of improvement which should arise from systematic training. A list of eleven exercises is tabulated, to be carried out every morning. These include dumbell exercises and hints on general hygiene and diet. The week by week training schedule is graduated until immediately previous to the Southern Championships; it reads:- Monday - 3 miles in 18 mins. Tuesday - 7 " " 37 " Wednesday - 3 " " 18 " Thursday - 3 " " 18 " Friday - Complete rest except for exercises. Saturday - 12 miles in 65 mins. Sunday - Stroll about 20 miles In addition, every morning, a stroll part way to work is recommended. Even in the light of modern experience it is an extraordinarily far-sighted document and of its benefits the performances of those who were influenced by it are perhaps the best yardstick. You will perhaps excuse my nostalgic reviews of the past, but at Parliament Hill recently on the occasion of the Inter-Counties Championship there was not one single member selected to represent his County. It appeared particularly incredible when I thought of the ability of many of our athletes only to remember how quickly they break off at a tangent for some "out of season event". Such actions seem almost escapist from the realities of the principle targets. This inevitably leads to the question, " what are the targets?" The answer to this must be, "The Championships sponsored by the governing bodies at the particular time of the year". These Championships must be given prime consideration if the maximum benefit is to be obtained from our great sport. I appreciate that taking lessons from the past is open to criticism but the conclusion is inescapeable that singleness of purpose is absolutely essential if the greatest success as an individual or as a club is to be achieved. Is it not worthwhile to discuss your training ideas with your section leader with a view to formulating a schedule for modern needs? For my part the influence of these early schedules on a very varied athletic career has been considerable. In conclusion, the best of luck and although the way to success may be difficult and weary, do not be diverted by the glitter of side-shows and above all ensure that there is thought and direction in all that you do. Sincerely yours. Harry Shields Harry Shields Harry Shields Southern Cross Country Championships English Cross-Country Championships Inter-Counties Cross Country Championships Parliament Hill

items.s: FIELD EVENTS GOSSIP Field events column by Field Events Secretary T.C. Jones: Belgrave men in the 1958 British ranking lists, hopes for the Sward Trophy, and the club's pre-season Open Meeting at Battersea on March 14th. In welcoming another New Year we look forward to the coming summer season with hopes of greater successes. Our performances last year were not, on the whole, as good as in some previous years but nevertheless it is good to see some of our men's names appearing in the British ranking list with the following marks:- Also appearing in the lists was Dick Harris, an ex-Belgravian now in New Zealand, with a 47'4½" Shot Putt and 146'9" in the Discus. Whilst mentioning Shot Putters we are pleased to welcome Derek McCorquindale who recorded a best of 50'3" and was in the English team at Cardiff. Young John Roche who is just over 15 must not be forgotten as his 5'7" in the High Jump was easily a best Club performance for a Belgravian of his age. His progress over the next few years will be watched with great interest, as also will that of John Sams who won both Southern and A.A.A. Junior 200 yards Hurdles Championships. With our best performers of last year, Derek McCorquindale and perhaps one of our reasonable Javelin throwers getting nearer the 200' mark we should put up a really good show in"The Sward", Trophy, especially as John Sams will then be a Senior and Charlie Jones will be out to make the grade at 440 yards hurdling. John Powell Jones who won the Welsh Shot Championship two seasons ago must not be left out of the reckoning as I hear that he has recovered from his back injury. Some winter and early season training should be got in with our sights on "The Sward" and pre-season competition will be provided by the T.V.H. meeting in February and our own Open Meeting on March 14th. The latter is at Battersea and the events are as follows:- Shot Discus Javelin Pole Vault High Jump Long Jump Triple Jump There are no prizes and no entry fees, but your entries are expected in full support of this Club venture. We have welcome news of Ted Gaworski in that he is back at work and progressing. He promises that he will be back on the Field at the earliest moment. T.C. items.label: No. 137
items.sum: Eric Hall's humorous account of the trip to the Great Britain versus France match in Paris, where Stan Vickers won the 10,000 metres walk with Hall second.
items.s: GAY PAREE Eric Hall's humorous account of the trip to the Great Britain versus France match in Paris, where Stan Vickers won the 10,000 metres walk with Hall second. A 10,000 metres walk was included in the Great Britain versus France match in Paris on the 13/14th. Sept. Stan Vickers and myself were lucky enough to get the trip. Behind that bald statement lies a wealth of incident which could fill this magazine for the next few issues. We arrived in Paris late Friday evening and found our quarters in the National Institute des Sports at Vincennes, some six miles from the centre of Paris. No doubt this was specially selected by the B.A.A.B. The quarters themselves were comfortable but the meals were of microscopic proportions. After what was by even continental standards, a very meagre breakfast a few of us adjourned to the nearest market to stock up for the rest of the stay. Stan was appointed C.[illegible]. stores and the rest of us supplied the money and the lingo. After a short lesson on French Stan was pushed into a shop and asked to buy some honey. In less time than it takes Peter Radford to run 100 metres he was back, protesting,"I can't understand a word she's saying". Apparently the poor girl didn't speak Hindustani! Stan's next attempt was very much better, he wanted some grapefruit, so after yelling it in French for some moments he was 'bout to give up when the girl turned on a dazzling smile and said, in perfect English,"Ah, you would like some grapefruit". That was the last we heard of Stan's French! Saturday afternoon was very warm, so after taking part in the march-past we decided to "do" the town. Only 5000 people were at the stadium so we didn't want to be conspicuous. Somehow or other we made our way to the Arc de Triomphe and there we made an error of judgement when someone suggested crossing the road, the person concerned being a sprinter- naturally! After a couple of attempts and some"lifting" by Stan and myself we made it. Stan was most disappointed as nearly everyone was American so he couldn't practise his French. The stadium was some 12 miles from our quarters so we were quite pleased with ourselves when we got safely back. This is a feat which Jack Goswell couldn't do in London, let alone Paris. Sunday was one of the hottest days of the year and in the morning we basked in the sun (that all too rare thing this summer). Stan and I duly performed in the afternoon and of course our European Gold-Medallist romped home in 47m.3s. with myself second, after some very anxious moments, in 48m.44s. Attane of France was third in 48m.57s. Not world shattering times but just good enough. Once again we forgot about the match in which, incidently, the walk did not count, and moved smartly to the Buffet- Bar to quench a hard earned thirst. On our return to the stands we found that while we had been emptying bottles, Stan Eldon had been doing the same to the steeplechase pit, much to the amusement of the 5000 staunch supporters who had turned up for the second day. The match itself produced some very fine running, but it was a very one-sided affair, with England winning all the track events and finishing up with nearly twice as many points as the French. As L'Equipe pointed out the next day, our overall supremacy was equalled by our victory in the final event, the 4 x 400 metres relay, which we won by eight seconds. As soon as the meeting was over we dashed back for a meal and were then taken to the Folies Bergere. I will not attempt to describe the various acts but leave it to what I feel sure are very adequate imaginations! We left the show at midnight and made for the Institute via several cafes and didn't finally arrive back until around 3 a.m. - much too late for bed! Much could still be written of Stan's adventures - his near arrest at the Folies, his missing the way home after volunteering to act as guide to three female members of the team - it only took him two hours to do two miles that night! It wouldn't really be fair to blacken his character any more. He probably had the last laugh on me next morning. Before we left London someone had most unkindly told Stan that it was my birthday on the Monday. Stan remembered this at the most inopportune moment and so at Le Bourget a full choir of British athletes sang "Happy Birthday", it was much worse than the Boeing 707 warming up outside! items.label: No. 137
items.sum: Plea to value the club's older, less active members, whose subscriptions and gifts fund its 43 championship trophies and its expenses.
items.s: A QUESTION OF AGE Plea to value the club's older, less active members, whose subscriptions and gifts fund its 43 championship trophies and its expenses. Having heard a number of comments recently regarding our older and less active members, with suggestions that we might be better off without some of them, leads me to wonder if these critics realise how much the Club owes to these enthusiastic supporters who, year after year, and without any hope of personal gain, continue to subscribe regularly to help provide facilities for the younger members, which, without such support would not be available. A study of the Club Handbook will show that we have 43 Championship trophies, valued, according to the Balance, at £1200. These have, in the main, been provided by or in association with, some of the "old" members to encourage competition among the younger ones. The financing of these Championships on track, field and road and also over the country, is only one of the many large items of expenditure which need the support of far more than the hundred or so active athletes who take part in them. Since Amateur Athletics remains one of the few things which are not State aided let us be grateful to those who, because of their affection for the name of Belgrave and in return for the pleasure they have gained in the past, continue to give their support wholeheartedly, generously and in a spirit of comradeship. A "Not so old 'un"

items.label: No. 137
items.sum: Light-hearted note on the 1958 Annual General Meeting, praising President Frank Webb.
items.s: A.G.M. 1958 Light-hearted note on the 1958 Annual General Meeting, praising President Frank Webb. A motley crowd turned up, including most of the "old faithfuls". The meeting always begins with orations from the chair with varying degrees of linguistic ability, but who cares! The old cry, "no change", heralds the appointment of the Officers who must have lots of time to spare, (wait for it) good show chaps! Our old friend Frank tried to create a diversion but was really shot down in flames by Bomber Lucas. The mystery of the missing vests could have caused acute distress to one of our members, but who said that the age of chivalry is dead and so, with age old charm, an apology was offered and dignity restored. Frank Webb is a worthy President, unassuming, no sting in his tongue. A.W.P. Bomber Lucas Bomber Lucas Frank Webb Frank Webb President A.W.P. A.W.P. A.G.M.

items.label: No. 137
items.h: A FEW WORDS FROM YOUR SOCIAL SECRETARY
items.sum: Social Secretary Bert Jordon's notes: poorly supported dances, thanks for the children's party of 11 January 1959, a coming Social and Dance, coaches for the London to Brighton relay, and a proposed summer outing.
items.s: A FEW WORDS FROM YOUR SOCIAL SECRETARY Social Secretary Bert Jordon's notes: poorly supported dances, thanks for the children's party of 11 January 1959, a coming Social and Dance, coaches for the London to Brighton relay, and a proposed summer outing. The Socials and Dances held so far this season have not been very well supported. I would like to see many more members taking advantage of these functions. We have a good class Band and those who do support us on these occasions have a very enjoyable time. Why not come along and see for yourself at the next Social, I am sure you will want to come again. Children's Party - Jan.11th, 1959 This function was a great success, the children enjoyed the entertainer "Uncle Jim" very much. He held their attention for a whole hour with his feats of magic and he ended with a Punch and Judy show, which the Mums and Dads enjoyed just as much as the children. I would like to take this opportunity of thanking, firstly the Ladies, Mrs Carter, Mrs Shepherd, Mrs Savage and Mrs Jordon for all their hard work, both on Saturday afternoon and Sunday, in preparing and serving the children's tea and serving refreshments for the parents, and also Mrs Lucas for her help with the children's tea and entertainments. Also Dick Savage for his efforts as Father Christmas, which he performed excellently, and for his help in the kitchen, also Bill Lucas and Bob Taylor for their hard work in entertaining the children, and Malcolm Robinson for his assistance in the kitchen, and Tom Carter for his general assistance during the afternoon, and all the people, too numerous to mention, who helped to make the party a success. There must have been many more children who could have been present but whose names were not given to me. So I would like to mention that children from twelve months to twelve years old are welcome to attend this annual party. There surely could be many more than the thirty-six who attended this year's For your future entertainment A Social and Dance will be held on Saturday 24th March. This will be the last of the season and I am hoping that you will all give it your support. London to Brighton Relay Two coaches have been booked for spectators to follow the National Relay on the 11th April. Tickets will, as usual, be 10/- each and they can be obtained from Bob Taylor. An early application will be appreciated, as it will enable us to book a further coach if necessary. Come along and cheer our team to Brighton. Summer Outing It is hoped to arrange an outing to a seaside resort on a Sunday in June or July. Would members please let me have their views on this proposal. Thanking you for your support during the season and looking forward to even greater support in the future. Bert Jordon. items.label: No. 138
items.sum: Editorial thanking contributors, welcoming shot putter Don McCorquindale, noting early-season form, praising "our Sten"'s win in Berlin and hinting the editors would like to hand over the gazette.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial thanking contributors, welcoming shot putter Don McCorquindale, noting early-season form, praising "our Sten"'s win in Berlin and hinting the editors would like to hand over the gazette. Dear Fellow Members, It never rains but what it pours and before going to press we have been inundated with contributions for the magazine from all quarters. So please, those critics whose voices are exercised more frequently than their pens, don't itemise what has been omitted but be thankful that a far greater number of articles have been submitted. Once again we have a fine weight putter in the Club, Don McCorquindale, who has made a fine start to the 1959 season. Charlie Jones must be greatly pleased with such an acquisition for our field events section. Brian Morris and John Davies have already recorded good times for the 440 yds. and 1500 metres respectively, whilst Alan Black and Malcolm Robinson look set for their best seasons yet. We are all justly proud of "our Sten" for his great win in Berlin. This was really one out of the bag and his margin over Matthews was quite astounding. Lastly, a note of warning and possibly of hope. We have edited the Belgravian now for almost three years and as active marathon runners we feel that we have made our contribution towards the revival of the magazine and that perhaps some other aspiring editors in the Club would like to try their hand. When the A.G.M. comes round again we hope to be able to hand over this gazette to a new editor. items.sum: Notice inviting members to join a Belgravian party travelling to the 1960 Rome Olympics for about £43.
items.s: ROME OLYMPICS - 1960 Notice inviting members to join a Belgravian party travelling to the 1960 Rome Olympics for about £43. You do not have to own a television set to be able to see the Rome Olympics! If you wish, you can see the Games from a seat in the stadium together with a party of Belgravians and friends. For approximately £43 you can travel by steamer and rail, via Newhaven, Dieppe, Paris and Modane to Rome, be accommodated in a good hotel where you will breakfast and have an evening meal and see the athletic events in the stadium on an all-day ticket! During the Games there will be two free days when you can partake in any of the many sight-seeing tours. It should be remembered that August and September are the best months for seeing Rome when the hot summer is beginning to close. If you wish to join the party, contact either of the following:- M.E. Robinson, R.T. Taylor and D.M. Shepherd. Special arrangements will be made to enable you to pay the money over a period. M.E. Robinson M.E. Robinson contact for Rome Olympics party R.T. Taylor R.T. items.sum: Report and results of the Horwood Cup walking championship, won again by Ray Middleton from John Knifton and newcomer K. Jones.
items.s: "HORWOOD" CUP CHAMPIONSHIP - DEC.13TH. Report and results of the Horwood Cup walking championship, won again by Ray Middleton from John Knifton and newcomer K. Jones. Ray Middleton repeated his victory of last year. Oscar Horwood, a great Club man, would have been delighted to see another very good winner on the list of fine walkers whose names are recorded on his cup. Ray has the potential of a champion just as surely as we saw it in others who have fulfilled that promise. He led in excellent style throughout. John Knifton, a few years younger than Ray, was placed for the third year in succession, which shows that hard discipline of training for several years is necessary to win this event. A newcomer, K. Jones, did very well to finish third. Bob Barnes continues to improve and was unlucky to lose third place to this tough opponent. The rest of the race was keenly fought, as always, and many unplaced were working as hard as those who gained the medals. It was good to see Joe Wilson going so well after his accident and Bert East must have taken part in about twenty-five "Horwood Cup" races since the cup was instituted. At the same time there were novices who will be tomorrow's victors if they persevere. Harry Evans, an old friend of Oscar's, was there to see fair play and to give advice where needed. The ceremony of prize-giving brings a satisfying conclusion to an afternoon's sport and we were reminded of the thanks we owe to those who regularly organise the provision of prizes when, for once, the prizes and medals had, unfortunately, not arrived Handicap result:- 1 M. items.s: HOG'S BACK ROAD RACE - DEC.20TH Report of the inaugural 9¾ mile Hog's Back Road Race from Farnham to Guildford, where Belgrave were fourth team behind Portsmouth, with Belgrave finishers. Despite the counter attraction of a cross-country match, quite an appreciable number of Belgravians journeyed to Guildford for this inaugural 9¾ mile race from Farnham. Dave Baulch and Chas. Walker were well to the fore early on, and with Colin Collis, Archie Bedford, Len Bishop and Bob Plummer quite well placed, it seemed as if we might gain a team place in this well contested race. Baulch stayed up very well and left Walker who, feeling the effects of a cold, suffered on the two-mile downhill finishing stretch. Collis, when well placed, was beset with stomach cramp and forced to ease. It was good to see some of our younger elements, namely D. Crookes and J. Radford finishing in the first half of a strong field. No one could deny Portsmouth their amazing win, as they ran in together, 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th, while we finished a close fourth. 9 D.L. Once again this meeting was televised and was quite well supported. Stan Vickers went through 2 miles in 13m.54s. and completed 3 miles in 21m.5s., a very fine performance under not particularly good conditions. John Sams, making his first appearance in a Belgrave fixture for years, had a rather generous mark in the 120 yards. The Boreham Benefit! (2 miles) was won this year by Derek Crookes, making his third successive Club handicap - a worthy successor to Steve. Steve, recently married, ran but lacked training. To illustrate my earlier point, D. Crookes and J. Radford competed Xmas and Boxing Day and on the latter both ran personal bests. Derek Crookes is rapidly becoming a junior Jim Heathfield. items.s: SURREY C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS Surrey cross-country championships: the youths were 11th team at Banstead and the seniors fifth at Epsom. Youths - at Banstead, Dec. 12th Under really sticky conditions, a field of approximately 80, comprising fifteen teams got off to a good start. The Bels were in the van and Eric Penny had to struggle from the start. Part of the course was only wide enough to permit of single file running, so it was necessary to be at the front right from the start. Our boys ran well but lack racing and need to train much harder and start faster. Belgrave were 11th in the team race, and our individual positions were as follows:- 20, E. We were further mortified to find that we had lost the six to score cup by the narrow margin of four points. Colin Collis, making a very successful comeback, was our first man home. items.h: MATCH v. BLACKHEATH & H.H.H. AT HAYES - JAN.10TH.
items.sum: Report of the 7½ mile cross-country match against Blackheath and Herne Hill at Hayes, won by Blackheath; John Moore was second behind Mike Maynard and Chris Thompson retired injured.
items.s: MATCH v. BLACKHEATH & H.H.H. AT HAYES - JAN.10TH. Report of the 7½ mile cross-country match against Blackheath and Herne Hill at Hayes, won by Blackheath; John Moore was second behind Mike Maynard and Chris Thompson retired injured. Despite the Mitcham '15' accounting for many of our members we were still able to produce fifteen runners for this fixture, as against sixteen by Blackheath and nine by Herne Hill. The 7½ mile course had been extremely muddy the previous week but had since frozen hard. As a result the going was particularly hazardous, and three runners retired with twisted ankles on the "plough" while many put caution before performance. Mike Maynard set a fast pace at the start and was comfortably leading after a mile from John Moore and Chris Thompson with Clive Shippen and the Blackheath captain, A.W. Wood, a further 50 yards down. After 4½ miles John Moore had established himself in second place, about 200 yards behind Maynard, while Wood and Shippen, still running together, had virtually caught Thompson. At this stage Chris badly twisted his ankle in one of the frozen furrows and although he tried gamely to continue he was forced to retire. However, he had done sufficient to show once more what tremendous potential he possesses, and Junior honours could no doubt come his way during the next two seasons. Meanwhile John Davies and Jim Heathfield were doing battle with a string of Blackheath men a little further back. Both of our boys lost ground on the dangerous stretches with a sensible "safety first" policy but made it up in the last mile or so of even going; John, in particular, gaining several places. Maynard won convincingly by about 450 yards from Moore who ran exceedingly well and was always moving away from the Blackheath man in third place. Thompson's mishap did not affect the match result which was won by Blackheath's superior packing. Results:- 2, J. Moore 46.18; 4, C. Shippen 47.46; 8, J. Davies 48.37; 14, J. Heathfield 49.48; 19, J. items.sum: Report of the R.A.F. seven miles walking championship at Harpur Hill, led throughout by Terry Clark.
items.s: R.A.F. SEVEN MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the R.A.F. seven miles walking championship at Harpur Hill, led throughout by Terry Clark. This year's R.A.F. race might be described as one of Belgrave's triumphs. It was held at Harpur Hill, in North Derbyshire, on 28th January; a day when the bright sunshine and clean, crisp air made racing pleasant in spite of the hilly terrain. The course consisted of one small lap and a larger one of fairly good roads with not too much traffic. Terry Clark headed the field from the start and was never overtaken. The good walking of a "dark horse" in the person of Flt.Lt. O.G.J. Hotston during the early stages of the race gave rise to surprise and a measure of anxiety. Usually a cross-country runner for R.A.F. Lindholme, this Officer went after Terry and tenaciously hung on to second place until he began to tire. A.C. Desmond of R.A.F. Bridgenorth and Essex Beagles came through after the first three quarters of a mile in an endevour to get on terms with Terry and, in the meantime, Bernard Eglinton was battling it out for fourth place with Nigel Deeks of R.A.F. Cosford and Met. Walking Club. The former subsequently gained a lead of about thirty five yards. At two and a half miles, Holston was slowing down perceptibly and the second Belgrave man succeeded in passing him at about three miles. The course was now a steady climb to the five-mile point, followed by a steep downhill gradient and an equally severe uphill grind of about a mile to the finish. Terry quickened his pace and disappeared from view but Desmond seemed to slow a little on the hills. Deeks made a valiant bid for third place in the last mile and a half, actually drawing almost level with Eglinton on the last hill. On this occasion, however, age prevailed by a mere ten seconds. 1 Cpl. T.B. Clark 57m. 13s. Belgrave 2 A.C. M. Desmond 59m. 55s. Essex Beagles 3 F/S. B. Eglinton 60m. 32s. Belgrave 4 Sgt. N. items.sum: Report of the Southern Counties cross-country championships hosted by Aylesford Paper Mills: Belgrave youths fielded only three, the seniors were fifth team behind Thames Valley Harriers and the juniors seventh behind Shaftesbury Harriers, with Belgrave results.
items.s: SOUTHERN COUNTIES C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS - FEB.14TH. Report of the Southern Counties cross-country championships hosted by Aylesford Paper Mills: Belgrave youths fielded only three, the seniors were fifth team behind Thames Valley Harriers and the juniors seventh behind Shaftesbury Harriers, with Belgrave results. Hosts for this year's event were Aylesford Paper Mills who, not for the first time, provided ideal facilities for championships of this nature. The course was ideal for runners and spectators alike, while the weather man had assisted the arrangements by providing perfect conditions underfoot and a fine sunny day into the bargain. YOUTHS EVENT (3 miles) Belgrave's day did not get off to a very good start, for with four to score in the team event we were only able to field three runners - Eric Penny, Mike Smithers and Roy Bagley. How many of our absent youths appreciated just how much their presence was needed? Eric, in 114th position, led our trio home; all of whom performed creditably. No doubt the efforts of these lads will be better rewarded when some of Tom Carter's promising youngsters move into their ranks. The event was won by Dave Harvey (Mitcham) who ran an excellently judged race to beat Smith(Deptford Park). It is interesting to note that Harvey is second string in his club to Harris, a 'flu victim during this event, and also that all these Mitcham youths are enthusiastically coached by the ex-Belgrave Mitchell brothers. We congratulate them on their excellent results. SENIOR EVENT (9 miles) Influenza had taken its toll of many leading athletes, but this made the team race more open than ever. Unfortunately, for a variety of reasons, Archie Bedford, John Davies, Colin Collis and Clive Shippen were unable to run, so with six to score and a "12 cup" in the offing we were able to start nine only. The number was eight to begin with but Malcolm Robinson, despite a suspect ankle, made a fine gesture in offering to run, thus making our entry look more respectable. Yet again the Arthur Whitehead "dustbin" sent the field on its way and after a ½ mile Pat Newell was 14th with Chanin(S.L.H.) leading from Ibbottson and Norris. John Moore had also got off to a good start, being in the forties, with Malcolm next man in the eighties. Charlie Walker, Eric Gebbett and Dave Baulch were labouring around the hundred mark. At two miles, with Maynard(H.H.H.) leading from Eldon and Knight, Pat was 15th, John 46th and our sixth scoring man in the nineties. At six miles, Eldon had established a substantial lead from Knight and Sando with Maynard 4th. Our lads had shewn considerable improvement in their team placings and were steadily pulling back the opposition with six men now in 87 and eight in 126. In the last mile the whole team made an extra special effort, pulling back over forty places amongst them. Special mention must go to our first and last man; to Pat Newell on his excellent 14th place and Alan Bishop for his most creditable 151st on this very fast course. Belgrave were the first team to finish seven, and also eight, runners but Old Belgravians will no doubt wince to hear that no club qualified for the twelve cup. Ex-members, Geoff Goode and Steve Charlton were seen running for their new clubs. Semi-retired Bagnall would have been our third scoring man with his 56th place!! Over 400 finished. 37 teams closed in. JUNIOR EVENT (6 miles) Apart from the unfortunate absence of Chris Thompson through injury, the Juniors were at full strength and following his excellent running the previous week hopes were pinned on a forward position by Alan Black. These hopes appeared to be well founded when, after a ½ mile, Alan was seen to be in third place, well backed up by Ken Miller and John Thresher in the early twenties and Trevor Hart in the sixties. A little after this, however, he had dropped back to join Ken and John and soon after dropped out altogether with severe stomach cramp; a nasty blow to both Alan and the team. After 2½ miles Howard(Watford) led the field from Lindsell (Portsmouth) and Baker(Walton). Ken Miller was now 29th, John Thresher 50th, Derek Crookes 92nd and Jim Radford 107th; Trevor Hart being forced to drop back a considerable way with trouble from a shoulder ailment. Derek and Jim moved through very strongly on the last lap to reach the sixties and nineties respectively. Boquets go to Ken Miller for his fine return to form after his recent chest trouble and to Trevor Hart for pluckily finishing the course. Despite being without their two best runners the team still managed to finish 7th out of the thirty teams to close in. Approx. 250 finished. 30 teams closed in. An excellent meal was provided by our hosts after the Championships, and the prizes were presented by their General Manager F.W. Amies Esq. Arthur Whitehead produced his most valuable result sheets again for distribution, and as usual they disappeared like gold dust; a fitting end to a day of keenly contested and exciting competition. items.s: COUNTY 10 MILES WALK CHAMPIONSHIPS. FEB.28TH Report of the county 10 miles walk championships: Belgrave's 'A' team won the Surrey title at Kingston led by Eric Hall, while a depleted team (as Cadogan A.C.) was fifth in Middlesex at Regents Park. SURREY - at Kingston Although the 'flu bug was still affecting our walkers, and overnight we had word that Ray Middleton had succumbed, it was with good heart that our two teams faced the starter. Our 'A' team won in devastating fashion with 17 points to Surrey A.C's. 33. The 'B' team, which was expected to be placed, was seriously weakened by re-arrangement to overcome the losses due to sickness and finished fourth. Comments on individuals must be headed by the continued great walking of Eric Hall who finished first. He was ably supported by George Williams 2nd, Ray Hall 6th and Terry Clark(still a junior) 8th. The fine walking of John Knifton in his first 10 mile race was encouraging. MIDDLESEX at Regents Park A very depleted team lined up for the start, and for the first time for many years we were unplaced. Ken Jones, who has the makings of a fine walker (he is an ex-runner) incurred the Judge's displeasure at an early stage and this further weakened our chances. How upsetting these decisions are, yet how important good judging is to the welfare of the sport. Do not be deterred Ken but take the opportunity to profit by your experience.
