items.h: NATIONAL C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS AT PETERBOROUGH. MARCH 7TH.
items.sum: Report of the National cross-country championships at Peterborough, lamenting falling support and Belgrave's record-worst senior score of 980 points, with Belgrave senior, junior and youth positions (Ken Miller is given as 49th in the text but 66 in the positions list).
items.s: NATIONAL C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS AT PETERBOROUGH. MARCH 7TH. Report of the National cross-country championships at Peterborough, lamenting falling support and Belgrave's record-worst senior score of 980 points, with Belgrave senior, junior and youth positions (Ken Miller is given as 49th in the text but 66 in the positions list). The National was, at one time, the event of the year for Belgrave, and both competitors and supporters talked of nothing else for weeks before. In this modern age, however, the race passes almost unnoticed - the runners treat it as a pennance and the supporters are practically non-existant. How can we expect to regain the championship with such an attitude. Our runners must approach this race with the will to win and not with the idea that providing they turn out they have done their duty. The non-active members of the Club, and those athletes not chosen to compete, must turn up in force to encourage, cajole, drive, plead and use every means in their power to ensure our teams meet with success. Nothing helps a runner more than to have adequate support and to know that the Club as a whole is behind him, willing him to give of his best. Special trains and coaches are almost invariably arranged at low costs to transport supporters to the race so there is no excuse for missing events of such importance. There is much satisfaction to be gained from seeing your club mates racing in big championships and opportunity is also provided to see the "stars" in action. When a club is going through a bad patch, such as Belgrave is at present, the need for keen support is greater than ever, so if you want to see the "Bels" back to their past glories show an interest in their training, racing in Club events and particularly in major championships. The least said about this year's race the better. We were never in the hunt and our final score of 980 points is an all time record, never, we hope, to be repeated. Even Pat Newell who was our main hope could not get going and finished in the most disappointing position of 59th. The remainder appeared to have no life whatsoever and were certainly not in the same form as at the Southern a few weeks earlier. Individual positions:- 59, P. Newell; 136, C. Shippen; 158, D. Baulch; 174, E. Gebbett; 205, A. Bedford; 248, C. Walker; 266, L.C. Bishop; 335, E. Short; 347, J. Heathfield. The Juniors fared little better than the Seniors and as the runners passed us soon after the start we wondered whether any of our boys were there. Only Ken Miller, in 49th place, was in the first hundred. Alan Black, our best junior, was well down the field and only started to run over the last mile or two, when he made about seventy places. items.s: SOUTHERN COUNTIES 7 MILE TRACK WALK. MARCH 7TH. Report of the Southern Counties 7 mile track walk and supporting 6 mile races, with "Our Stan" absent through 'flu and a judging decision against George Williams, plus Belgrave placings. The main event was preceded by a Junior 6 miles in which John Knifton walked well to finish 4th. He was ably supported, a little way back, by Brian Gibbs. Another supporting event for 6 miles in the hour badges was then held and it was very pleasing to see Fred Denny finish second. It was a great pity that in the main event the holder, "Our Stan" was unable to take part as he was still laid low with 'flu. I am sure all will agree that his presence adds lustre and interest to any meeting. We still had five representatives in the field of forty and although major honours did not come our way a good reckoning was given. From our point of view this meeting was marred by an unpredictable judging decision given against George Williams when he was laying a comfortable second. George's heart is big enough to overcome this set-back but these unfathomable judgments are disturbing. 13 R.C. Hall 57.55 21 B. Eglinton 61.58 26 J. Morris 64.01 27 J. items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the Ilford road relay, where Belgrave finished second to Woodford Green A.C., who set a course record.
items.s: ILFORD ROAD RELAY. MARCH 14TH Stage-by-stage report of the Ilford road relay, where Belgrave finished second to Woodford Green A.C., who set a course record. This has always been a popular event with our boys and acts as a relief immediately after the cross-country season. Our poor showing in the National the week before gave us little hope of a win but we were soon to be proved wrong. Dave Baulch took the first stage and brought us in a creditable fourth in 18m.3s., twenty-three seconds behind the leaders, Thames Valley. Eric Gebbett ran the second stage in 18.45 and took us up to third with T.V.H. still in first place, forty-three seconds ahead. Ranjit Bhatia did 18.28 on the third stage but was forced to give way to George Knight, who put up a lap record of 17.21, and we were back to fourth again. Polytechnic had gone into first place and forty-six seconds covered the first four teams. John Davies performed well to do 18.40 on the fourth lap and maintained his position although losing some ground to the leaders who were then over a minute ahead. Brian Hallowell was given the fifth stage and in doing 18.38 took us back to third, one minute and twelve seconds behind Poly who were still leading by one minute from Woodford Green Len Bishop kept us in third position with 19.02 but could not close the gap on Poly and Malcolm Robinson went off, 1.26 behind, on the seventh stage. His time of 18.53 was a little disappointing but it kept us in the same position. Woodford had taken over the lead from Poly and we were lagging by over 1½ min. Charlie Walker, on the eighth stage, was also disappointing with 18.49 and dropped us back to fourth after a battle royal over the last half-mile with Alan Perkins(Ilford) and Bert Ingles (T.V.H.). Pat Newell was in good form and, with an excellent time of 18.09, brought us up to second, exactly one minute behind Woodford, and it was left to John Moore, on the last stage, to hold this position with Woodford the winners in a course record time and T.V.H. third. 1st Woodford Green A.C. 3h.4m.42s; 2nd Belgrave 3h.6m.25s. 3rd Thames Valley H. 3h.7m.14s. items.sum: Report of the R.W.A. 10 mile walking championship at Sheffield, where Belgrave won the team title with Stan Vickers second, plus a list of members walking for their counties.
items.s: R.W.A. 10 MILE CHAMPIONSHIP. MARCH 21ST. Report of the R.W.A. 10 mile walking championship at Sheffield, where Belgrave won the team title with Stan Vickers second, plus a list of members walking for their counties. To arrive at ST. Pancras station and find our Hon. Secretary rubbing shoulders with Tommy Trinder made me think that Jack Goswell's musical talents had been rejected and that our Hon. Treasurer had spared no expense to ensure the happiness and comfort of our team. However, it turned out that Fulham F.C's. supporters were travelling on the same train and they obviously felt that Alf had talents which could be of use to them. Altogether seventeen of us travelled to Sheffield where coaches were waiting to take us to the venue. The course was a typical Northern one of the out and back variety with some pretty stiff climbs on the way out. From the start "Claret and Gold" dominated the proceedings with Stan Vickers challenging Matthews, the eventual winner. Stan was not, unfortunately, at his best, having only recently recovered from 'flu and Matthews went right away, to win by over two minutes. Eric Hall gave one of his usually polished performances to finish third, and he was followed by George Williams who walked in excellent style. A ding-dong battle for 4th team position developed between the two Rays(Hall and Middleton), which Ray Hall eventually won by proving the stronger over the last two miles. Terry Clark gave a creditable display in his first Senior R.W.A. championship. It is unfortunate that the times are suspect owing to a misunderstanding at the turning point. The journey home was enlivened by the usual musical interlude from J.W.G., which does so much to soothe and quieten a tired body and mind. items.s: T.V.H. ROAD RELAY AT CRANFORD - MARCH 28TH Stage-by-stage report of the T.V.H. road relay at Cranford, used as Brighton relay preparation, with Belgrave 'A' finishing eighth. We entered five teams for this event which we were supporting for the first time for many years. The main object was to give our runners experience of this type of competition as a preparation for the Brighton relay and also to make last minute selections for this race. A number of those entered could not attend and we eventually started four teams of which three finished. The runners on the first stage were Walker(A), Collis(D), L. Bishop(C), and E. Bishop(E). Collis led our boys home in seventh place with a time of 23.49 against the leaders (St. Albans) 22.52. Walker was 12th with 24.24, Len Bishop 17th in 24.57 and Eric Bishop 26.02. Jim Heathfield took over from Collis on the second stage for the 'D' team with Bhatia running for the 'A', Shippen for the 'C' and Conway for the 'E'. Ranjit, with a time of 24.15, caught and passed Jim to finish 10th., Jim being in 11th place, Clive 13th and Conway 26th. Archie Bedford continued for the 'A' and did 24.30 to retain 10th position. Eddie Short, running for the 'C' remained in 13th place but Dennis Jones dropped the 'D' back to 14th. The 'E' team had shot its bolt and had no runners on this stage. The fourth and last stages were run by M. Robinson(A) who did 24.14 to take us up to 8th, J. Masters(C) who did 24.43 moved up to 12th and David Jones(D) who fell back to 15th. Colin Collis really pulled one out of the bag to be our only runner under 24min. and earned his place in the Brighton team. It was grand to see Colin running so well. The remainder of the times were very mediocre compared with performances by other clubs. items.s: STOCK EXCHANGE 25 MILES WALK - APRIL 4TH Brief report of the Stock Exchange 25 miles walk, in which Ray Hall finished second to R.E. Green of Surrey W.C. It was again my pleasure to act as attendant to Ray Hall and as usual we were blessed with grand weather. The race started promptly at 10.30 a.m. and by the time Westerham was reached it was apparent that the race rested between Ray and Green of Surrey W.C. At the top of the long climb up Botley Hill Green emerged in front, and so the position remained to the finish in spite of a great effort by Ray over the last two miles. Ray's record time of last year was never in danger. Result:- 1st R.E. Green 3h.47m.53s. 2nd R.C. Hall 3h.48m.32s. Ray Hall Ray Hall 2nd Green Green winner R.E. Green R.E. Green 1st 3h.47m.53s. R.C. items.sum: Syd Roberts's account of an R.W.A. Southern Committee dinner at which Stan Vickers received record plaques, the International Trophy and the Fowler Dixon Style award.
items.s: R.W.A. HONOURS STAN VICKERS Syd Roberts's account of an R.W.A. Southern Committee dinner at which Stan Vickers received record plaques, the International Trophy and the Fowler Dixon Style award. On 12th March a dinner was held at the "Feathers" Hotel, St. James's, S.W.1., sponsored by the R.W.A. Southern Committee, the main purpose of which, was to present British Native and British All Comers' Record Plaques to Stan Vickers for his new records which he set up last year. Whilst the function was not too well supported, Belgravians constituted about half the total assembly. Norman Easlea, Vice President of the A.A.A. and a past President of the R.W.A., in presenting the two plaques to Stan, gave a glowing account of his achievements over the past three years culminating in his outstanding performance at Parliament Hill last September. Norman was followed by Timber Woodcock who then presented to Stan the new International Trophy for the most outstanding performance in International Competition during 1958. This trophy, a very handsome one, was won by the British Team in Italy in 1957 and has a Belgrave interest as George Checkley was a member of that team. Permission was subsequently given by the British Board for it to be adopted as an International Trophy. Further tributes were then paid to Stan by Alf McSweeney whose club promoted the race in which Stan set the new records, by Ernest Neville who also presented to Stan the Fowler Dixon Style award which he won in the A.A.A. Championships last year, and Harold Whitlock who spoke of the great assistance given by Stan to other members of the team in the European Championships at Stockholm. Having been well and truly loaded up with trophies Stan was then called upon to reply and he made it quite clear that without the assistance of numerous people he is quite certain that he would never have broken any records. He mentioned, in particular, Ray Hall who endured all sorts of agonies in accompanying Stan during training and Matthews of Sutton Coldfield who battled with him during the actual race. A further presentation to one of the retiring R.W.A. Auditors and the customary toast of the Chairman completed a most enjoyable and interesting evening. items.sum: Gloomy report of Belgrave's 11th place in the National London-Brighton relay, never higher than tenth, won by Derby and County.
items.s: NATIONAL LONDON-BRIGHTON RELAY - APRIL 11TH. Gloomy report of Belgrave's 11th place in the National London-Brighton relay, never higher than tenth, won by Derby and County. The report on this race can usually be made interesting but how can anyone raise enthusiasm over a team which at no time during the whole race was higher than tenth and at one stage was as far back as sixteenth? The tale of woe really began during the week prior to the race when firstly John Davies was forced to withdraw because of foot trouble and then Clive Shippen contracted enteritis and had to stand down. John had been allocated the first leg and this was given to Charlie Walker who could not, this year, impress the selectors sufficiently to gain more than the first reserve designation. A quick switch of Eric Gebbett from the fifth to the fourth leg let in Jim Masters on the Redhill stage which has almost become his own property by divine right. The race started in fine weather but soon after Purley was passed ( we joined the race at this well known place as our Cross-Country Secretary resides there!) it began to rain. Our spirits were at a very low ebb on finding our team back in 13th place, and the weather did nothing to improve them. They were raised subsequently, for brief intervals, at the prospect of a position in the first half of the field! The whole story is most dismal; Charlie Walker struggled into tenth place on the first leg in a poor time, Malcolm Robinson floundered along on the second and lost three places, his time of 26.18 being the fifteenth best of the day, and Colin Collis,who was entrusted with the vital stage from Mitcham to Purley after his brilliant run in the T.V.H. relay, had an almost complete breakdown and finished in a distressed condition in 15th place. At this point we were 3m.42s. behind Coventry Godiva who were then leading. We now hoped that Eric Gebbett would redeem our fate but this was not to be and we remained in the same position but dropped to 4m.24s. behind the leaders, Derby and County, who were never again to be headed. Even Jumbo Masters could do nothing to put the matter right and fell back to 16th with a gap of 5m.55s. between us and Derby. Truly a hopeless position but Alan Black set out to prove that his loss of form over the previous few weeks was purely temporary and with the fifth fastest time of the day brought us back to 14th. Archie Bedford, although on the wrong side of forty, put up a plucky effort across Gatwick Aerodrome and, despite being forced to give way to Shaftesbury, can be said to have run true to form. Pat Newell must have been very dispirited waiting for well over six minutes after the leaders had passed by for his turn to come and this obviously affected his performance, for he could make no impression on those ahead and remained in fourteenth place. Next came Dave Baulch, making his last appearance for Belgrave (so he says), and he set off as though he really meant Belgrave to reach Brighton first. Running with more zest than most of the team put together he whipped past two of the opposition and took us to twelfth. Bhatia, on his first, and we sincerely hope not his last Brighton, took over in cold, wet and dreary conditions far from suitable for his type of running and, with a very good effort, he gained one more place. John Moore could make no more progress and Brian Hallowell on the last stage was over two minutes behind the team in front and could do no more than maintain his position despite a time which was the fourth fastest of the day. Inquests gain nothing but it is evident we must look for new faces before the October race for Southern Clubs. On this showing I would forecast that only Alan Black, Dave Baulch, Renjit Bhatia and Brian Hallowell will retain their places in the team - I wonder how right I shall be. items.sum: Report of the club 20 miles walk championship, led from the start by Eric Hall, with Cyril Yescombe third in a big personal best.
items.s: CLUB 20 MILES WALK CHAMPIONSHIP - APRIL 18TH Report of the club 20 miles walk championship, led from the start by Eric Hall, with Cyril Yescombe third in a big personal best. Perverse Mother Nature was in a cold and boisterous mood when our walkers faced the starter for the 20 miles Championship. Once again we welcomed some visitors from the Met. Police A.C. in the field of eighteen starters. Eric Hall went into the lead immediately, accompanied by Terry Clark who only completed two laps of the course. Halfway times were not outstanding; Eric and Terry Clark were still leading with Ray Hall in 3rd place closely followed by Cyril Yescombe and George Beecham who were about three minutes in front of George Checkley. Johnny Morris was walking a very steady race but one or two of the back men were travelling too fast and suffered from the cold in the later stages of the race. Over the last five miles George Beecham dropped back to fifth place after an unhappy time but Cyril Yescombe held on to third place and, having walked his fastest 10 miles in the first part of the race, completed the course in a very fast time which was over 10 minutes better than he had ever done before. This split the handicap wide open and Cyril treated us to an even bigger and better grin. Johnny Morris's steady walking (20 miles at an almost identical speed each mile) gave him second handicap prize. Eric improved on the previous best time for the race on this course by over twenty seconds and gained third handicap prize. And so to Imber Court with a true Belgravian effort for the 'National 20'. items.sum: Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary, greetings from 1899 Hon. Secretary F.A. Bool, news of Len Fletcher in hospital, thanks to Frank Simmons for winter coaching, and a call to support the Track Championships at Hurlingham.
items.s: FROM THE HON. SECRETARY Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary, greetings from 1899 Hon. Secretary F.A. Bool, news of Len Fletcher in hospital, thanks to Frank Simmons for winter coaching, and a call to support the Track Championships at Hurlingham. It is with considerable pleasure that we advise the appointment of Les Stokell as Junior Hon. Secretary.His address is:- 174, Frant Road, Thornton Heath, Surrey, and all our junior members are asked to record this address on their summer fixture card, and make themselves known to Les at the earliest opportunity. He will, of course, work in close cooperation with other Club officers; and we expect, under Les Stokell's guidance, to see the younger element in the Club progressively go from success to success. Les is probably the ideal man for the job he has undertaken. As a schoolmaster he will know the problems of the younger member, as a qualified Physical Training Instructor he is in a position to advise and assist on many athletic problems. As a former member of our teams and as an International runner (he represented Canada at the Vancouver Empire Games) Les has a lot of knowledge to impart and experience to pass on; as a strong personality with tremendous enthusiasm and competence he can well become one of the greatest assets Belgrave have ever had. We were pleased to have greetings and good wishes recently from Mr. F.A. Bool, a Life Member, who became Hon. Secretary of the Club in 1899, and succeeded A.H.N. Edwards who had occupied this position for the first twelve years of the Club's existence. Mr Bool recalls the early racing, including sprints, on the Embankment. Still resident in Chelsea he follows the Club's activities with the greatest interest. Len Fletcher, one of our great walkers from 1925 onwards, is again in West Middlesex Hospital; but it is now hoped that a new course of treatment will bring almost complete recovery. We sincerely hope so and send Len all good wishes. Congratulations and thanks to Frank Simmons on the success of the winter coaching and training sessions at Chelsea Barracks. No doubt the hard work done there will be reflected in better performances than ever before on the track this coming season. Very special attention is called to our Track Championships on Saturday June 6th at HURLINGHAM PARK TRACK, S.W.6 and it is hoped that every Club member will come along and bring his friends. There is ample accommodation for all. It is hoped also that our athletes will show their appreciation of an excellent track and first class arrangements and give us bumper entries in all events, and keenly fought out Championships. Hurlingham Track is easily reached from Putney Bridge Station (District Line), and many bus routes run nearby. There is ample car parking accommodation at the track. Let's make this a really memorable occasion! Les Stokell Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary; schoolmaster and PT instructor; represented Canada at the Vancouver Empire Games F.A. items.s: SOCIAL NOTES FROM BERT JORDAN Bert Jordan's social notes on the coach trip to the Brighton Relay and details of the 1959 Annual Dinner at Barrington House. We had three coaches for the very popular Brighton Relay, and enjoyed a very good view of the race, being able to cheer our man on each leg of the race. On the return journey we made a stop at The Apple Tree, Crawley, and spent a very pleasant two hours enjoying the Belgrave Choir's rendering of popular camp songs. We arrived at Clapham Junction at 11 p.m., a very enjoyable day having been spent by all, despite the damp atmosphere. items.sum: The cross-country secretary's review of a disappointing 1958/9 winter season for Belgrave, race by race, with a call for modern training and a revival of club spirit.
items.s: CROSS COUNTRY SECRETARY'S NOTES The cross-country secretary's review of a disappointing 1958/9 winter season for Belgrave, race by race, with a call for modern training and a revival of club spirit. These notes will reach you well after the end of the cross-country season but I hope you will forgive me for recapping on the winter activities. To say that the overall results were disappointing is putting it mildly. At the beginning of September I was hopeful that 1958/9 would start a revival for Belgrave and we would recover some of our lost glory but the Surrey Road Relay at Woking found us taking a back seat behind Herne Hill, Walton and South London. The following week we took part in the Polytechnic Relay (8 x 3 miles) and it was encouraging to finish three complete teams. The 'A' team were fifth, the 'B' team were ninth for which they qualified for the medals awarded to the first 'B' team, and the 'C' team twenty-fifth. Good times were recorded by Baulch, Bhatia, Davies and Newell. These two races,followed by our own 5¾ miles road race and 3 miles yacht handicap, preceded the London to Brighton Relay for Southern clubs on October 11th and we had every reason to think we were set for a place - in actual fact we had to struggle hard to secure sixth place to qualify for the National Relay in April. On October 25th we revisited Chelmsford for their annual relay after an absence of some years. A strong team,on paper,took eighth place, 2½ minutes behind Woodford. A cross-country relay at Reigate Priory on November 1st gave us seventh place with minor clubs like Deptford Park, Brighton, Hercules and Rochester ahead of us. On November 22nd we lost our hold on the L.C.C. Championship, taking third place behind Highgate and Queens Park Harriers. Charlie Walker and John Moore did well to take 8th and 10th places respectively. The first major cross-country race, the South of the Thames Junior, was held at Epsom Downs on November 8th and Ken Miller(20th), John Moore(26th), Malcolm Robinson(34th) and Clive Shippen(35th) ran well to give us 3rd team award behind South London and Walton. For the next two months we engaged in inter-club fixtures with reasonable success and also held our 7 miles Championship in which Charlie Walker caught Pat Newell on the wrong foot and, against the form book, chalked up another win in this race. The first Saturday in January is always set aside for the county championships and this year the Surrey race was held at Epsom Downs. Although we packed well together we could do no better than fifth, with South London, Herne Hill, Walton and Surrey A.C. taking the earlier positions. Malcolm Robinson was unfortunately forced to retire when well placed, thus depriving us of a possible place. The 10 miles Championship on January 24th reversed the result of the "seven" and gave Pat Newell an easy win over Walker with John Moore again taking third place. Eight minutes covered the first twelve runners, a very wide spread and not very encouraging for the big championships to follow in February and March. The first of these was the South of the Thames Senior which was held from our own headquarters at short notice owing to extensive flooding at the planned venue at Maidenhead. This is a race which we have won on a number of occasions and most of our leading runners are ineligible. Nevertheless our twelfth position was far from satisfactory over our own familiar terrain. The winning team Portsmouth, finished seven men before our first runner, John Moore, who was 49th, and South London, who were second, placed six men in front of John! On February 14th we travelled to Aylesford for the Southern and were surprised by the much improved running of our team which took fifth place with 345 points after T.V.H.(169), Woodford(208), Portsmouth(283) and S.L.H.(305). It was grand to see the lads making steady progress throughout the race - another five miles would probably have secured us a place! Special mention should be made of Pat Newell who took 14th position in very good company - a great effort. Three weeks later the National was held from the Hotpoint Factory at Peterborough but the hope of a good position, after our improved form in the Southern, did not materialize and we scored a record number of points - 980. Let the individual positions speak for themselves - Newell 59th, Shippen 136th, Baulch 158th, Gebbett 174th, Bedford 205th and Walker 248th. The annual visit to Ilford for the local club's relay followed the National by seven days and produced second place behind Woodford Green who beat the course record with 3h.4m.42s. Our time of 3h.6m.25s. is the second best we have shown over this course. Strangely enough it was five years ago when we caned the record to win in 3h.6m.1s. - is this a reflection on our present strength when times generally are much faster? On March 21st we held our road Championship and Pat Newell added yet another victory to his ever growing list of Club Championships with a record breaking run of 28m.21s. Dave Baulch took second place and Malcolm Robinson was third. We visited Cranford for the T.V.H. road relay on Easter Saturday and started four teams but were without a number of our best performers, and in consequence were not in the running for leading honours. The 'A' team were 8th, the 'C' team 12th and the 'D' team 15th. Colin Collis, in a welcome return to form, produced the fastest time of our boys. The last effort of the winter season is the National Relay over the London to Brighton course. Our team on paper appeared to be our best for some years, but again we were to be greatly disappointed and, after much floundering in the lower half of the field, we could do no better than 11th for the second year in succession, some nine minutes behind the winners, Derby and County A.C. Now we have to qualify in the race for Southern clubs in October in order that the "Claret and Gold" shall be seen on the Brighton road next April. Thus the season came to an end on a despondant note and my hopes of six months earlier had not been realised, A few bright specks in the shape of the Southern and the Ilford relay, in an otherwise dark sky indicate that our prospects may not be as poor as they would appear. In fact I know that our past glories will return, but not before we have all taken complete stock of ourselves. Athletes and Officials alike must change their ideas. Obviously a club having a membership such as ours must again come to the fore, but if this is to be accomplished we must discard obsolete methods of training which produce a general fitness but do not bring the speed and strength required for the modern level of athletics. Circuit training and regular exercises with the weights must become standard to the schedules of everyone, not just the few. This combined with longer and more varied running sessions, a la Herb Elliott, will ensure faster times and increased confidence. It only needs an average improvement of 45 seconds per man for us to again win a Brighton relay and to reduce our National score by over 500 points. This improvement is well within the capabilities of many of our runners and with the advent of our leading juniors such as Alan Black, Ken Miller, Chris Thompson, Alan Peckings and Derek Crookes, to mention just a few, in to senior competition with, I hope, the return of such performers as George Flanagan, Charlie Dabbs and Ron Linstead, I look to the future with considerable anticipation. If small clubs like Derby, Sheffield and Portsmouth and clubs like South London and Thames Valley who are no larger than ourselves can do well then so can we. Therefore I want you all to analyse your training methods to see where you went wrong - set yourself an improved target and don't give up until it is attained. Use Club events throughout the year to achieve your ambition and don't be sidetracked by other subsidiary interests. Remember that in trying to put Belgrave back on the map you yourself may also attain honours and I can assure you that there is nothing more satisfying than winning your county colours as a prelude to representative and International recognition. A revival of that pre-war spirit which took a small group of our members to team and individual honours, in combination with a greater attention to training, will produce the results which, I am sure, are not far away. Why not start now to build up that spirit by getting together with other members and resolving to become Belgravians whose names will be added to that select roll of "never to be forgottens". A sense of friendly rivalry will do much to gain this object - go to it!! Baulch Baulch 158th National Bhatia Bhatia Davies Davies Newell Newell 59th National Charlie Walker Charlie Walker 8th L.C.C. items.s: CROSS-COUNTRY SEASON 1958-9 Tribute to Arthur Whitehead's organisation of eleven cross-country events using Club facilities in 1958-9, with the list of events and duties. It is impossible to estimate the benefits that "back room" workers bring to hundreds of participants in the great winter activity of cross-country running. We are indebted to Arthur Whitehead for his organisation and assistance in the following events which, during the past year, have involved the use of Club facilities. Needless to say no other club approaches the help and co-operation we give to the sport and none can boast of such a competent band of workers as that which Arthur has at his disposal. This is not only a substantial contribution to the sport but a great encouragement to competitors. In addition it is felt that the Club must benefit by the wide publicity obtained through acknowledgements in the programmes of the events concerned and also by the fact that our colours are in evidence at all these meetings. items.sum: Track secretary Dave Shepherd urges members to support all club fixtures and keep in touch with section officials.
items.s: TRACK SECRETARY'S NOTES Track secretary Dave Shepherd urges members to support all club fixtures and keep in touch with section officials. Members should by now have received their fixture cards for the track season and it is hoped that all concerned will note that they are expected to support all Club fixtures - it is, in fact, an obligation. I would like to point out that these fixtures do not arrange themselves, but that a vast amount of work is put in by Section Secretarys, Captains and Vice Captains to make a coherent programme. If you have any queries, get in touch with your section Secretary, Captain or Vice Captain. Don't wait for them to come to you - go to them. Tell them what you are doing in training or what you mean to do. They can only help you if you help yourself. All the best! Dave Shepherd Dave Shepherd Dave Shepherd

items.sum: Report of Belgrave's senior and junior performances in a track match against Mitcham, Deptford Park and Surrey A.C. at Carshalton.
e: Match v. Mitcham, Deptford Park & Surrey A.C.
items.s: MATCH v. MITCHAM, DEPTFORD PARK & SURREY A.C. - CARSHALTON,MAY2ND. Report of Belgrave's senior and junior performances in a track match against Mitcham, Deptford Park and Surrey A.C. at Carshalton. Despite a rather weak representation, those of our men who did turn up performed quite creditably. Seniors Charlie Jones took second place in both sprints, clocking 10.2 and 22.9; in the second string Alan Jackson was third in 23.9. In the 440 Dave Mitchell was second in 53.4 whilst Alan Jackson won the second string event in 53.5. A very good performance came from John Thresher who finished third in the 'half' in 1m.59.7s.In the second string event Dave Taylor was second in 2m.9s. Malcolm Robinson, improving every time out, recorded 4m.26s. to take third place in the mile, his fastest time to date, whilst Alan Black was fourth in the second string event in 4m.37.6s. Don MacLean, now running more like his old self, finished second in the two mile event to Hugh Foord with a time of 9m.33.8s: other places:- K. Miller 11th(10m.3s.), J. Heathfield 14th(10m.29s.) Juniors We had a small but keen contingent with Captain Brian Kolbe scoring fourth in the 'half'(2m.6s.) and second in the 220 in 25.7. Eric Penny was fourth in the mile, whilst new members Mike Smithers and Roy Bagley both finished fifth in the first and second string 440 event with times of 58.5 and 59.5 respectively. items.s: GORDON STEWART TROPHY - DRAYTON GREEN, MAY 9TH Report of the Gordon Stewart Trophy meeting at Drayton Green, where a weakened Belgrave team was third in the senior match and fourth in the junior. As this meeting clashed with the Sward Trophy we were poorly represented. In the Senior events, John McNaughton and Bob Taylor reached the 100 yds. final, which John won in 10 4 with Bob 4th suffering from a pulled muscle. Alan Peckings was our only representative in the mile but found the pace too fast ; the winner was M. Barratt of Ealing in 4m.19s. John Thresher again beat 2 minutes in the 880 yds. taking 3rd place behind Blagrove. In the same event Dave Taylor did 2m.6s. Don MacLean was our fastest man in the 2 miles, finishing 3rd in 9m.56s..Our other runners were K. Miller (10m4s.) David Jones(10m.22s.) and Ted Pallent(10m.50s.) Match result:- Shaftesbury 33, Ealing 28, Belgrave 11, Maidenhead 4 In the junior events Eric Penny recorded his fastest mile to date with 4m.43s. for fourth place. Although running well, Mike Smithers and Derek Wade failed to reach the final of the 100 yds. Brian Kolbe led all the way in the 880 yds. only to be passed in the home straight; his time was 2m.4s. items.sum: The outgoing editors' farewell editorial, thanking contributors and praising the coaching of the club's youngsters.
items.s: EDITORIAL The outgoing editors' farewell editorial, thanking contributors and praising the coaching of the club's youngsters. Dear Fellow Members, In all probability this is the last Belgravian editorial which will flow from this pen, for it is hoped that new editors will take over the magazine after September. We feel that our contribution over the last few years, though small, has helped to ensure the recording of Club activities, successes and failures, and, we trust, in a manner and vein acceptable to most. We have not pleased everyone all of the time and have not been immune from personal attack (once for something we didn't even write!). But the magazine is there for everyone to air his views and the greater the interest of any individual in Club affairs the more eager he becomes to expound his theories and invite criticism. And what better way than through the Belgravian? We are indebted to Clive Shippen for his well prepared reports, to Alf Harley, whose knowledge of Club history is second to none and whose writings are always of such great interest, and to all those members whose contributions have enabled us to produce the magazine during our term as editors. It is our hope that even greater support will be extended to the new editors. In passing we must pay tribute to the great efforts being made by Les Stokell and Tom Carter in recruiting and training the fine band of youngsters who are now so successfully performing in Belgrave colours. Here lies our chance to build future teams of National class and we ask that all members, old and young, see to it that the necessary words of encouragement are given to these lads; we all know what it means to be noticed "by those who matter". items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes: a timekeeping qualification for E.T. Ryan, a visit from Wally Bayliss, Jack Bidgood's M.B.E., an athletics clinic introduced by Don Brown, and tickets for the White City Floodlit Meeting. We congratulate our Vice-President E.T. Ryan on qualifying to be added to the list of First-grade Timekeepers. He is a very worthy addition and we count ourselves fortunate on having his services and of our ever-reliable Dick Savage. How nice to see our former President, and Hon. Secretary for 11 years, Wally Bayliss, at one of our evening meetings recently. Welly was a great figure in our Club life for many years and his wager (hush!) of a pound to a penny on Belgrave when they held a commanding lead in the Brighton Relay, which was lost in the last few yards, has become one of the Club legends. Let's see you again soon, Wally! Congratulations to Vice-President Jack Bidgood on the award of the M.B.E. in the Queen's Birthday Honours List. We know it to be well deserved. We have had the very good fortune to be introduced to a private Athletics Clinic in the Knightsbridge area, equipped with the most modern apparatus and staffed by qualified physiotherapists with a very deep interest in our sport. Already one of our Olympic athletes has had successful curative treatment of an injury and other prominent members have received the benefit of the most modern treatments at nominal cost. We are indebted to our former Champion and member of many years standing, Don Brown, for this valuable introduction; and any members who feel they would benefit from the facilities available should, in the first instance, contact Don at Kensington 3336 for an appointment to be made. Our Club benefits financially each year from the promotion of the Floodlit Meeting (this year on Sept. 30th) at the White City. You will help yourself athletically by witnessing one of the finest meetings of the season - as this promotion always is; and you will be assisting our Club and many others that we meet in sporting rivalry if you go along. Tickets at all prices may be booked through Frank Webb, 50 Longford Avenue, Southall, Middx., but it must be done quickly. E.T. Ryan E.T. items.sum: Report of Belgrave's depleted team finishing 5th of eleven clubs at the Sward Trophy meeting at Chiswick, won jointly by L.A.C. and T.V.H.
items.s: SWARD TROPHY MEETING Report of Belgrave's depleted team finishing 5th of eleven clubs at the Sward Trophy meeting at Chiswick, won jointly by L.A.C. and T.V.H. May 9th brought round "The Sward" once again at Chiswick. On paper our team was, I think, the strongest we have ever been able to enter, but injuries, illness and other matters seriously depleted it. As we have no really adequate reserves we were unable to supply competitors in the 120 yds. hurdles, Pole Vault, Discus or High Jump. Tolson had pulled a muscle, Norman Caves had contracted tonsilitis, Andorka was sitting very important exams and Mal Ash threatened to retire; I was unable to change his mind. However, those who did turn out put up some fine performances and I am sure that, with the help of our absentees, we could have troubled L.A.C. and T.V.H. who tied for the trophy. Percy Porter gave us a good start with 4th place in the hammer (155'9"), Derek McCorquindale, in his first outing for Belgrave, showed his class and won the shot with 49'0¼" and our Captain Dave Ansell took second place in the long jump with 21'4½" and, deputising for Norman Caves, 5th in the triple jump at 42'3½" (a personal best). Charlie Jones had his first outing over the 440 yds. hurdles and was 5th in 58·8s. He is bound to improve a lot on this with more competition and increased confidence. John Sams, who last year won the A.A.A. Junior 200 yds. hurdles, was running for the first time as a senior in the 220 yds. hurdles. I am sure he was disappointed at not reaching the final but National Service and shortage of training took their toll. Next year perhaps a win! We also had Alan Black running only his second steeplechase as a senior. Unfortunately he bruised a heel on the third lap when landing from a hurdle and was forced to change his hurdling leg but with true Belgrave spirit he kept going and finished a very creditable 6th in 9m.53·7s. John Ware was our javelin man and he threw up to his early season form but 158'4" was not good enough for a place in that class of competition. We scored 19 points for 5th place out of eleven clubs. As usual there were some relays and running events for which we had invitations. Our 4 x 110 yds. team failed to materialize and in the 4 x 440 yds. we were fifth. Frank Wright, Pat Fox, Alan Jackson and Brian Morris constituted our team. The medley relay saw us finish in 6th place. We had only three men in the two miles team race and finished well down but Malcolm Robinson ran a personal best of 9m.24s. to finish seventh. C.J. items.sum: History of Belgrave's performances in the News of the World London to Brighton relay (later the National Relay) and the Southern Relay from 1924 to 1959, signed A.A.H.
items.s: BELGRAVE AND BRIGHTON RELAYS - 1924 to 1959 History of Belgrave's performances in the News of the World London to Brighton relay (later the National Relay) and the Southern Relay from 1924 to 1959, signed A.A.H. The first relay race on the Brighton road organised by the "News of the World" took place in 1924. Belgrave did not merit an invitation to compete on this occasion and sixteen clubs, all Southern, took part with Surrey A.C. proving the winners in 4hrs. 50min.0·2s. Each competing club fielded a team of ten men. In the following year, Belgrave were still absentees, but Birchfield Harriers entered for the first time and proved equal to their great reputation by winning from a field of seventeen teams. In 1926 we received an invitation to compete, following a qualifying race, and Hallamshire Harriers from the North were also in the field for the first time. We were never conspicuous at any time; seventh position at Merstham was our best, and at Brighton we were 14th. On the ninth stage (then 5 miles 486 yds. up Dale Hill) Bert Footer returned second fastest time. In 1927 we again qualified, but in the relay itself we suffered grave disappointment for we were never nearer than ninth, and eventually finished 17th. Our one small mead of satisfaction was the running of A.E. Smith whose time on the Mitcham to Purley stage was third fastest. In 1928 we were (not unexpectedly!) called on to qualify in a trial race once again, and this we did in emphatic fashion, winning the trial by over two minutes. In the Brighton Relay itself we managed to improve by 11½ minutes on our time of the previous year and finished 12th in the race. We were never higher than 10th and never lower than 14th throughout; and derived satisfaction from our evident solidarity even if brilliance was lacking. 1929 marked a turning-point and gave us our first set of medals in this race. For the first time we included in our team Arthur Allum and Arthur Penny (both to win International cross-country honours later) and the brothers Jack and Joe Flower. Our seventh position earned us the special award medals. Joe Flower excelled himself in running the second fastest over stage 2, and placed us second at Mitcham. Even more improvement was shewn in 1930, when we finished fourth and earned a set of place medals. Our star runners were Allum, who did fastest time over his stretch and Syd Warboys, running for the first time who was second fastest on the long fifth stage of those days of 6 miles 352 yards. In the following year we actually finished fifth, but many thought our performance had more merit than that of the previous year. We suffered a bitter blow when Arthur Allum, having made four places in 2½ miles and seeming all set to peg back more, sustained an ankle injury and had to concede two of the places gained. Arthur had great difficulty in finishing and had to be carried away once the change-over had been effected. In this race another of our future Internationals, Tom Carter, made his debut. In 1932 the sporting papers advised the public that the Belgrave team had deteriorated and would not be in the first half-dozen - whereat we were secretly very pleased! The strongest field ever was promised; for all the leading clubs in the country were to be represented. Over the first eight stages we were either fourth or fifth - remarkable consistency. On the ninth relay yet another of our Internationals, that great character Bert Footer, showed his teeth and took us into third place, which was well held to the end by our Captain, Bill Webb. The two clubs to finish in front of us were Salford Harriers and Birchfield Harriers. Behind us were Aldershot Command A.C., South London Harriers and Surrey A.C. in that order, with fourteen other clubs following on. Every one of our runners set up a new Club record over his stage. Obviously the conditions must have been favourable, but here were ten magnificent performances. In those days we had on the road a double-decker bus, which served as grandstand and dressing room. The inside was curtained off and we actually dropped our man at his relay point, picked up our finishing runner and then passed through the field to the next change-over point and so on throughout the race. What a hopeless task it would be these days! Needless to say a very happy bus load of Belgravians returned to London on that day in April 1932. In 1933 third position was again ours, and Salford Harriers, from Manchester, and Birchfield Harriers were again in front of us.But once again we were the first Southern club home, and the future hope of the South to win a sporting victory over the Midlands and North. That came in 1934 - and how excited we were! April 14th was the date and the late Bill Rice was entrusted with the first stretch from Westminster and handed over third. Tom Carter held the position and next Harry Shields set about the opposition to some purpose. He quickly took the lead and also the baton carried by the leading team (the first Belgrave man to carry it). He still gripped it firmly and defiantly at Purley even though the Polytechnic Harriers runner got his nose in front in the last yard! Jack Flower (4th stage) had a three seconds lead over the Poly when handing over and 2 min. 2 sec. lead over Birchfield. Arthur Penny ran our fifth leg and finished 61 sec. ahead of the Poly with Birchfield nearly three minutes away; we were well on our way to our first victory! Syd Warboys increased our lead over the next stretch, and then we ran over successive stages two newcomers, Bert Shaw and Alf Taylor. Both ran well but nevertheless at Hickstead, Polytechnic and Birchfield had made some inroads into our lead. Bert Footer, on the Dale Hill stretch that he new so well, ran brilliantly, recording second best time over the stage to hand over nearly two minutes in front of Poly with Birchfield four minutes further back. Our great little International handed over to another of that gallant band, Arthur Allum, who sped on his way over the last stretch of 6 miles 904 yards to return the fastest for the stage, and gave us a winning margin of 2 mins. 6 sec. over Polytechnic Harriers, and 4 mins 9 secs. over Birchfield. Great was our delight! 1935 - we were now English Cross-country champions and holders of the Relay Trophy, the challenged, no longer the challengers. Birchfield Harriers tried all they knew to give us a beating and at the commencement of the last stage were only 17 seconds behind, but we ran out winners by 37 seconds. Newcomers to our team were Jim Ginty (one of our finest runners ever), Dan Patience and Syd Ring. Our hat-trick of wins was accomplished in 1936 and we were the first club to have three wins in a row, even though Birchfield could boast five wins in all. Two new boys in our team were Pat Parker and Ted Stimpson - both destined to become Cross-country Internationals. Our winning margin on this occasion was 13 seconds only from Birchfield - a most exciting race, marred only by the death of C. Young of Queens Park Harriers who was killed on the road. This was the first of the races to start from Mitcham and teams still consisted of ten men. 1937 was our Jubilee Year and naturally we wished to excel, but as so often happens at such times, we were doomed to disappointment. After taking the lead on the second relay (Pat Parker gained eight places) we held it all the way to Brighton and to within half a dozen yards of the tape, when Mitcham A.C. (represented by Dennis Brickwood, now well known as one of our members) managed to gain an inches win in almost the last stride! Birchfield were a mere 12 seconds behind us - what a race! Our team newcomers were Les Cohen and Bill Lucas, then a junior, but destined later to win Olympic and International honours. In 1938 we slipped back to third position, Mitcham A.C. again winning, with Birchfield second. Those were the days of mass unemployment, and many Welsh International runners were finding their way on to the nursing staff of a certain mental hospital in S.W. London, whence they became members of Mitcham A.C. Much high feeling was caused at the time, but one thing is certain, and that is that there were some grand runners and sportsmen among these Welsh runners. In our team for the first time were Len Herbert, due to become an International later, Harry Verney and Charlie Smart. Mitcham's hat-trick of wins was recorded in 1939 when we were second and Birchfield third. All our runners on this occasion had previous relay experience and one of the best performances was by Charlie Smart on the fifth leg. Then came War and it was "good-bye" to Brighton Relays until 1947. In our Diamond Jubilee Year we were again the winners, and in no uncertain manner, for we led on every stage except the eighth when we were second for a short while, but Len Herbert quickly took us to the fore again. Blackheath Harriers were second and Coventry Godiva third. Rather naturally there were new names in our team in Vic Blowfield, George Lucas, Stan Eales, Eric Herbert and Albert Frost. It is interesting to note that of our ten runners, six were past or future Internationals. Our 1948 win owed much to Bill Lucas who started the last lap 31 seconds behind Birchfield and passed the finishing line twenty seconds to the good! Newcomers to the team were Tom Clinton, Ken Stimpson, Martin Williamson and Eddie Short. Twenty-five clubs competed in 1949 and we accomplished our second hat-trick of wins, thus achieving more wins in the nineteen races held than any other club. Birchfield, Tipton and Reading A.C. finished 2nd, 3rd and 4th in that order. On April 1st 1950, old friends of ours for many years past on track and country, Thames Valley Harriers, scored their first win. It was definately not our day although we took the fourth set of medals, for Blackheath and Reading also anticipated us into Brighton. The first of the National Relays was staged in April 1951 over the Mitcham to Brighton course, and we were the winners from Thames Valley H. by nearly three minutes. Our team ran in this order:- C.W. Walker, L.W. Herbert, A. Bedford, W.E. Lucas, J.C. Smart, E. Herbert, J.W. Brown, J. Bromley, E. Short and L. Adams. The Southern Relay held later in the year provided us with another win - our fifth win in the last six races - and the minor places were filled by Blackheath H. and Polytechnic H. In 1952 Birchfield Harriers gained their first Relay win since 1931, beating us by 25 seconds with the Scottish Club, Victoria Park A.A.C. in third place. In this race Pete Newell made his debut, coming in as reserve on the fifth stage. He took us from tenth to fourth position and accomplished fastest time - what a reserve to have up one's sleeve! In the Southern Relay held later in the year we had yet another win by almost a minute from T.V.H.; Essex Beagles were third. Jack Brown, Arthur Bruce, Len Adams and Ray Tooby all broke stage records, with Eddie Short also doing so but finding one better runner on the day in Ken Norris of Thames Valley. The National Relay of 1953 found us slipping back to fourth place behind Thames Valley H., Birchfield H. and South London H. Bill Lucas recorded fastest time over the eighth stage. In the Southern Relay held in October we finished second to Essex Beagles with T.V.H. third. In 1954 the National Relay reverted to the old pre 1936 full length course from Westminster to Brighton (54¾). Our position was a meritorious second to South London Harriers with Essex Beagles third. Teams comprised eleven men and our team did exceedingly well although we were very conscious of the fact that five of our members were over 35 years of age, and of the need for some young replacements. The Southern Relay in October gave Herne Hill their first win with Thames Valley H. and ourselves second and third. We move more into the days of recent history and 1955 found us fourth in the National Relay behind S.L.H., Poly and Sheffield. The Southern Relay gave us a real shock - we were sixth! From 1932 onwards we had always won a set of medals in this event and now we were turned away empty. In 21 consecutive races we had been inside the first four places (on nine occasions, winners) and this is a record any club would be glad to have; but this fall from grace was all the harder! In 1956 we were fifth in the National event, S.L.H. winning for the third time in succession. We were happy to see two of our younger members Charlie Dabbs and George Flanagan performing so well. The Southern race gave us the chance of being in the "placings" once again, and we were third to Thames Valley H. and Herne Hill H. Jack Brown, as so often, ran splendidly for us. The 1957 National race also found us in third place, with S.L.H. winning once again. Ours was a satisfying performance. The Southern relay in October had added distance due to the re-laying of the road round Gatwick Airport, and twelve runners constituted a team. Thames Valley H. had an easy win but we took second place with Woodford Green A.C. third. As we were 18th at the end of the first relay we did well to come through to second at the end of the race. Last year we dropped to 11th in the National race and 6th in the Southern Relay. This year, as recorded elsewhere, we were placed 11th again in the National Relay; and in October we shall be able to try ourselves out once again with the other chosen clubs in the South. Our form in the last two years has borne no comparison with that of earlier days. It is true that many of our younger runners who by now should be establishing reputations in these relays have been prevented by injuries from turning out as regularly as we would have wished, but time is still on their side. In addition we have some excellent junior runners maturing and there can be little doubt that those golden days we enjoyed for so long can soon come back. But they will not return without plenty of purposeful hard work added to great enthusiasm and solid mutual team support in training, as well as in racing. These, we may be certain, will be forthcoming, and may we see their results soon! A.A.H. items.s: FINCHLEY H. 20 MILES ROAD RACE - APRIL 18TH Report of the Finchley 20 miles road race, with Belgrave winning the team race and the Belgrave finishers' positions and times. This very popular event again attracted a large entry and there were actually 163 starters. Some tremendously fast running ensued and the winner (O'Gorman of St. Albans) covered the course in 1h.43m.26s.- 3m.25s. faster than the previous record. With such a fast winning time many meritorious performances "down the field" are apt to be overlooked, but Colin Collis deserves special mention for his 11th place in 1h.50m.50s as does Bob Plummer for his best ever time of 1h.52m.54s. In the team race we scored the same number of points as T.V.H. but our fourth scoring man finished ahead of two of their scoring members and so clinched first place. items.s: MATCH v. HERCULES A.C. 13TH MAY. Report of the evening match against Hercules A.C., which began with the club 7 miles walk championship for the Frank Elson Cup, with the walk result. The evening commenced with the Club 7 miles walk Championship for the Frank Elson Cup. Notable absentees were Stan Vickers, the holder, and Eric Hall, last year's runner up. However, form had altered very little for Ray Hall, Hugh McGreechan and George Beecham, 3rd, 4th and 5th last year, filled the first three places this time in the same order! Although the turnout of Seniors and Juniors for the match with Hercules was quite good, they were outnumbered by the boys and youths present. Les Stokell and Tom Carter have a most enthusiastic bunch of youngsters under their wings; it gladdened one's heart to see so much promising young talent in Belgrave vests. A most exciting Senior 100 yds. was won by the versatile Charlie Jones in the good time of 10·2; Ron Holtum and S. Deane each clocked 10·3. The half-mile was notable for the last lap performance of John Thresher. With just over 500 yds. to go John was boxed in by a group of runners 12 yds. behind the leaders. Entering the back straight for the second time he made his effort to catch the leaders. Rubbery legs in the last 40 yds. prevented his doing so and Malcolm Robinson passed him on the line . However, he was undoubtedly the fastest over the second lap and its good to see him consistantly breaking 2 minutes these days. In the mile Derek Crookes gave a most welcome show of form by finishing third in a time of 4m.25·1s. Don Maclean also running well again did 4m.21s. and Alan Black 4m.25·7s. The standard in the long-jump was also high. Dave Ansell, runner up in the Sward Trophy a few days earlier could only manage 4th place this time with a similar distance! Jim McGrath, our new member from Northern Ireland who seems to be another Mal Ash, jumped a most creditable 21'0" to finish 5th. The junior sprints illustrated our sad lack of young sprinters but this was offset to some extent by the promising debut of Linley in the 440 yds. His time of 52·6s. should be cut considerably under the guidance of Frank Simmons, as he has the stamp of a class runner. Our junior Captain, Brian Kolbe performed creditably in both the 220 and 440 and is improving each time out. Eric Penny ran a very well judged race to win the mile in 4m.45·7s., an encouraging early season time. Result of 7 miles walk. 1, R.C. Hall 55.47; 2, R. Middleton 56.10; 3, G.S. items.sum: Report of the rushed evening match against H.H.H. and Q.P.H., with senior, junior and youths match scores.
items.s: MATCH v. H.H.H. & Q.P.H. MAY 20TH. Report of the rushed evening match against H.H.H. and Q.P.H., with senior, junior and youths match scores. Owing to a late start, and an already overcrowded programme for an evening meeting, the events had to be rushed through in double quick time; giving the appearance of some hybrid relay meeting. However this did not stop the athletes from putting up some good performances. Sylvan Deane won both the sprints in 10·5 and 22·8 and a now free from injury Gerry Leroy made a welcome comeback to win both second string sprints in 10·4 and 23·5 . Brian Morris and John Davies showed their class by cantering home in the 440 and 880 respectively and virtually clinched the match for us. An excellent start to the season was made by Norman Caves in the triple jump with 45'4", only 13" less than his highly ranked best of last year. Jim McGrath showed his versatility by adding the discus to his list of events, and continued his battle of the "half-inch" with Dave Ansell in the long jump. Jim and Dave seem to be inseparable in their long-jumping performances. In the junior match Brian Kolbe (2m.4·5s.) was our only winner although Eric Penny was narrowly beaten in the mile. The junior section must be hungrily awaiting the arrival of some of our promising youths. Les Stokell's lads did their duty in the youths match by beating Herne Hill. A few personalities will no doubt soon arise from their ranks and their progress watched with growing interest. Keep at it boys! items.label: No. 139
items.h: VANCOUVER TROPHY MEETING AT WOODFORD MAY 23RD
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's under-strength team at the Vancouver Trophy meeting staged by Woodford Green A.C. in a fierce wind.
items.s: VANCOUVER TROPHY MEETING AT WOODFORD MAY 23RD Report of Belgrave's under-strength team at the Vancouver Trophy meeting staged by Woodford Green A.C. in a fierce wind. This meeting was inaugurated in 1955 by Woodford Green A.C. to commemorate the performances of Elliott and Johnson in the previous year's Empire Games at Vancouver. The home club were virtually at full strength, but many athletes from some of the other clubs were conspicuous by their absence. Our own John Davies, Brian Morris, Clive Ryan, Frank Wright and D. McCorquindale were competing elsewhere, and with Stan Vickers Eric Hall, Norman Caves, Mal Ash and Andorka also unavailable our team could not be said to be truly representative of the name of Belgrave. Nevertheless, the lads who did carry our colours performed with considerable credit and had no small portion of bad luck. Conditions would have been ideal but for a fierce wind which affected almost every performance. Ron Holtum just failed to qualify for the final of the 100 m. recording 11·8 in his battle against both wind and competitors. In the 200m. we were out of luck again when S.Deane, who clocked 22·7s. was also unable to qualify. However, Dave Carter joined the finalists with a workmanlike performance a provided us with a very valuable point. In the 400m. C.Lindsay of Q.P.H. showed considerable speed and strength in negotiating the antics of the wind to record a phenomenal 47·7! How Brian Morris would have liked to have been there! Our own Alan Jackson (51·9) was also unable to reach the final but ran a sound race. When he has the courage to make his first 220 a little faster his times will undoubtedly improve. Dave Mitchell and John Thresher, both of whom are new arrivals to the senior ranks, each narrowly missed qualifying for the 800m final. They both ran very spirited races and in a couple of seasons time should prove to be outstanding performers. In the 1500m. Malcolm Robinson, our only entrant, found himself up against opponents such as Earl, Linford, Chapman and Ellis, but with his usual show of determination and ever-improving ability he secured a point with a time of 4m.2·4s., another best performance. In many events we were unable to field two competitors, which meant a possible wastage of points before we started. The 5000m. appeared to be another such event when a call was put out for the runners to assemble. Simultaneously, a certain Irishman, red-faced and panting, burst upon the scene having, seemingly, run a four minute mile from Woodford Station. Having had his clothes virtually dragged from him John Moore was ushered over to the starting line where he just had time to take a deep breath before travelling a further 5000 metres. John must be congratulated on his running although his performance, of course, was not one of his best. Don Maclean ran well in the first half of the race but when it became obvious that he wouldn't score he eased down to save himself for the steeplechase, in which he had volunteered to run. In the high hurdles Jim McGrath showed his prowess by qualifying for the final. Charlie did likewise in the 400m. hurdles and was a creditable fourth in 57·9s. Both Percy Porter and John Ware did well in finishing 3rd and 2nd in the hammer and javelin respectively. Jim McGrath led in the long jump until the final round where two competitors"pulled one out of the bag". Only 2¾" separated the first four! Both Jim and Dave Ansell, who was fourth, recorded 20'3", the wind accounting for a good two feet. Dave went on to a fourth place in the triple jump while Jim completed a "Mal Ash" type performance by finishing third in the pole vault, narrowly failing at 12'0", an excellent days work. Stan and Eric were sadly missed in the 3000m. walk, although Ted Smith and John Knifton gleaned a valuable three points between them. Prior to the 3000m steeplechase Clive Shippen paid the penalty of insufficient warming-up by pulling a thigh muscle when negotiating a hurdle. Thus Don Maclean faced yet another race as our sole competitor as this time there was no late arrival to join him. In doing 10.21 Don left behind several fresher opponents. As far as the match result was concerned Woodford Green were in an unassailable position quite early on. Of Belgrave's 32 points, 23 were obtained on the field and 9 on the track, from which you may form your own conclusions. C.S. Held on a very hot day at Imber Court this race was notable for the way in which Tom Missen and Don Thompson, both of Metropolitan Walking Club, absolutely slaughtered the opposition. It was also notable for the performance of George Williams who came in at the last minute to replace Eric Hall, who had leg trouble. To finish fifth in such a class field at his first attempt over the distance deserves great praise. Credit must also be accorded to Terry Clark, only just out of the junior stage, for his very fine effort in finishing ninth. Although we lost the team race we did retain the Nijmegen Cup for the first club to finish eight men, indeed this is the fifth time in succession that we have won it. Teams:- 1st Met. items.sum: Report of the Surrey Championships at Motspur Park, at which Belgrave were represented in every event and swept the two miles walk, signed C.S.
items.s: SURREY CHAMPIONSHIPS - 29/30TH MAY. Report of the Surrey Championships at Motspur Park, at which Belgrave were represented in every event and swept the two miles walk, signed C.S. Without doubt Motspur Park has an atmosphere all of its own. A fast track in a pleasant, well-sheltered setting, together with a large appreciative crowd of spectators reclining on the grassy banks and the usually fine weather, make this meeting a rather special occasion for competitor and onlooker alike. A large proportion of the crowd consists of semi-retired athletes, still dabbling, who have not yet managed to resist the lure of an athletic meeting. At one time they would have returned home determined to make a "come back", but now, alas, the County Junior and Youth performances are sufficient cause to not only turn this group to full retirement but to swell their ranks by the addition of many more disillusioned Seniors. At Whitsun, Surrey's athletes allowed the Inter-County Trophy to slip across the river to their Middlesex rivals. But on thisday they made it quite clear that it had gone for no more than a year's holiday. Performances were improving all round but most noticeably amongst the younger competitors. Mitcham A.C. and Hercules A.C. were the most prominent but Belgrave were unique in being represented in every event - that is if one is allowed to count the announcer! Yes, Bill Lucas was on duty once more. Bill's announcing is second to none and he must be congratulated on the way he carried this marathon task. Highlights of the meeting were, a 1m.49·6s. "half" from Brian Hewson, a 48·7s. 440 by junior John Strachan of Hercules and a 13m.49·6s. conquest by his clubmate Ernie Earl over the redoubtable Mike Maynard in the three miles. For many this meeting started and finished on Friday evening, and no less dramatically than in the Senior mile heats. County standard is 4m.24s., yet Giddings of Deptford Park failed to qualify for the final with a time of 4m.13·7s.! and our own Malcolm Robinson likewise with a personal best of 4m.19s. In the two miles walk Belgrave swept to victory by filling the first three places; George Williams winning from Ray Middleton with John Knifton a good third in his first year of senior competition. On Saturday Clive Ryan and Charlie Jones comfortably qualified for the 440 final despite being drawn against each other in their heat and having to fill first two places. Clive recorded 49·9 and Charlie 51·0. In the final Clive was drawn on the outside lane, while the holder, Woodland of Hercules, was blessed with the inside. However, Woodland had to put up a Best Championship Performance of 48·4 in beating Clive's 49·4. Charlie was fifth in 51·3. Eric Penny ran well on Friday evening to qualify for the Junior mile final but found the opposition too strong next day. The first four broke the Best Championship Performance and the first seven were inside 4m.23s.! Harvey of Mitcham (4.16·8) led from start to finish to win from Harper of S.L.H. (4.19·1) Eric Shirley made his first appearance at the Championships and won the senior mile from A.S.Rogers of Mitcham in 4m.11s. - sixth man here clocked 4.14·4! Sylvan Deane (10·4) was narrowly beaten in his 100 yds. heat, being passed in the last ten yards in a blanket finish. The leading white-vested runner in the second heat of the 880 went by unrecognised as Belgravians cheered on Malcolm Robinson in the main bunch. When the first lap time of 54·8 was announced eyebrows were raised and on closer inspection it was seen to be Frank Wright. A barrage of voices carried Frank down the back straight and although caught in the final straight he qualified through second place in 1m.57·2s. - a good solo run. In the third heat John Thresher ran a personal best of 1.58·5. Belgrave's only representative in the three miles was Don Maclean who recorded 14m.57·8s., and as the crowd left was seen to be reclining against a post in the centre of the arena in a rather deflated state - a fitting end to the day. items.sum: The new editors introduce themselves, explain this 28-page issue, and pick out Ray Hall, Peter Eldridge, Gerry LeRoy and Charlie Dabbs as performers to watch in Olympic year.
items.s: EDITORIAL The new editors introduce themselves, explain this 28-page issue, and pick out Ray Hall, Peter Eldridge, Gerry LeRoy and Charlie Dabbs as performers to watch in Olympic year. Dear Fellow Members, This issue marks the arrival of a new Belgrave year, a new President, and as you can see from the head of this page - new Editors. We thank the Bishop brothers for helping to establish our journal as a regular, healthy and expressive organ of Club activity, and we will endeavour to maintain the high standards they have set. We hope to introduce new ideas in future issues and are quite prepared to face adverse criticism. A big post-bag indicates a lively readership, so let us have your ideas too. The Autumn issue of the Belgravian always has plenty of news to cover. This,together with a back-log of results to last June, has enabled us to produce the biggest issue for many years - 28 pages. We should hastily point out however, that for ecconomic reasons it is not possible to continue publishing more than 20 pages, so the accent will be on quality rather than quantity. Although the summer season was not one of our most succesful there emerged several performers who could well gain higher honours next year. In the forefront of these is Ray Hall who has been outstandingly consistent in his walking, and whose quest for Olympic honours will be followed with great interest. Peter Eldridge and Gerry LeRoy, in their first fully active season for some time, showed that very little lies between them and representative honours of high note, and Charlie Dabbs, who at long last triumphed over persistent injury and established himself as one of the country's leading distance runners by his magnificent performance in the R.R.C. 25km event. Success leads to success and as a result many other stars are likely to be swept along in the wake of these athletes. We are firmly of the opinion that Belgrave is now equipped with the right sort of material to commence a succession of highly successful seasons- and what better year to start than Olympic year, 1960! Ray Hall Ray Hall walker; consistent season, Olympic hopes Peter Eldridge Peter Eldridge Gerry LeRoy Gerry LeRoy Charlie Dabbs Charlie Dabbs magnificent performance in the R.R.C. 25km event R.R.C. 25km Olympic Games

items.label: No. 140
items.sum: Profile of the newly elected President T.C. "Charlie" Jones, a member since 1926, covering his hurdling, field events, walking and administrative work.
items.s: THE PRESIDENT - 1959/60 Profile of the newly elected President T.C. "Charlie" Jones, a member since 1926, covering his hurdling, field events, walking and administrative work. Our newly-elected President, T.C."Charlie" Jones, has certainly grown-up with the Club for he became a member as far back as October,1926, and has been very much in evidence ever since in all our activities. His early interest in our sport was derived from his father who became a member on the Club's formation in 1887, and could tell many an interesting story of the early days; and of the matches Bels v Bats (the long-since defunct Battersea A.C.) on the roads over the Chelsea Bridge—Battersea Bridge circuit. Charlie was also a cricketer of some skill, and as junior and youth athletic events were infrequently held at the time, he spent most week-ends in perfecting his fast bowling. Despite his activities on the cricket pitch he was at all other times to be found at Battersea Park Track- the focal point of all our Summer interest in those days. The hurdles always fascinated Charlie and his first club award was for the event. Later he was to win the Surrey County 440 yards Hurdles Championships, and later still to gain Surrey County place medals in the Hop Step & Jump and Javelin Championships. He competed in our Junior Cross-country teams, and in later years established himself as one of our best runners at 440 and 880 yards. His long-striding action was a delight to watch, and only inability to translate that terrific stride into a sprint over the last thirty yards or so prevented him from carrying off many Championships. His interest has always been extended over the full range of field events, and he became a Club Champion at the triple jump and was responsible for many excellent performances in this event and the long-jump. To add to this story of athletic versatility must be added the fact that Charlie was always (and still is) a most accomplished stroller both at home and abroad; and had he decided to try himself out as a race-walker it is certain he would have achieved further successes. Charlie had the good fortune, shared with many others, to be part of that tremendous enthusiasm which permeated the Club in the late 1920's and 1930's, when our star was in the ascendant, when each month saw more battle honours won, more athletic history made. Even the slowest man in the Club felt he was pushing the man in front of him, who was forcing the man ahead of him to give of his best, and so up to Club team level when the reserves compelled the selected team men to run every inch of the way. Charlie epitomised this intense Club spirit and was at every Championship urging and working for our successes. On the administrative side Charlie has done yeoman work and served in a variety of offices and been in on higher councils for the greater part of his Club life. His legal knowledge has been of the greatest help to us, his especial work for Field Events and Coaching within the Club still continues; and his work in the administrative field has been almost as versatile as his active career in our colours. We may be sure that Charlie Jones will serve us well as President. Let us resolve to serve him and the Club equally as well. A.A.Harley. T.C. "Charlie" Jones T.C."Charlie" Jones newly elected President 1959/60; member since October 1926; won Surrey County 440 yards Hurdles Championship Charlie Jones Charlie Jones President A.A.
